#239. It’s Getting Too Dry for Even Cactuses to Survive

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (963 w)

It’s Getting Too Dry for Even Cactuses to Survive

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (963 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The humble cactus is an icon of resiliency.
  • Recent findings suggest that yet cacti are in serious trouble, due to habitat loss and the poaching of species for private collections.
  • “The public perception of cacti tends to be of these organisms that are extremely drought-adapted and are just resilient, can handle anything that you throw at them,” said Michiel Pillet, a conservation ecologist at the University of South Florida and lead author of the paper.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The humble cactus is an icon of resiliency. Stuck in a desert with little rain and abundant searing sun, these plants don’t just survive, they thrive—and in turn provide habitat for owls and other birds, and flowers for bats and other pollinators.

Recent findings suggest that yet cacti are in serious trouble, due to habitat loss and the poaching of species for private collections. Now we can add worsening droughts to those woes, according to a upcoming study in the journal Nature. Researchers modeled a future of not just relentlessly rising temperatures but also the attendant dry spells, finding that the majority of nearly 1,000 cactus species will lose habitat as the climate radically changes. More than a quarter of those species could lose at least 80 percent of that habitat by 2100.

“The public perception of cacti tends to be of these organisms that are extremely drought-adapted and are just resilient, can handle anything that you throw at them,” said Michiel Pillet, a conservation ecologist at the University of South Florida and lead author of the paper. “In reality, cacti are absolutely amazing—and they’re my favorite plant group, clearly—but they’re not that different from other plants.”.

It has been revealed that that means cacti need water. In the deserts of the southwestern United States, for example, they rely on seasonal monsoon rains, which tend to make July or August the wettest month in a given year. Because this is still a desert, cacti have evolved a range of adaptations to survive, like a waxy skin that helps them retain that bounty of rainwater. “Just like other plants, they evolved under conditions that they’re used to,” Pillet stated. “When you take them outside of those conditions, they might not be able to handle that.”.

Think of these cacti like sick hospital patients. Someone might be admitted for heat-related illness, as their body struggles to cool itself. At the same time, though, they might be dehydrated. Cacti are dealing with the same stresses, as global temperatures rise and dry spells intensify. “When we consider drought conditions, then it turns out that they’re much, much sicker than we previously thought,” Pillet stated. “These results really do change the outlook of cacti, and most likely plants more broadly under climate change.”.

In a recent development, instead of simply modeling these threats going forward, the researchers turned to the citizen science platform iNaturalist, where people upload photos of plants and animals. This provided 650,000 observations of cacti in the wild, helping paint a clearer picture of how species might be faring.

Really, this isn’t a simple matter of cacti withering and dying. Sure, if relentless droughts take hold, individuals can’t get water. But the stress could be temporally complex, too. “Now we can move towards questions of: What life stages are most affected?” Pillet remarked. “Is it the adults or is it the seedlings? But also, which processes? Is it reduced growth or is it increased mortality? Or are plants failing to flower?”.

Put another way: Cactus species could be suffering from sublethal effects of drought—the lack of water may not kill them immediately but still interfere with their reproduction. And without procreation, populations shrink. In the Sonoran Desert, for example, the iconic, towering saguaro is reproducing less frequently during prolonged droughts, because they’re not always flowering.

Part of the problem is that while desert ecosystems may look tough and hardened overall, they’re in fact quite fragile. “They don’t recover quickly once they are disturbed, or once they are degraded, just because there’s so little water and such higher temperatures,” stated Marcos Robles, the Nature Conservancy’s lead scientist in Arizona, who wasn’t involved in the research. “It takes multiple decades to recover, and in some cases, they don’t recover.”.

Now drought is compounding with other stressors, like habitat loss and poaching, to drive cactus species to the brink. On the opposite end of the spectrum, too much water from rising seas has led to the local extinction of the Key Largo tree cactus in Florida. Higher nighttime temperatures are a problem, too, since that’s when saguaro and other cacti respire to avoid water loss. “If the nighttime temperatures are very high, they can’t do it,” said Rod Haenni, president of the nonprofit Cactus and Succulent Society of America, who wasn’t involved in the paper. “Then if you water on top of that, the plants just rot.”.

Sources indicate that still, some cactus species may persist by picking up and leaving. Well, not individual plants, but populations could creep into areas with climates that more closely match what the species adapted to all those millennia ago. A similar thing is happening in the Arctic, actually, where some plants are marching farther north in “search” of increasingly agreeable weather and more water.

In a recent development, in the end, the purpose of this sort of research is to better inform where conservation professionals might concentrate their efforts. They can’t stop droughts, of course, but they can evacuate enough cacti to establish populations in botanical gardens, where they can be cared for as the climate grows more unrecognizable to even the hardiest desert vegetation. Species can even be reintroduced to the wild in some cases, so long as drought and high temperatures don’t remain a threat to a population.

Governments, too, need to protect the lands where cacti are threatened, Haenni said. This new research, he added, could make that happen. “Hopefully, it’ll wake people up,” Haenni said. “But the problem is that a lot of the governments involved are indifferent to this. There are a lot of people in the countries who are not indifferent, but they’re not running the governments.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, I’ve spent the past few weeks thinking about how Apple built up the best deal in enterprise AI.
  • The Xserve has been dead since 2011, but its spiritual successor sits on a desk rather than in a rack.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple @ Work is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Mosyle is the only solution that integrates in a single professional grade platform all the solutions necessary to seamlessly and automatically deploy, manage, and protect Apple devices at work. Over 45,000 organizations trust Mosyle to make millions of Apple devices work ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

In a recent development, I’ve spent the past few weeks thinking about how Apple built up the best deal in enterprise AI. Two things happened that make me think Apple knew that all along (or maybe they didn’t and got lucky). Meta released its most capable open-weight model yet and optimized it to run on a Mac Studio. I also spent time with Osaurus, an app that runs a usable local AI model on something as small as a 16 GB Apple silicon laptop without needing a network connection. They even have two models that will run on 8 GB.

The Xserve has been dead since 2011, but its spiritual successor sits on a desk rather than in a rack.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train people, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

Sources indicate that for the last few years, the narrative has been that Apple fell behind in AI because it didn’t have a frontier model. Siri AI got delayed, and the Apple Intelligence rollout was not great. In hindsight, I think Apple was right not to run that race, as the frontier-model business has turned into somewhat of a capital bonfire. Every frontier lab is spending billions on GPUs to be the best for a few months at a time, and the moment a model is good enough, someone else releases an open-weight version that runs on hardware you already own.

It has been revealed that open-weight models prove it: Muse Spark Open has 816 billion parameters, 42 billion active parameters, and a million-token context window, and Meta is giving it away. Apple didn’t build that LLM. It built the hardware that runs it. With that being mentioned, Siri is still far behind.

Sources indicate that look at what Apple has shipped while everyone was waiting on them to try to compete with Anthropic or OpenAI. With Apple silicon’s unified memory, the GPU can use up to 512 GB of memory on a single Mac Studio, instead of being limited to whatever fits on a graphics card.

Industry observers note that MLX is Apple’s machine learning framework, and it’s built specifically for the unified memory architecture of Apple silicon. If you’ve used NumPy, the API will feel familiar right away. On top of that, MLX includes higher-level packages for neural networks and optimizers, along with function transformations for automatic differentiation and graph optimization, so you can build more complex models without giving up efficiency. It also has bindings in Swift, C++, and C, which means it runs on any Apple platform.

Apple’s own Machine Learning Research post shows four M5 Ultra Mac Studios running Muse Spark Open at over 36 tokens per second, which is faster than you can read, while peaking around 300 watts per machine.

It has been revealed that apple’s unified memory architecture lets the M5 Ultra’s integrated GPU use up to 512 GB per Mac Studio, so two machines can hold an entire model. And the chip’s 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth is fast enough to read the small slice each token needs. The result is two Mac Studios behave like one supercomputer with a terabyte of unified memory.

We tested a range of agentic workflows running entirely on-device, using Muse Code powered by Muse Spark Open, including shipping real iOS changes to Ice Cubes (an open-source Mastodon client) — bug fixes, new features, full build — and driving DaVinci Resolve end to end, with the model reviewing footage frame by frame to find the strongest moments and crop them vertically.

Sources indicate that that’s the Xserve pitch, rebuilt for 2026. Apple killed the Xserve in 2011 because nobody wanted a Mac in a data center. The Mac mini came along and provided some new use cases over the years. Now, a couple of Mac Studios can host a model that would otherwise require a rack of Nvidia hardware and a power budget to match, and it does so quietly enough to sit under a desk. Apple wasn’t trying to compete with OpenAI, Anthropic, or Nvidia. It was building the infrastructure for everything except the frontier model, and it looks like that’s where the market is going. A firm like MacStadium has to be loving this future as well.

It has been revealed that the Mac Studio story is the headline, but what matters most to most IT teams is at the other end of the lineup. I had Terence Pae, co-founder and CEO of Osaurus, on the Apple @ Work podcast last week. Osaurus is a free, open-source AI tool for the Mac. It helps manage local models that work offline, but it can also call a frontier model when needed. A really cool feature, when it does this, is that Osaurus runs a small local model first to find names, phone numbers, and account numbers in whatever you pasted, and swaps them for placeholders before anything goes to Claude or OpenAI.

Osaurus has no servers and no customer database. If the manufacturer went out of business tomorrow, the app would keep running until macOS broke it. Individuals use it for free. Workspaces, the paid tier, is for teams who want to share agents across their own Macs. There’s a Windows beta as well, which I think helps Apple’s case more than it hurts it. When the same app runs on both platforms, the Mac’s unified memory is the difference.

In talking with him, Terence mentioned he wouldn’t be surprised if a local model matches what today’s frontier models can do by this time next year. I believe him, and that’s the point. The frontier will keep moving, but good enough keeps moving too, and good enough is what most employees need most of the day. Apple spent the AI race building memory, bandwidth, and a framework instead of trying to match the frontier, and the narrative was that they were behind.

Now the most capable open-weight model in the US is optimized for the Mac.

Pixel Watch update brings a sweet redesign I wish was on more apps

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google has been at its gradient redesign schtick for a while now to varying levels of success, but its latest redesign has just landed on the Pixel Watch for the Media Controls app, and I love it.
  • Quietly rolled out, the Media Controls app on Pixel Watch has picked up a redesign to its app icon, adopting the same gradient look we’ve seen across several other Pixel Watch apps.
  • The difference here is that Google’s styling expands beyond a simple coat of paint.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google has been at its gradient redesign schtick for a while now to varying levels of success, but its latest redesign has just landed on the Pixel Watch for the Media Controls app, and I love it.

Quietly rolled out, the Media Controls app on Pixel Watch has picked up a redesign to its app icon, adopting the same gradient look we’ve seen across several other Pixel Watch apps.

The difference here is that Google’s styling expands beyond a simple coat of paint. The new look extends to the edge of the icon with play/pause in the center and a ring indicating playback around the border, just like the actual app itself – the app, to be clear, hasn’t been redesigned.

Sources indicate that I’ve personally been a bit mixed on these redesigns, but this one really nails it in my book. I wish Google would do this sort of thing more often. The white borders are nice in some cases, but I very much miss the whimsy of the icons that took up the full size available to them – that mid-2010’s icon was the absolute peak in my opinion.

Pixel Watch has been quietly rolling out more of these icon redesigns in recent months, with the other most recent additions including Alarm, Stopwatch, and Timer from around August/September.

Industry News: GitHub availability report: October 2026

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2050 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.
  • Recent findings suggest that the short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate.
  • It has been revealed that as of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.

Recent findings suggest that the short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate. However, write outages, monitoring gaps during data migrations, and a regional network disruption reinforced the need for capacity growth to be paired with safer operations, stronger isolation, and validated regional recovery.

It has been revealed that as of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US. Azure served 63% of migrated-service reads, 66% of monolith reads, and 52% of Git reads. We also completed a compute expansion across all nine Central US Kubernetes clusters, more than doubling capacity.

That capacity is already carrying real growth. Migrated-service traffic has increased 82% since March, with Central US absorbing the growth beyond the highest weekly-average load previously served from our existing datacenter. This gives GitHub more room to grow without pushing the original environment beyond its prior operating range.

Recent findings suggest that we also made several targeted reliability improvements. Actions changes increased capacity for critical Azure control-plane requests. A separate NAT-gateway mitigation reduced usage by 85%; four production jobs failed during the change, compared with approximately 800 expected without the mitigation. Connection limits and other client improvements now also reduce the chance that a dependency interruption becomes a broader reconnect storm.

We removed concentrated sources of database load as well. A high-traffic GitHub Actions endpoint handling more than 250 million requests per day moved to a more efficient service path, reducing peak database reads by 85%. Requiring at least three characters before searching repository topics reduced slow or terminated queries for that pattern by approximately 98%.

In a recent development, reliability was still not where it needed to be. The October 7 write outages exposed an unsafe interaction between database orchestration and production routing. An October 29 Azure network disruption affected all three Central US availability zones and at least 34,128 signed-in people. More details on these and other incidents follow.

The East US 3 buildout is about one week behind blueprint. The next phase starts with its first validated traffic ramp in the first week of December, while we continue hardening migration safety, dependency isolation, and regional recovery.

The principle remains the same: availability, then capacity, then features.

Duration: approximately 3 hours and 45 minutes.

According to recent reports, customers may have seen GitHub Actions jobs on GitHub-hosted runners stay queued much longer than usual, and some workflow runs failed to start. During the worst stretch, which lasted about 90 minutes, most jobs on GitHub-hosted runners did not start within five minutes. Impact eased as we failed over to healthy regions and added capacity. Self-hosted runners were not affected. GitHub Pages sites that build with actions were slow to update, though existing sites continued to serve normally. Some customers also saw errors in repository lists, licensing and billing pages, and some Copilot features.

Actions jobs stayed queued or failed to start because the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners stopped working reliably. A partial networking failure on our cloud provider’s side disrupted some of the connections between one of our datacenter regions and the cloud-hosted databases that service depends on. Instead of failing fast, the service waited for those calls to time out. The waiting calls piled up until the service ran out of memory and restarted.

Jobs then shifted to the same service in a healthy region, which did not have enough capacity for the extra demand and began failing too. At the same time, runners that went several minutes without receiving a job shut down and were slow to be replaced, so fewer runners were available to pick up jobs.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 6 minutes of failed or slow requests across github.com, followed by approximately 3 hours and 30 minutes during which enterprise migrations were paused.

Recent findings suggest that customers may have seen server errors or slow responses when signing in, working with repositories and pull requests, calling the API, or using GitHub Codespaces. Retrying a short time later would have succeeded, and delayed webhook deliveries caught up soon after. At the peak, about 1.3% of all requests failed or timed out, and about 6.4K organizations saw at least one failed or slow request.

Migrations were paused for customers using GitHub Enterprise Importer, and were resumed once a fix was deployed.

According to recent reports, A surge in migration activity caused GitHub Enterprise Importer to send a burst of very large queries to a shared database. These queries took much longer than usual and, together with normal traffic, used all of the database’s available connections, preventing other github.com features relying on the same database from completing their requests.

The importer did not reduce its load when the database became overloaded. The impact ended within minutes, once the importer finished its queued queries and the database’s connections were released.

To prevent a recurrence, we paused migrations until we deployed a mitigation that runs these queries in smaller batches.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Sources indicate that duration: two separate write outages lasted approximately 10 minutes and 9 minutes, totaling about 19 minutes. The second was a recurrence of the first, with the same cause.

Customers may have seen errors when pushing code, signing in, updating pull requests or concerns, or making changes through the API. Webhooks, GitHub Apps and OAuth, actions, code scanning, codespaces, and Copilot were also affected. Viewing content was largely unaffected. Data that was already saved was not lost, and actions that failed during the outages succeeded when retried after recovery.

Web and API request failures peaked at 8.9% in the first outage and 9.3% in the second, affecting more than 12,000 and more than 11,000 organizations, respectively. Some organizations may have been affected by both outages.

During regular maintenance, we replaced machines that manage where database writes are sent. One new machine started with outdated records that still listed retired database servers. Once it was automatically elected leader, it published routing settings that sent writes for several core databases to those retired servers. Incorrect settings passed our existing validation and took effect immediately. Later, an automated maintenance task did not honor a pause on maintenance and triggered another election, and because the new machine had not yet been removed, it became leader again.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 28 minutes.

According to recent reports, customers may have seen delays in GitHub Actions workflow status updates, logs, and checks. About 5% of jobs on GitHub-hosted runners experienced delayed starts, a very small share of workflow runs failed, and some requests to the actions jobs REST API returned errors. GitHub Pages deployments and workflow and check webhook events generated by actions runs were also delayed. For part of this time, live updates on github.com and code search were degraded.

Sources indicate that an internal actions service that stores workflow logs and run status lost connections to some of its cache servers in one cloud region. Every server running that service then retried those connections at the same time. Together, those retries saturated the network connections between GitHub’s data center and that region, disrupting other services that use the same link.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Sources indicate that customers may have seen delays in pull request updates, GitHub Actions workflow status updates, and webhook deliveries. After a push, new commits were slow to appear on pull requests. Workflows triggered by the push started late. Status checks from actions workflows could look stuck on pull requests, which held up merges that require those checks to pass. These features recovered within about 2 to 3.5 hours.

Audit log events were affected the longest. Recent activity took longer to appear when customers searched their audit logs, with delays of up to 1 hour and 50 minutes. Audit log events were fully caught up after about 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Some webhook deliveries from this period may be missing from webhook delivery history, though the webhooks themselves were delivered.

Some servers in our event streaming platform were close to their memory limits, and memory use on these servers grows with the number of client connections. When requests to these servers failed, upcoming connections were opened immediately, which increased the number of connections and the memory they used. The increase in memory use slowed down and overloaded the servers.

It has been revealed that we took the overloaded servers out of service, and their traffic moved to other servers. Those servers then became overloaded too, and the problem spread to more servers over the following hour. We began rebalancing overloaded partitions onto brokers that had available capacity and this mitigated the issue.

Audit logs took the longest to recover. The service that writes audit log events kept restarting on errors from the platform for more than two hours and fell further behind. Once stabilized, it could only write events at a limited rate, so the backlog took several more hours to clear.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 32 minutes.

Customers may have seen errors when using several GPT-family models in Copilot. Requests using these models in Copilot Chat in IDEs and on github.com, the Copilot CLI, Copilot code review, and the Copilot coding agent returned errors or did not complete. About one in 10 requests to the affected models failed. Other models continued to work, and choosing another model avoided the errors. Auto model selection reduced the errors by sending some requests to an unaffected model.

Code scanning autofix and code quality, which are built on one specific model without an alternative model to switch to, were affected more heavily.

It has been revealed that copilot reaches these models through an upstream model provider and uses a credential to authenticate with that provider. That credential became invalid, the provider began rejecting our requests as unauthenticated, and our service returned those rejections to clients as authentication errors. Copilot features that use these models send their requests through that provider, so they began failing at the same time.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 9 minutes.

Sources indicate that customers may have seen some requests to github.com hang for up to about 10 seconds and then fail with a server error. Pull request merges and Git operations over SSH and Git LFS were hit hardest. At the worst point, about 43% of merge attempts failed, compared with about 3.5% of API calls. Complications, GitHub Pages, notifications, and sign-in for GitHub Apps and OAuth apps also saw intermittent errors.

A database connection pool used by many github.com services reached its limit, and for several minutes no connections were available. New requests that needed a connection waited until the connection timeout expired and then failed.

Recent findings suggest that the pool was already running near capacity when some update requests started holding their connections far longer than expected. Each one began writing a change, then ran a separate lookup that could take several seconds, keeping its connection reserved but unused the whole time. With little headroom, those held connections helped tip the pool over.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Recent findings suggest that follow our status page for real-time updates on status changes and post-incident recaps. To learn more about what we’re working on, check out the engineering section on the GitHub Blog.

Today, we laid out our vision for GitHub as the most comprehensive, end-to-end software delivery system in the world.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Products such as Microsoft Teams and Outlook have been out of service for much of Friday.
  • Microsoft has said its services have been fully restored after a worldwide outage affected several of its tools, causing disruption.
  • The tech firm stated early on Saturday morning that efforts to address the underlying problem had been completed and customers using Outlook, Teams and Copilot should no longer be affected.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Products such as Microsoft Teams and Outlook have been out of service for much of Friday.

Microsoft has said its services have been fully restored after a worldwide outage affected several of its tools, causing disruption.

The tech firm stated early on Saturday morning that efforts to address the underlying problem had been completed and customers using Outlook, Teams and Copilot should no longer be affected.

Recent findings suggest that the outage hit more than 70 countries, disrupting everything from business operations to government services and personal users. More than 430 million people use the affected products worldwide.

Microsoft apologised for the technical issue, which it remarked was introduced during a "network capacity upgrade" and was not caused by a cyber-attack or an artificial intelligence agent.

Experts noted the event was a "stark reminder" of how heavily businesses and vital services rely on a small group of significant tech providers.

Owners began reporting they were having trouble accessing Microsoft 365 products on Thursday.

By Friday, the far-reaching matter was affecting institutions from the Japanese government and the Philippines Supreme Court to the Australian spy agency, and trains, hospitals and courts in North America.

Services were beginning to recover by Friday afternoon UK time, nearly 24 hours after the challenges first began to emerge.

Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost?

Courts, spies and MPs: How the Microsoft outage has been felt around the world.

In the UK, some parts of the NHS were affected, as were some schools and police forces.

UK cyber minister Liz Lloyd mentioned the incident had "limited" impact on critical frontline services such as 999 calls and that there had been no disruption to the transport network.

In Canada, however, the national rail network said passengers may not be able to receive email updates about their trips, and hospitals across the country also had challenges with emails.

In the US, staff members from the House of Representatives told Politico it had set back an entire day of legislative work as everything was on Microsoft's Outlook.

Singapore's government acknowledged some of its systems had been impacted, and in India, the outage disrupted work for many on Friday.

In Turkey, advisers and officials attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya were left frustrated by being unable to access Outlook.

The problems also affected smaller businesses and individuals.

Pete notes his business has been brought to a standstill.

Peter Pentz, a winemaker in South Africa, said his entire business had been effectively brought to a "standstill".

His winery's communication with exports was also brought to a standstill, he said, and "critical production work" had been halted as the Cape West Coast winery "relies on these systems for parts of our day-to-day operations".

Georgia from Staffordshire in England said she had been due to complete her first house purchase after waiting eight months to get to this point - but the outage has delayed that.

"The solicitor mentioned there may be a delay due to not being able to contact other agencies," she noted.

"We're not the only one completing today - there are hundreds of houses and for them to ring everyone in time is unfeasible.".

Microsoft first acknowledged users in the Americas were unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes at 17:54 GMT on Thursday, and shortly after warned the disruption was possibly affecting Microsoft 365 globally.

It launched an investigation and engineers began working to restore services, but by 04:36 on Friday Microsoft was reporting only a "partial recovery" in some parts of the world.

By 13:32, the tech giant said there had been "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" across much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in the Asia Pacific region.

Microsoft noted it restored services gradually due to the scale of the problem and to help ensure services remained stable once they were up and running again.

"We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," a Microsoft spokesperson noted.

"We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously.".

A full post-incident report will be released once Microsoft has completed a review.

Experts remarked that while workers may have been happy to not have email access for a working day, the incident demonstrated the dependence many organisations have on these cloud-based services.

"The global Microsoft outage is a stark reminder of how heavily we rely on a handful of big tech providers," stated Rob Demain, chief executive of cybersecurity firm e2e-assure.

Matt Saunders, field chief technology officer at tech consultancy Adaptavist, remarked it would be challenging to mitigate against a similar problem.

"Classic IT disaster planning strategies suggest using a second service for resilience, but in practice, it's almost impossible for a business to function without tools such as Microsoft," he said.

"In the wake of this outage, organisations must have a plan in place for how to work without such tools, for when incidents like this occur.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Second Circuit has refused to shield Kalshi and Coinbase from New York and Connecticut while their appeals proceed.
  • A federal appeals panel has left Kalshi and Coinbase without interim protection in two Northeastern states.
  • Sources indicate that the ruling came a few hours after the panel heard lawyers for Kalshi, Coinbase, the CFTC, Newly introduced York and Connecticut.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Second Circuit has refused to shield Kalshi and Coinbase from New York and Connecticut while their appeals proceed. The ruling lets both states press state-court cases against the companies' sports event contracts and deepens a circuit split headed for the Supreme Court.

A federal appeals panel has left Kalshi and Coinbase without interim protection in two Northeastern states. The Second Circuit found that the companies had not made the showing needed for an injunction pending appeal. The order did not say which part of that showing they failed to meet.

Sources indicate that the ruling came a few hours after the panel heard lawyers for Kalshi, Coinbase, the CFTC, Newly introduced York and Connecticut. The court took up Kalshi’s two appeals together with Coinbase’s appeal of Judge Oliver’s August decision. That decision allowed Connecticut to keep pursuing its claim that Coinbase’s sports event contracts are illegal gambling.

The order lets both states keep enforcing their gambling laws. They are pursuing state-court suits to force the sports event contracts offline. Gaming attorney Daniel Wallach called the ruling a major win for both states. He said one remand order now separates them from returning the cases to state court and seeking preliminary injunctions there.

Sources indicate that kalshi had already lost at the district level. Federal courts refused it a preliminary injunction in New York in July and in Connecticut in August. On July 31, 2026, New York sued KalshiEX, accusing it of running an illegal gambling operation through its prediction market. Attorney General Letitia James had sued Coinbase and Gemini in April 2026 on similar illegal gambling claims.

It has been revealed that the stakes in Latest York are high. InGame reported that the state case seeks billions of dollars in damages, and that the CFTC has told Kalshi to disobey the state-court order if it ever takes effect.

Connecticut moved earlier. In December 2025, the Gaming Division of its Department of Consumer Protection ordered Kalshi and two other sites to stop offering unlicensed online sports wagering. On August 26, 2026, Attorney General William Tong, Consumer Protection Commissioner Bryan T. Cafferelli and Gov. Ned Lamont unveiled a lawsuit to stop Kalshi offering unlicensed sports wagers in the state. Gov. Kathy Hochul, James, Tong and Lamont each won re-election on the day the order was issued.

It has been revealed that the decision joins a lengthening list of circuit court rulings siding with states against prediction markets in 2026. It cuts against Kalshi’s argument that its contracts are “swaps” that only the CFTC can regulate. That argument prevailed at the Third Circuit, which ruled that Newly introduced Jersey cannot regulate sports bets on prediction markets.

Nine federal judicial rulings within the Second Circuit have now gone against Kalshi, Coinbase and/or the CFTC in efforts to block state gambling enforcement through emergency or preliminary relief.

That includes today’s Second Circuit ruling denying Kalshi’s….

— Daniel Wallach (@WALLACHLEGAL) November 4, 2026.

Industry observers note that the federal regulator has also gone to court against states. On April 2, 2026, the CFTC sued Arizona, Connecticut and Illinois over their actions against CFTC-registered designated contract markets. On April 24, 2026, it sued Upcoming York in the Southern District of New York. It asked that court to declare that federal law gives it exclusive authority over event contracts. It also asked for a permanent bar on the state enforcing preempted laws.

Industry observers note that the outcome matters for state sportsbook markets and for the reach of CFTC jurisdiction. With the circuits now split, attention turns to Washington. New Jersey’s petition seeks review of the Third Circuit’s April 6, 2026 decision in case 25-1922. Kalshi is preparing to file its response to that petition.

I checked Gemini’s newly introduced Memory summary to see what it knew about me – how to see and edit yours

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (650 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Like any AI, Google Gemini wants to remember things about you.
  • Also: I tried Claude Sheets on 3 tasks – and it saved me hours of work.
  • With a fresh option called Memory summary, you’re able to view the details that Gemini has gathered about you over time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Like any AI, Google Gemini wants to remember things about you. The purported reason is to help tailor and personalize your conversations. But remember that your personal details may also wind up training the AI or even being reviewed by actual humans. With that in mind, you might want to find out just what Gemini knows about you. And now you can.

Also: I tried Claude Sheets on 3 tasks – and it saved me hours of work.

With a fresh option called Memory summary, you’re able to view the details that Gemini has gathered about you over time. These may be tidbits from your conversations or things that you directly told the AI. Even better, you can add or remove any details just by editing the memory or issuing your request directly to Gemini.

This new capability is available in Gemini across the board, so you can access it at the Gemini website, in the mobile iOS and Android apps, and in the Windows and Mac desktop apps.

Launch Gemini via the web or in one of the mobile or desktop apps. In the left pane displaying your previous chats, select the Settings icon at the bottom. At the Settings screen, select Personal Intelligence and then click or tap Memory summary. If the option is grayed out, it means the Memory feature is turned off. To proceed, turn it back on. You can always turn if off again afterward if you wish.

According to recent reports, you’ll then see the individual details by category. My summary arranged the information across such categories as Essentials, Business & Career, Reading & Interests, and Culinary Preferences. Go down the list to see the individual items in each category. To view a recent history, tap the three dot-icon at the top and select Memory history. This shows you the latest changes and updates to Gemini’s memory.

Also: Stop sharing your passwords with AI agents.

It has been revealed that what if Gemini’s memory includes details that are too personal or just incorrect? No problem. You can alter the AI’s memories of you. At the website or in one of the desktop apps, click the pencil icon at the top. Now you’re able to directly edit the text to add, remove, or revise specific details. After you’ve made your changes, just click Save.

Sources indicate that for example, my summary said that I lived in Madison County. I have no idea where Gemini got that notion, as I live in New York. Here, I revised the text and saved the changes, which then synced across the Gemini website and apps.

The mobile apps have no direct editing capability. But there’s another method that works both on mobile and on the desktop. Just tell Gemini what change you want to make. At the prompt, type and speak your request, and the AI will carry it out for you.

Also: The best and worst AI for your privacy, ranked.

As an example, my summary stated that I run a business called Batter Up selling collectible baseball cards. That’s not at all true. I had once referred to such a store only to test Gemini’s image creation skills to design a logo for a baseball card seller. Here, I simply told Gemini that I don’t run a business called Batter Up and asked it to remove that item from its memory. Poof, that detail promptly disappeared.

Google isn’t exactly known as being privacy-friendly, and that extends to Gemini. In this case, though, I give the manufacturer credit for offering this easy way to control the AI’s memories. I do find the memory feature useful as it recalls details about me that help personalize and direct its responses. But I don’t like Gemini or Google knowing too much about me. Now I can keep memory enabled and just control what it remembers about me.

Tech Report: Helping teens navigate online news and information

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the Future Report reveals UK teens use of algorithms, video, and AI for discovery and learning.
  • In a recent development, online spaces are where children and young people discover upcoming ideas, keep up with current events, and learn about the world around them.
  • For many (83%), information comes through algorithm-driven recommendations — which children see as positive for introducing them to new ideas they may not see otherwise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the Future Report reveals UK teens use of algorithms, video, and AI for discovery and learning. Navigating trustworthy information is vital and requires a shared effort by platforms, educators, and parents to boost digital literacy, empowering youth to engage in democracy safely.

In a recent development, online spaces are where children and young people discover upcoming ideas, keep up with current events, and learn about the world around them. This is highlighted in Google’s The Future Report, which gathered the views of 6,000 UK teenagers to better understand the opportunities and challenges that technology presents for young people.

For many (83%), information comes through algorithm-driven recommendations — which children see as positive for introducing them to new ideas they may not see otherwise. Young people are also increasingly accessing video-based content and prefer this for building understanding, particularly of difficult topics. They are also engaging with AI, using tools like AI chatbots for creativity and learning on a daily basis.

According to recent reports, while the report highlights the positive ways in which the internet is used for discovery and learning, it also points to the challenges young people face in accessing high-quality, trustworthy information. Teens recognised that the proliferation of AI-generated and manipulated content was making the online information environment increasingly complex to navigate. This is echoed in Internet Matters’ own research, which found that the growth of this content is leaving children feeling less trusting of the news they encounter in their feeds and more concerned about their ability to distinguish between what is true and false online.

Industry observers note that addressing these challenges will be essential if we are to preserve the educational benefits of online spaces. Children and young people must have access to high-quality, accurate content, alongside the skills to critically engage in an increasingly complex information environment. This is especially important in the UK, which is set to lower the voting age to 16, with the aim of increasing lifelong democratic participation. However, this will only be possible if young people feel equipped to engage confidently with the news, politics and current affairs they encounter online.

According to recent reports, encouragingly, Google’s research found that many teenagers are already using strategies to verify online information, including cross-checking sources (49%), checking the credibility of websites and authors (48%) and speaking to parents and trusted adults about the content they have seen online (45%). However, the responsibility for navigating a changing and complex information environment should not rest with young people alone.

It has been revealed that platforms, educators, and policymakers all have a role to play in helping children and young people access trustworthy information and develop digital and media literacy. Schools must be supported with clear direction set by government, alongside the resources and training needed to teach these skills effectively in the classroom. Tech companies also have an notable role to play by making their platforms and services safe and media-literate by design. This means supporting children to have age-appropriate experiences and embedding features that help young people evaluate, question and contextualise what they see.

Parents will also continue to be children’s main source of information about online safety, and who they turn to when they need support. Yet they are also navigating many of the same challenges as their children. As a result, we must ensure that they too feel confident and able to support children — whether this is through building their own media literacy skills, improving access to easy-to-use parental controls or providing advice on where to access high-quality content.

Through this shared approach, we can build a safer and more empowering digital environment where every young person can confidently participate and thrive.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This week, Apple started shipping the HomeView, its first display made for the smart home.
  • Recent findings suggest that on iOS, iPadOS, and macOS today – the only flexibility you have on dark mode is whether or not it automatically switches on towards night time.
  • With HomeView, you can enable ambient dark mode.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This week, Apple started shipping the HomeView, its first display made for the smart home. On the HomeView, there’s one particularly nice feature that I’d love to see make its way to all Apple platforms: Ambient Dark Mode.

Recent findings suggest that on iOS, iPadOS, and macOS today – the only flexibility you have on dark mode is whether or not it automatically switches on towards night time. While this is generally helpful and certainly appreciated, it isn’t super granular. Of course, you can adjust the time when it switches, but generally speaking its just a one time toggle.

With HomeView, you can enable ambient dark mode. In display settings, once you enable automatic dark mode, there’s the usual two settings you’d see on other Apple platforms: sunrise to sunset, as well as a custom schedule. HomeView takes it a step further with ambient mode, where the ambient light sensor determines whether or not you should be in light or dark mode.

Sources indicate that of course, a sunrise to sunset schedule generally works for most cases. However, if you’re up late at night with your lights turned on, you still might prefer light mode in an instance where macOS would generally be in dark mode. Similarly, if you wake up later in the day with your curtains shut, at say 11am, you might not want to immediately see light mode on your phone the second you open your eyes.

There are tons of good reasons for why someone would prefer ambient light-based automatic light and dark mode switching. HomeView software is the first Apple platform to enable this, and I’d love to see it come to iPhone, iPad, and Mac starting next year with OS 28.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Italian regulators have fined social media giant Meta â¬805m (Â£670m; $887m) for accessing Android users' photos without their specific consent.

Italy's Data Protection Authority noted Meta did not properly inform about 20 million smartphone people that it had access to their photos and videos via a feature of the Facebook app.

It has given Meta, which also runs WhatsApp and Instagram, 60 days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent separately.

The fine is among the largest an Italian authority has ever imposed on a tech tech giant.

A Meta spokesperson told the BBC that it planned to appeal.

The charge is related to a feature that suggests photos and videos from a user's phone gallery as ideas for posts.

Industry observers note that facebook requested access to owners' photo galleries through a single app-wide authorisation. A preceding notice did not make clear that this would also allow Facebook to generate suggestions based on photos in their gallery, according to the Italian regulator.

The regulator stated it had taken into account "the high number of people affected" and the fact that the feature was "still ongoing for those who have not updated the app and for those who have already given their consent to the system".

It also cited "Meta's lack of co-operation" in its decision.

Meta told the BBC: "We strongly disagree with the [regulator's] assessment of the facts, its application of the law and the disproportionate level of the fine.

Recent findings suggest that "This is a straightforward feature which helps people post photos and videos to Facebook. People must give permission on their device before it can operate and they can change this permission at any time via their settings.".

Last month, Meta was hit with its largest fine ever for its business practices.

A judge in the US state of New Mexico ordered the tech giant to pay $25bn (Â£18.6bn) after it found that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Streaming giants are always finding new ways to upgrade the user experience and adapt to evolving usage patterns, and Peacock is the latest platform to take its mobile app in a new direction with its biggest overhaul yet.

NBCUniversal revealed a latest era of the Peacock mobile app this week (November 11), showcasing a roster of fresh upgrades it hopes will not only enhance the experience, but increase user engagement and get viewers to spend more time browsing its seemingly endless library of titles.

The streamer claims it's already started testing the upcoming tools and will continue into 2027.

"Our ambition is for Peacock to be more than a place to watch," said Jim Denney, Chief Product Officer, Global Streaming & NBCUniversal Media Group.

"With this new mobile experience, we’re evolving Peacock into an entertainment platform that gives fans more ways to discover, participate, and strengthen their connection to their favorite stories, teams, and franchises, turning viewing into deeper engagement and lasting fandom and loyalty".

One of Peacock's most notable mobile upgrades is the addition of vertical video — which the platform claims is integral to creating an experience that's separate from the one you get on a TV. Netflix jumped on this a while back, so it was only a matter of time before Peacock followed suit.

The new Clips Feed exists as its own section, designed to give you a new means of discovering new titles across entertainment and sports that isn't just simply scrolling the homepage.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

Sources indicate that peacock is also launching its new Franchise Hubs as a way to browse more content but with a community or fandom focus. This section of the app packs interactive games, live moments, and relevant episodes and podcasts centered on specific franchises, from Minions, Love Island USA, The Traitors, and more.

It has been revealed that as well as short-form video, Peacock is jumping on the AI bandwagon, introducing conversational AI search to give you another way to find newly introduced content. With this new function, you can browse titles by name or, if you can't decide what to watch but know what mood or theme you're looking for, it can pull up content based on that information, which you can refine as the conversation progresses.

Audience behavior evolves; there's no doubt, so in order for streaming platforms to adapt to these shifts, they have to make some changes.

In the case of Spotify, for example, its Messages feature lifted a pain point with users by allowing them to share music and podcasts with their friends directly in the Spotify app, rather than having to screenshot everything and send it to group chats on other platforms. Those kinds of features are genuinely helpful, but even then, Spotify has also plagued its in-app hubs with short-form video, and I want to see the back end of it.

When Netflix first unveiled its vertical video feeds, I wasn't surprised per se, but I certainly grimaced at the very thought of it. And now that more services are taking advantage of it, it's suddenly becoming the new norm.

Sources indicate that but what gets under my skin most is how these vertical feeds are pitched to viewers. The streaming behemoths claim they're useful discovery tools, but at the crux of it, it's just another way to increase your screen time and how long you spend in apps. Doom-scrolling has taken over the social media landscape as it is; I don't need it to get in the way of how I browse movies and demonstrates.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, rep. Charlie Geren filed a constitutional amendment on the first filing day of Texas's 2027 session that would let voters decide on casinos and sports betting. A Democratic House and a supportive lieutenant governor-elect improve its odds, but a two-thirds Senate vote and a fight over the Senate's leadership stand in the way.

Industry observers note that texas lawmakers have their first gambling-expansion measures of the 2027 session. Rep. Charlie Geren, a Fort Worth Republican, filed House Joint Resolution 52 on November 9, the first day of bill filing, and Democratic Sen. Carol Alvarado filed a Senate resolution on casinos and sports betting, SJR 11, the same day. Voters would get the final say on a constitutional change giving lawmakers the power to permit and oversee casinos and sports betting.

Recent findings suggest that the resolution would require lawmakers to limit casinos to a capped number of facilities statewide. Initial license terms would run at least 40 years. The Legislature would decide where sports betting could take place. The ballot wording would describe licensing, application fees and a tax on casino and sports wagering revenue at a limited number of locations.

Sources indicate that geren framed a statewide vote as the end of the debate either way. A rejection at the ballot box would close the question permanently, he stated.

Recent findings suggest that the political ground has moved since Geren’s last attempt. Democrats won control of the Texas House in the November 3 election. Republicans held on to the Senate. As a state representative, Goodwin backed the 2023 gambling measure. The office she won was held by Dan Patrick, who blocked gambling expansion for years.

The constitutional route keeps the bar high. An amendment needs two-thirds of both chambers, then a majority of voters. Approved amendments go on the November ballot after the session ends. In 2023, online sports betting passed the House with 101 votes. Geren’s casino resolution reached only 92. The casino measure fell short of the threshold that the betting measure cleared.

The Senate is the harder test. Republicans control the chamber, and any amendment needs two-thirds support there. On November 9, Patrick urged Republican senators on conservative radio to strip Goodwin of her powers as Senate president before she takes office. Her influence over the chamber, including any gambling bill, now hangs on that fight.

Goodwin has signaled a conciliatory approach. Her transition team noted she wants to work with Republican senators and believes Texas is “best served by a deliberative, collaborative body.”.

Industry observers note that texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, arguably the casino and sports betting industry's biggest boogeyman in the Lone Star State, will leave office next year. What comes next in a crucial 2027 for the largest remaining state without major casino gaminghttps://t.co/u6WLlaAj3S.

— Ryan Butler (@butlerbetstrade) November 4, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that industry money has struggled to change the Republican map. In the March primaries, anti-gambling incumbents beat challengers backed by the Las Vegas Sands-funded Texas Sands PAC and Texas Defense PAC, to which Miriam Adelson had given $9 million. Even so, Texas Sands PAC has pledged to keep investing in and organizing for Texas candidates who favor bringing casino gambling to the state.

Recent findings suggest that that leaves Geren’s measure dependent on a Senate whose leadership is still contested. A simple majority could strip Goodwin’s powers once the chamber reconvenes in January.

#223. This AI Tamagotchi Turns Everyday Objects Into Needy Virtual Pets

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (952 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

This AI Tamagotchi Turns Everyday Objects Into Needy Virtual Pets

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (952 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that you forgot to water the plant.
  • Sources indicate that that's the idea behind OATs, or Object Agent Twins—micro-agent AI avatars on tiny E Ink displays designed to pair with everyday household objects.
  • You might remember Tamagotchi, the popular egg-shaped toys from the ’90s that housed digital pets requiring real-time care and attention.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that you forgot to water the plant. Instead of seeing yellowing leaves, you see a cute plant-shaped pet on a tiny screen, looking sad and dejected. Maybe that'll give you the push you needed to grab the watering can. As you pour water into the soil, the plant pet on the screen gets excited and happy.

Sources indicate that that's the idea behind OATs, or Object Agent Twins—micro-agent AI avatars on tiny E Ink displays designed to pair with everyday household objects. The tech was created by Daehwa Kim, a fifth-year PhD student in Carnegie Mellon's Future Interfaces Group. Kim presented the project at the ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology in Detroit in early November, a forum where academics and industry experts explore human-computer interfaces, and she earned two Honorable Mention awards.

You might remember Tamagotchi, the popular egg-shaped toys from the ’90s that housed digital pets requiring real-time care and attention. Kim’s goal was to bring a similar experience to physical objects in our lives. “We bring this joy of caring from virtual to physical objects,” she tells WIRED. While folks have encouraged Kim to sell OAT kits online, she hasn't decided whether to pursue it as a business opportunity.

According to recent reports, kim claims everyone spends all day staring at mobile devices, and AI agents—even if they're designed to handle tasks on your behalf—still demand attention from your smartphone screen. OATs were a way to bring those interactions out into the real world.

Giving AI a physical body isn't latest, as companies rush to create “the next smartphone,” whether that's failed attempts like the Humane Ai Pin, OpenAI's upcoming hardware created in collaboration with famed ex-Apple designer Jony Ive, or Meta's Muse Charm. The pocket-sized gadget houses Meta's popular Muse AI agent and is expected to launch in December. Increasingly, though, companies have leaned on “cuteness” in their strategy for widespread adoption.

In a recent development, OATs have an E Ink display connected to internal and external sensors that can track things like moisture, temperature, humidity, light, occupancy, and motion. (The hardware is relatively cheap, around $20 for the main module.) The sprites are created with Google Gemini's Nano Banana image-generation service, creating a suite of emotions for various states based on the sensor data. You can set all of this up through a web portal, where you can name your OAT and choose which sensors to use for the object you're attaching it to.

In a recent development, the web app will generate “Positive” and “Negative” behaviors based on your object's name and description. So if the OAT is attached to a plant, positive triggers could be “consistent air temperature readings” and “low humidity levels” if the plant of choice prefers dry environments. However, you can customize these behaviors to suit your specific plant type.

It can be used for very simple things. Want to use your skateboard more often? Attach the OAT to your board, and if it hasn't detected motion for a few days, the avatar will look sad and lonely. You don't want that, do you? As Kim says, “These kinds of inanimate objects can be more expressive.” When you hop on the board, the OAT avatar will be happy, with fun faces.

In a recent development, the catch is that the system's battery life is really short, showing why this is more of a proof of concept than anything else. OATs last around three to four days, but paired with the sound-level sensor, they'll only last a day. It has a USB-C port for charging the lithium-ion polymer battery.

Kim claims she distributed OATs to many people and found that they used them in three different ways. One is, “Am I being used?” Like when you attach an OAT to a coffee machine and have the avatar get excited when the machine starts grinding beans. The second is for warning people near an object. For example, 3D printers release toxic fumes during use, and attaching an OAT to one can warn people that the device is operational. And the third is to track their own behaviors. Someone attached an OAT to a dumbbell to track how often they lifted weights, encouraging themselves to exercise regularly so they wouldn't disappoint the AI pet.

The demo at the symposium was popular, and Kim turned it into a competition to see who could come up with the most interesting ideas about what objects to pair with the OATs. Kim's website features a gallery with sprites people made, from an animated conference badge to a panda avatar for an Owala water bottle.

But the demo also ignited a huge discussion about anthropomorphizing artificial intelligence, and whether it’s proper to give these sprites humanlike traits and emotions to make people feel connected with them.

It's already a topic in play within the AI industry. Companies often refer to their chatbot behaviors in human terms, like when they “hallucinate.” Anthropic unveiled a “dreaming” feature this summer where its AI agent cleaned up its local memory as a background process. These anthropomorphized terms can distort moral judgments about AI and cause people to overly trust the tools.

Kim notes that's why OATs have very limited interactions, restricted to expressive emotions and the E Ink display.

It has been revealed that “Anthropomorphism can be very useful in certain ways, like helping people to change their behaviors,” Kim claims. “People name their car, and they name their bike. I rarely see people who name their iPhone. I feel like in the future of computing we will have more of a relationship with AI, but we should definitely be careful not to abuse this.".

What teenagers really think about online safety and AI

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (657 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Blog

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Future Report reveals UK teens are curious, digitally confident, and critical of online content.
  • Read the Future Report and you meet a generation that is curious, capable and far more thoughtful about technology than we often give them credit for.
  • Too often, public debates frame young people's digital lives as problems to be solved.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Future Report reveals UK teens are curious, digitally confident, and critical of online content. Rather than viewing technology solely through fear, policies should support youth and parents together—fostering resilience, media literacy, and safe, empowering AI use.

Read the Future Report and you meet a generation that is curious, capable and far more thoughtful about technology than we often give them credit for. Of the 6,000 UK teenagers surveyed, 77% mentioned they always or often stop to consider whether what they find online can be trusted. That should make us optimistic, and it should inform how we think about keeping them safe.

Too often, public debates frame young people's digital lives as problems to be solved. Screen time to cut, platforms to restrict, harms to count. The report describes teenagers who are "digitally confident, curious and optimistic" while staying alert to the risks. That is much closer to what we hear from parents, who know what a great generation they are raising. They have concerns, but they also see children who are creative, funny and often remarkably sensible online. If policy starts only from fear, we risk designing for the worst case and failing everyone else.

In a recent development, when we think about online safety, we usually list what we hope to prevent. The risks are real, and parents are right to want them gone. But there is a second list we rarely write down and that one includes what gets lost when we take access away. The learning, the creativity, the conversations and the confidence that come from using technology well.

Industry observers note that those skills need to be developed over time in age appropriate ways. Knowing to check what you're consuming online is something that is learned through practice and with support. Trying things, getting some wrong, and working out what to do differently builds resilience. You can see it grow with age. The report tells us that 52% of 16 to 18 year olds always check what they find, compared with 33% of 13 to 15 year olds.

That learning takes place with the help, guidance, and involvement of parents and teachers Eighty-one percent of teens say they would ask a parent for help with misinformation, scams or cyberbullying, and that barely drops as they get older (83% of 13 to 15s, 79% of 16 to 18s). Teens want their parents involved with three in ten saying that parental supervision helps them get the balance right.

The same goes for AI. Two thirds of teens use it at least a couple of times a week, for creative projects (67%) or learning (65%). What's striking is how they use it. They value AI when it helps them understand, not just when it gives answers. One 15-year-old in the report said she needs to know "how it's been worked out" for her schoolwork. That is exactly the instinct parents and educators want to develop.

If we can, the opportunities are incredible. Older teens are already using AI to learn a language (20%), teach themselves to code (19%) and prepare for job applications (17%). This is a generation using technology to stretch themselves, and as an organisation dedicated to improving outcomes for children that’s exciting to read.

It has been revealed that there is clearly more work to be done. The report is honest about the gap teenagers perceive. Twenty-six percent of older teens worry their parents can't recognise AI or fake content. Parents need to be brought on the journey to an AI enabled world alongside everyone else. They need platforms that are safe by design, the confidence to respond calmly when things go wrong, and the chance to learn about AI alongside their children.

Recent findings suggest that this generation is giving us real reasons to be hopeful. Our job is to make sure every child gets to build these skills, with the adults in their lives beside them.

Han Won-seok confessed in a video on the YouTube channel of his lawyer.

A candidate who came first in South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam has admitted cheating by using a miniature camera, mobile phone and AI tools.

Han Won-seok confessed in a video on the YouTube account of his lawyer, Lee Don-Ho, adding that he had confessed to the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency and offered details on how he cheated.

The 34-year-old scored 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, getting just one of 160 questions wrong, which initially raised suspicions and sparked online speculation.

Standardised national tests play an outsized role in career trajectories for South Koreans, making their results - and efforts to unduly inflate those results - of great importance.

"I cheated in both the first and second rounds of the tax account exam by using electronic devices and generative AI," Han said in the video published on Sunday.

"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating.".

When accusations he had cheated first began to surface, Han had denied any wrongdoing - but said he had changed his mind after thinking about the feelings of the candidate who had come second in the exam.

He went on to apologise to the other entrants who had passed the tests fairly.

"It seems that because of me, other successful candidates are being suspected," he suggested.

The Ministry of Employment and Labour and the Human Resources Development Service held an emergency meeting after Han admitted cheating.

The South Korean president's policy chief Ha Jun-kyung said upcoming measures would be introduced to prevent cheating and warned "past crimes" would be "tracked down and apprehended to the very end".

Those found to have used AI to cheat in the tax accountancy exam will have their qualification revoked and will be banned from retaking the test for five years, the government remarked.

The scandal comes just days before the east Asian nation's annual college entrance exam, a crucial hurdle for students.

Can smart glasses exam cheating be stopped?

A series of cases involving exam cheating with AI glasses in South Korea has universities and schools scrambling to rein in the use of the technology.

Han remarked he had only cheated to try and earn money and get a job that would make his parents proud of him again.

Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency told Korean news agency Yonhap on Sunday that it was looking into the case.

"We received a written confession through the test taker's lawyer this morning regarding cheating on the tax accountant exam," it confirmed in a statement.

It added that the case had now been assigned to investigators.

Because of the significance of the national exams, instances of cheating are not uncommon in South Korea, and cases involving the use of AI have become more prominent as the technology becomes more sophisticated.

Last month, two college applicants were reported to have used AI glasses to try and cheat their entrance exams at two Seoul universities.

Education ministry data also indicates there were four cases of cheating through AI glasses at middle and high schools in the past 12 months.

Exams watchdog warns of rise in high-tech cheating.

In September, Apple introduced the latest Beats 360 headphones, the first overears from Beats since the Beats Studio Pro in 2023. That noted, the older Beats Studio Pro still remain on sale at a lower price point – so it begs the question, which Beats headphones are more worthwhile?

According to recent reports, one of the biggest differences between the two will be the price. The Beats Studio Pro, since they’re older, are regularly available on discount. Right now, you can pick up Beats Studio Pro for $199-249 on Amazon, compared to Beats 360, which aren’t discounted from their $349 launch pricing.

Recent findings suggest that despite being older and cheaper, the Beats Studio Pro have a couple advantages over the Beats 360. On top of the fact that they’re $100-150 cheaper, you may very well still want to consider them.

Sources indicate that the biggest advantages, in my view, have to do with the form factor. The Beats Studio Pro can fold down into a much more compact size, whereas Beats 360 don’t fold at all. This means it’s easier to carry around the Beats Studio Pro.

Industry observers note that beats Studio Pro also offer a headphone jack, whereas Beats 360 don’t have any sort of wired audio at all, even over USB-C. This means Beats Studio Pro are easier to use in environments where bluetooth audio isn’t convenient, such as with a game console or on an airplane.

One of my favorite things about the Beats 360 is that they offer UltraPlush cushions you can swap into, but those cost extra. Beats Studio Pro by default come with UltraPlush cushions, so you can have a more comfortable experience out of the box.

According to recent reports, of course, Beats 360 are newer, so by default they do a number of things better. That includes:.

Recent findings suggest that out of everything on this list, I’d say clearer transparency, stronger noise cancellation, and automatic device switching make the biggest difference. In my testing, its hard to hear with the transparency mode on the Beats Studio Pro, so I end up taking the headphones off to have conversation. With Beats 360, that isn’t the case.

It has been revealed that as for noise cancellation and automatic device switching, I feel that if you’re buying Beats for the sake of having Apple headphones, you should buy the ones that offer true automatic device switching – and those are the Beats 360. Noise cancellation is more of a personal preference, but if you value having the best noise cancellation, the Beats 360 are noticeably better.

According to recent reports, lastly, the Beats 360 do have the customizable design going for them. While customization is more aesthetically pleasing, it also has an advantage longer term – when the earcups start wearing down over the years, you can quickly replace them on the Beats 360.

According to recent reports, while it’s hard to overlook the fact that Beats Studio Pro come in at a much lower price point, I’d generally say that if you want a great pair of headphones that offer an Apple experience, you probably shouldn’t buy the Beats Studio Pro. The Beats Studio Pro are a fine pair of headphones for the price, but you certainly aren’t getting all of the same ecosystem creature comforts that Beats 360 offer.

That mentioned, Beats 360 simply do not offer a headphone jack or a foldable design, and if those things matter to you, then Beats Studio Pro might still be the way to go. Beats Studio Pro also offer a ton of different color options that aren’t available on Beats 360, while costing $150 less.
