💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you thought the foldable craze got crazy when only Android OEMs were involved, it got even crazier with the Apple iPhone Duo.
  • A report by Smart Analytics Global (SAG) on global foldable shipment performance in Q3 2026 highlights one Android OEM's staggering lead.
  • It has been revealed that this is important—the form factor, specifically.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you thought the foldable craze got crazy when only Android OEMs were involved, it got even crazier with the Apple iPhone Duo. A recent analytics report for Q3 2026 spells out how crazy things got and what 2027 could have in store.

A report by Smart Analytics Global (SAG) on global foldable shipment performance in Q3 2026 highlights one Android OEM's staggering lead. The report states that global foldable shipments declined 2% YoY, which translates to "over 7.5 million units shipped." However, Samsung saw a 13% YoY increase this past quarter, thanks to the Galaxy Z Fold 8, accounting for 69% of the foldable market share.

It has been revealed that this is important—the form factor, specifically. The Fold 8 is the company's first wide-foldable. Many other OEMs, such as Chinese companies, have also adopted this wider, often shorter foldable design. SAG's report states Samsung experienced "double-digit shipment growth in both South Korea and Europe," as well. A notable competitor, Huawei, accounts for 14% of the foldable share in Q3.

The Pura X View was a significant contributor, despite the report noting a small YoY decline in shipments.

Recent findings suggest that SAG then flips the script. While the market has struggled, it forecasts "a new growth cycle" next year. Shipments might grow 55% YoY in 2027. Wide foldables might account for most phone shipments next year, driven by Samsung's device, the Apple iPhone Duo, and others from Chinese makers.

Some of this data is a little interesting. This was a while ago, but in 2024, Huawei topped Samsung in foldable shipments. The Chinese OEM became the world's leader in foldable shipments. This was a "turning point," one could say, for Samsung. It came at a time when many believed Samsung had become complacent with its Galaxy Z series: the Flip and Fold.

Samsung's shipments fell 42% year-over-year in Q1 2024, while Huawei increased by a massive 257% YoY. Currently, you have Huawei's Pura X View, the industry's first wide foldable, which didn't perform as well for the firm as the Fold 8 did for Samsung. SAG's 2027 outlook is certainly intriguing, but it will take consumers buying new phones to make it happen.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

In the broader phone market, global shipments plummeted in Q3, marking the lowest level in 14 years. The market dropped 20% YoY. Still, Samsung claimed the top spot because of the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra.

Recent findings suggest that everything is in flux right now. Some analysts foresee a turnaround, while others firmly believe we're in for more trying times in 2027. The main thing is pricing. If phones are priced well and buyers can afford them, things will change. But we've seen how prices have gone. Moto's Signature 27 is $1,599, and that's not even a foldable—it's a standard slab phone. Other foldables are $2,000; I know we were all paying attention to Apple's iPhone Duo launch. Wide foldables are cool (I almost got one), but plenty of variables are getting in the way of a turnaround.

There are two main reasons people still buy standalone cameras despite having an iPhone in their pocket wherever they go. The first is lens quality: iPhones have small plastic lenses compared to the far larger and more sophisticated glass lenses used with dedicated cameras.

Recent findings suggest that the second is sensor size. All other things being equal, a larger sensor will capture more light and provide a higher quality image. Current smartphone sensors are absolutely tiny compared to those used in even mid-range consumer cameras.

Squeezing more pixels into a given sensor size tends to sacrifice low light capabilities in return for higher resolution. This is less likely to be an problem with a telephoto lens, which is normally used outdoors rather than inside.

What I’d really love to see is a significantly larger sensor for the main camera, with no increase in resolution. This would improve low light performance and overall image quality.

#120. In elephants, the resilience of communities has its limits

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1349 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

In elephants, the resilience of communities has its limits

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1349 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Elephants live in some of the most complex and resilient societies in the animal kingdom.
  • In a recent development, anastasia Madsen, a behavioral ecologist at the University of California, San Diego, and her colleagues analyzed 12 years of observations of wild Asian elephants in Sri Lanka.
  • Udawalawe National Park in southern Sri Lanka was created in the 1970s around a reservoir on one of the country’s four major rivers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elephants live in some of the most complex and resilient societies in the animal kingdom. Individuals die or move away, calves grow up, and newcomers join, but the local communities as a whole usually hold together. Long-term studies of African savanna elephants have shown that, even after poaching or other spikes in deaths, survivors tend to rebuild their lost connections over time. But a upcoming study suggests that resilience may not keep the community intact when steady losses accumulate over time.

In a recent development, anastasia Madsen, a behavioral ecologist at the University of California, San Diego, and her colleagues analyzed 12 years of observations of wild Asian elephants in Sri Lanka. They found that, once losses began to outpace newcomers, the elephants’ society didn’t just get smaller. It fractured.

Udawalawe National Park in southern Sri Lanka was created in the 1970s around a reservoir on one of the country’s four major rivers. “Before that, it was basically a tropical deciduous forest,” said Shermin de Silva, an ecologist at UC San Diego and senior author of the study (de Silva started the Udawalawe Elephant Research Project in 2006).

The reservoir had brought farming and settlers, some of whom lived inside what later became the park. When they were moved out, the land they had cleared for their crops turned into grassland that, according to de Silva, looks very much like an African savanna. With far more food than the original forest offered, the park became famous for its big elephant herds.

But the savanna was only a stage in the forest’s comeback. Without fires and clearing, invasive plants like lantana took over. “In some places, they’re like an impenetrable thicket. Not even elephants really like to go there because there’s no food for them,” de Silva said. This is a problem because elephants tend to move where the grass is. A park with less forage, the team claims, stops attracting elephants from outside while, due to limited food, fewer calves reach adulthood.

Her team watched this transformation from a vehicle, driving random routes along the park’s roads about three days a week. The team identified elephants mostly by their floppy ears, which collect holes, tears, and cuts with age. “Their ears are very individually distinct, so it’s like a fingerprint,” de Silva said. Between 2007 and 2018, the team identified 443 adult and subadult females that roamed the park.

Sources indicate that the team focused on females because males lead more solitary lives, ranging widely in search of mates. Females live in a so-called fission-fusion society. “It’s kind of similar to humans,” Madsen stated. “You might have your work friends, you might have your family, and you’re not always with those same individuals at the same time, but they’re all part of your social network.” Unlike African savanna elephants, where families follow older matriarchs, Asian elephants move more independently. This may be because Asia’s rainy environment ensures that food and water are rarely far apart and usually easier to find, so following an experienced individual brings less benefit.

Industry observers note that madsen reconstructed the elephants’ social network for each year, measuring the strength of each relationship by how often two animals were seen together. “You can think of it as a probability that you will see those two individuals together,” she explains. An algorithm commonly used for analyzing human social networks then picked out communities—clusters of elephants with many strong ties to one another.

Sources indicate that for the first few years of the study, these communities seemed to hold very well. But then cracks started to appear.

Sources indicate that around 2012, the elephants that died or left began to outnumber the newcomers. By 2018, about 69 percent of the females seen at the start of the study were gone, even though Asian elephants can live 60 years or more. Soon after the balance tipped, communities grew smaller, more numerous and more isolated from each other. “As individuals are being lost from the network, there’s nobody filling it back in,” de Silva says.

It has been revealed that A shrinking population naturally makes for a smaller network, so the team checked whether this was just a numbers game. They looked at a population of 59 elephants seen every year of the study, which the team referred to as residents. “If it was just an artifact of the data, those core individuals should have fairly consistent relationships. But that’s not what we saw,” Madsen said. “They were changing their relationships with each other, even though they were still there.” Among these residents, the fracturing came one to three years after the decline began.

Sources indicate that madsen suspects some of the lost elephants were the glue holding groups together. “If you go to a city hall meeting, it’s maybe the same group of people that constantly comes in. You’re not friends with every single other person in that group, though,” she said. “There could have been some key individuals that were lost that were holding these subgroups together.”.

Sources indicate that the first ties to go were the weakest, the casual acquaintances. These weak relationships, Madsen says, could represent animals that merely tolerate each other: “Tolerance is really important in a society, especially in large animals. If they get into conflict, it could be serious.” These weak ties, researchers argue, may still be important because they can carry information between communities.

Recent findings suggest that de Silva links this fracturing to the disappearing grass. “As the competition becomes more severe, your social sphere sort of shrinks,” she said. “It’s as if they’re emphasizing the quality over the quantity of the relationships.”.

Before the breakup, some network statistics fluctuated from year to year, which complex systems scientists call flickering. “If you have a light bulb that’s right on the edge of dying, it might start flickering,” Madsen said. “It’s on, it’s off, it’s on, it’s off. And then suddenly it dies.” Spotted early, she argues, such signals could serve as an early warning sign. “Hopefully, park managers and conservationists can detect that and intervene before the population collapses,” Madsen said.

Recent findings suggest that the challenge is that this detection requires long-term data, and we don’t have that for many populations. What worries the researchers most is that, without early detection, we may only recognize problems after it’s too late. “If you are taking the boards out of a ship and you’re not replacing them, the ship starts to take on water,” Madsen mentioned. “There was a point of no return where there was structural damage, but you might not have noticed it until later.”.

The study’s data end in 2018, but de Silva claims things haven’t improved. Her team predicted a decline in the park’s elephant population in 2019, and it now appears to be happening faster than expected. “They don’t appear to be breeding very well. A lot of the calves are not surviving,” she stated. Many adult females die in their 30s and 40s, and they should be living roughly twice as long.

Part of the reason they die so young is conflict with humans. Female Asian elephants have no tusks, so ivory poaching isn’t the main threat. Instead, elephants get shot when they raid crops or startle people. Occasionally, de Silva claims, they also eat explosives hidden in pumpkins some locals place to get rid of wild boars. But the bigger problem, she says, is that elephants can’t survive in the protected areas alone.

In a recent development, more than half of Asian elephant populations live in poor-quality habitats, and the species has lost nearly two-thirds of its likely historic range. “Management really has to be about entire landscapes,” de Silva remarked. “Roads and infrastructure, irrigation canals—those are the things that are hurting the elephants. It’s not really a wildlife management problem.” Her team now works with farmers outside the park, testing crops elephants are less likely to damage. “Their long-term persistence really depends on people and elephants being able to share the space safely,” she said.

Science, 2026. DOI: 10.1126/science.aef6714.

#119. Where was Nvidia’s security team?

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1110 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

Where was Nvidia’s security team?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1110 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that outsiders had little reason to notice when Nvidia’s longtime chief security officer and head of product security stepped down in August.
  • According to recent reports, at the time, David Reber, who spent four years as CSO and seven at Nvidia overall, said he was leaving for health reasons.
  • According to recent reports, reber’s replacement, Saša Zdjelar, previously spent 17 years at ExxonMobil in Houston, leaving as a senior IT manager before spending one year at Salesforce and several years at the cybersecurity organization ReversingLabs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that outsiders had little reason to notice when Nvidia’s longtime chief security officer and head of product security stepped down in August. Just two and a half months later, CEO Jensen Huang himself left the company over growing questions about his extramarital relationships — starting with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore data center company that U.S. investigators suspect of funneling Nvidia chips to China, then widening to reports about two separate affairs with Nvidia employees.

According to recent reports, at the time, David Reber, who spent four years as CSO and seven at Nvidia overall, said he was leaving for health reasons. “This wasn’t a pivot I had planned. But I know what needs to come first: family and health,” he wrote on LinkedIn in late August, disclosing that he’d been diagnosed with young-onset Parkinson’s more than two years ago.

According to recent reports, reber’s replacement, Saša Zdjelar, previously spent 17 years at ExxonMobil in Houston, leaving as a senior IT manager before spending one year at Salesforce and several years at the cybersecurity organization ReversingLabs. Zdjelar didn’t respond to questions Thursday about the transition or what the security team knew.

Recent findings suggest that nothing public connects Reber’s or Zdjelar’s role changes to the Megaspeed matter, but it seems fair to wonder what Nvidia’s security team knew about the government’s scrutiny of Megaspeed and about Huang’s relationships, and whether anyone raised concerns. Reber didn’t respond to questions Thursday. Nvidia also has not answered our related questions.

Recent findings suggest that relationships between a CEO and his employees typically fall to HR, legal and the board, not security. But security specialists say any affair — even one inside the office — can give a foreign intelligence service leverage over an exec who wants it kept quiet.

According to recent reports, still, spotting the clues isn’t easy. The way intelligence services collect information, much of it through everyday conversation rather than hacking, makes it especially difficult for security teams to identify risks, according to retired senior intelligence officer Nicholas Eftimiades, who says he has trained more than 1,000 corporate security professionals.

In a recent development, some people inside Nvidia clearly knew parts of the picture. Nvidia’s top lawyer was engaged with the government’s Megaspeed inquiry more than a year ago, The New York Times reported earlier this week. (Nvidia has remarked it regularly contacts officials.) Reports about Huang’s relationships with employees suggest colleagues also knew of them, even if the behavior is not expressly forbidden by Nvidia’s code of conduct. The Times cited five Nvidia employees who said he was involved with a vice president who reported directly to him; Reuters, citing two people, later reported a second relationship. What’s unclear is whether any of that reached security.

Even if it had, Eftimiades, who wrote Chinese Espionage Operations and Tactics in 2020, told TechCrunch that a security team’s resources are often limited. For one thing, they’re often underfunded because, unlike some other cost centers, they don’t drive revenue. It’s astonishingly common for CEOs to answer a security team’s warnings with “not a nickel more than compliance,” he stated.

Many companies also define security overly narrowly, specialists say. In an opinion piece in The Hill, Don Aviv, CEO of the corporate investigations firm Interfor International, and author Jeremy Hurewitz, wrote, “Too many companies still approach security primarily as a matter of protecting facilities, preventing cyberattacks, and responding to physical threats.” The two argued that “[s]ecurity teams need to pay greater attention to insider threats, including the cultivation of executives and employees by foreign intelligence services, suspicious business relationships, conflicts of interest and attempts to obtain sensitive information through trusted personal contacts.”.

It would be surprising if Nvidia’s security team didn’t have a more expansive remit than most companies given its scale and business partners, but it’s possible.

According to recent reports, in fairness, some of it is simply beyond what any team can do. Speaking generally, not about Huang, Eftimiades offered a hypothetical in which a CEO complains that he can’t do something because “I’m fighting a board who doesn’t want to do this.” That tells an intelligence asset who the obstacle is. The service then asks, “Who’s the sticking point here?” and looks for ways into that person’s email and phone.

In a recent development, what a rival intelligence service wants is often less technology than policy insight, including who’s pushing to change export rules and who the biggest blocker is. “Intel world tends to be like cancer,” he remarked. “Once it gets into the body, it looks to spread and looks to reach out.”.

According to recent reports, the playbook isn’t new, Eftimiades added, “particularly for China.” Any executive dealing with the country “will tell you that they’ve been approached.” He noted there are also “tons of diplomat stories” of U.S. diplomats walking into a hotel room to find a woman on the bed. He said what’s newer compared with Soviet era spying is the relationships these services cultivate now often last years, not weeks.

Sources indicate that technology can augment that human intelligence, Eftimiades said, pointing to IMSI catchers as one example. The devices mimic a cell tower so that nearby phones connect to them. A basic version can cost about $1,000 and fit in a suitcase, he said, though government-grade models cost far more, and there were a couple of cases involving Chinese espionage where these factored in last year.

Eftimiades indicates no one knows yet if the devices were used against Huang, whose phone was presumably hardened such that compromises could be detected, if not stopped altogether. But what Nvidia’s security team knew, and whether it could have acted on it, will only become clearer as the board’s independent investigation and federal inquiries proceed.

Industry observers note that in the meantime, Eftimiades said he hopes the whole episode is “a wake-up call” for U.S. industry, which he said is mostly “clueless” about China’s tactics. “We have lost trillions [of dollars] in intellectual property,” is his guess. “Whatever we think we’re doing isn’t working.”.

#118. How to get the most protection from your Ring camera security system

How to get the most protection from your Ring camera security system

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Simply putting the camera on your front door may not be enough.
  • It has been revealed that let's be blunt here.
  • Recent findings suggest that if you are going to use Ring, it's vital to maximize your setup's efficiency.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Simply putting the camera on your front door may not be enough.

It has been revealed that let's be blunt here. There are good reasons to skip Ring for your home security, from ongoing privacy concerns to some key features relying on a subscription. At the same time, it remains the most practical security platform for a lot of people, at least in the US. That's especially true if your smart home platform of choice is Alexa, which is likewise owned by Amazon.

Recent findings suggest that if you are going to use Ring, it's vital to maximize your setup's efficiency. Some of the company's products can be costly, and your goal here is to deter and record intruders (although you'll need a Ring subscription to do this), not just maintain an illusion of security. If that's all you care about, you might as well slap a few ADT stickers on your home along with a "Beware of Dog" sign.

Efficiency isn't about covering the widest area — it's about thinking like a thief, yet spending as little as possible for the results you need. You also need to be concerned about minimizing false alerts.

Your first consideration should be capturing all possible points of entry — and we mean all of them. Don't just position cameras over your doorways. If you've got a side alley, for example, it's possible that an intruder could climb a fence and break in without ever appearing on your door-based video feeds. Give your outdoor cameras overlapping views when possible, and make sure they're installed around 9 feet high, excluding doorbells. This will not only ensure a wide field of view, but make it harder for intruders to smash or tamper with your equipment. That mentioned, cameras should also be easily visible beyond your property. Any halfway intelligent thief is going to think twice if they know they're being recorded.

Ring is eager to sell you indoor cameras, but these aren't actually necessary unless you're hoping to monitor a child, pet or guests. By the time an intruder makes it indoors, all you're really doing is capturing further evidence of their crimes. If you do buy indoor cameras, position them high in the corners for broad coverage, with an eye toward entryways.

Recent findings suggest that once cameras are in position, be sure to spend time customizing their Motion Zones via the Ring app. This can prevent unwanted motion detection from objects such as passing traffic or trees blowing in the wind. But really, you'll also want to turn on Advanced Motion Detection if a camera supports it, and most importantly, Smart Alerts. These let you narrow alerts to people, packages and/or vehicles, so when you receive notifications on your phone, you'll know to take them seriously instead of tuning them out. Smart Alerts do require a subscription, so remember that before you come to depend on them.

A factor that's all too easy to neglect is redundancy. You should always have a backup battery available for your cameras powered by removable batteries, for example, because it can take hours to fully recharge one. You may also want spare cables or installation tools.

Even more critical is the quality of your Wi-Fi network, since you need a stable signal for uninterrupted video. Be sure to test for any weak spots or dead zones, and consider upgrading to a mesh system if you can't fix them with better router placement. You don't need to go with Amazon's eero routers, but if you can't afford any downtime whatsoever, look into models with cellular backup features. These can keep your entire network online at the cost of a monthly fee. You may want power backup too, however, and that can get very expensive on the whole-home level.

Sources indicate that lastly, don't forget to consider supplementing your cameras with door and window sensors (tied to a Ring Alarm system), as well as automatic lighting. While newer Ring cameras do have great night vision, lights from Ring or otherwise can improve video clarity further and make intruders visible to everyone. Just make sure lights aren't blaring into your neighbor's windows or too easily triggered by people passing by.

Breaking: Nvidia’s fresh boss is expected to rein in its AI financing, WSJ reports

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jensen Huang at Nvidia’s GTC Berlin keynote, 21 October 2026.
  • Recent findings suggest that nvidia’s interim chief executive, Colette Kress, is expected to rein in its financing of the AI industry, The Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday.
  • In a recent development, kress, Nvidia’s finance chief since 2013, was already wary of some of the deals Huang made, according to the Journal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jensen Huang at Nvidia’s GTC Berlin keynote, 21 October 2026.

Recent findings suggest that nvidia’s interim chief executive, Colette Kress, is expected to rein in its financing of the AI industry, The Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday. Jensen Huang had already started that pullback in his final months as CEO, the Journal’s Robbie Whelan, Anissa Gardizy and Kate Clark wrote. He told neocloud partners to get their customers to pay upfront.

In a recent development, kress, Nvidia’s finance chief since 2013, was already wary of some of the deals Huang made, according to the Journal. Startups that counted on Nvidia’s support now expect an even bigger pullback in Nvidia financing.

In a recent development, nvidia confirmed its financing programme in July. About a month later, Huang and Kress started questioning the return on some of the deals, the Journal reported.

In August, Nvidia cut the scale of its commitment to OpenAI’s data centre lease in Piketon, Ohio. OpenAI signed the lease with SoftBank’s SB Energy. Nvidia scaled back after Kress became sceptical of the deal, according to the Journal.

Huang also told his finance team that massive cloud providers planned to use other chips. That left Nvidia with more chip wafers and memory than it needed, which it had already committed to buy. He asked staff to find a way to judge whether the guarantees Nvidia gave smaller companies were worth it. By the end of August, Nvidia had paused some deals that were in progress, the Journal reported.

In October, neocloud chief executives met at Nvidia’s GTC conference in Berlin. Huang told them to secure payment upfront from their customers rather than simply rent out his chips. That is according to people in attendance who spoke to the Journal. Two executives who heard his remarks, and one briefed on them, gave his words as:.

Industry observers note that “You’re not charging what you should be charging. I don’t even need you guys. I could just give all this capacity to Elon! Elon wants it.”.

Recent findings suggest that nvidia took part in a record 129 venture deals over the past year, the Journal reported. It did 49 in 2023. That was 27% of global venture deal value. Nvidia’s latest quarterly filing lists $36bn of off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, the Journal mentioned. Those are its neocloud backstops.

Some founders of companies with little or no revenue told the Journal they could struggle to raise money without Nvidia. UBS analyst Tim Arcuri estimated that a pullback could take $50bn or more out of the market.

According to recent reports, several deals are still open. Nscale is negotiating with Nvidia and other investors to back a $45bn data centre for Anthropic in West Virginia. Nvidia had been in talks to guarantee its debt. Nvidia offered to license Reflection AI’s technology and hire some of its staff. That deal was not done before Huang left. Nvidia is also finalising an investment in Thinking Machines Lab at a $40bn valuation, according to the Journal.

Huang defended Nvidia’s investments in an interview with Fortune in London in October. He stated Nvidia only takes minority stakes, so other investors must back the companies too.

“We’ve created an industry that the VCs alone cannot fund,” Huang told Fortune.

It has been revealed that marc Boroditsky is chief revenue officer at Nebius, a neocloud Nvidia has invested in. He told Fortune:.

“If it’s all going to come down to Nvidia’s capital, we would have run out already,” Boroditsky remarked.

According to recent reports, huang resigned as CEO on Thursday, and the board named Kress interim chief executive. She keeps her finance role. An Nvidia spokesperson told CNBC:.

Industry observers note that “We are in the process of selecting a search firm for the NVIDIA CEO role. We have not formally engaged any potential candidates.”.

Huang has discussed a return with allies, the Financial Times reported. On Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News that the board should look outside the manufacturer. He also wants answers from the board within 10 days on its export compliance, Axios reported.

Industry observers note that nvidia reports its third-quarter results on Tuesday, 17 November. The earnings call will be Kress’s first public appearance in charge of the tech giant, The Information noted.

Amazon has a new meal delivery partner to offer Prime members free delivery: Uber Eats. If you’re always overpaying because of Uber Eats’ or Amazon’s delivery fees, an Amazon Prime membership may be worth it — especially before Black Friday deals sales start.

Recent findings suggest that the new perk also comes with $20 off the first two Uber Eats eligible orders of $25 or more for the first 14 days, plus Amazon-exclusive offers. Recent findings suggest that in order to get free delivery and $20 off your order, go to the Uber Eats tab at the top of your Amazon app or Uber Eats on Amazon’s website. Place your order as usual with a participating restaurant but make sure the $20 discount applies at checkout.

In a recent development, I tried the newly introduced perk and promo out for Saturday’s dinner. However, I will say the tip, a nearly $10 service fee, tax and the delivery fee all added up to the cost of another meal — which is worth paying attention to when you order.

It has been revealed that but you may wonder what that means for the GrubHub partnership that both Amazon and GrubHub touted for years — dating back to 2022. Before now, your Prime subscription included a GrubHub Plus membership at no additional cost. GrubHub Plus included no delivery fees, lower service fees and 5% back on pickup orders.

Industry observers note that the new partnership rolled out the same day that Lyft and DoorDash confirmed that they’re teaming up for a new subscription, Lyft Go. An Amazon spokesperson said in an email to CNET that the GrubHub and Amazon partnership ended on Thursday. There’s no telling how long Amazon will partner with Uber Eats.

It has been revealed that “We continuously evaluate our third-party offers to ensure they provide the best possible value for Prime members,” the spokesperson mentioned. “As part of that ongoing evaluation, we identified an opportunity to deliver an even better restaurant delivery experience.”.

Recent findings suggest that however, a GrubHub spokesperson said in an email to CNET that if you have a Prime membership and activated GrubHub Plus, you’ll have the membership until Dec. 31, 2027.

GrubHub shared a joint statement from Amazon and GrubHub in an email to CNET:.

Sources indicate that on Nov. 5, Grubhub and Amazon have decided to end the Prime-exclusive Grubhub Plus offer, and Amazon customers will no longer be able to place Grubhub orders through Amazon.com or the Amazon Shopping app. Amazon and Grubhub are proud of the partnership and the value provided to Prime members over the years. As the agreement concludes, both companies remain committed to serving our customers and delivering a great customer experience.

Industry observers note that the latest Uber Eats perk is now available to all Prime members, including those with Prime Access and Prime for Young Adults. And if you’re looking for another dining option, your Amazon Prime membership still offers free same-day delivery on perishable grocery orders over $25 when you order from Amazon Grocery.

Industry News: AO3 is back online but with limited features

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (377 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The outage lasted two weeks but full functionality is expected to resume soon.
  • In a recent development, after two weeks in the dark, popular fan fiction website Archive of Our Own (AO3) is back online.
  • In a recent development, AO3 was taken offline at the end of October due to "evidence of a security incident" that OTW mentioned would result in two to four weeks of downtime.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The outage lasted two weeks but full functionality is expected to resume soon.

In a recent development, after two weeks in the dark, popular fan fiction website Archive of Our Own (AO3) is back online. However, Organization for Transformative Works (OTW), the nonprofit organization that runs AO3, said that some features have been temporarily disabled as a compromise to bring the site back earlier than the four-week mark, according to an upgrade post on the website. OTW said that features like icons and external work importing are right now disabled, while works can only be downloaded in HTML format. The organization clarified that these features will be restored and that no icons have been deleted.

In a recent development, AO3 was taken offline at the end of October due to "evidence of a security incident" that OTW mentioned would result in two to four weeks of downtime. Now that the open-source fan fiction repository is back online, its customers may still run into some problems, according to OTW. The organization said it implemented an "intentional measure to help manage traffic," so users may experience delays with the website loading but can refresh to continue trying.

It has been revealed that as for the site's data, OTW mentioned that none of it was deleted, adding that user "works, bookmarks, kudos, etc. are still safe." OTW also managed to pause AO3's draft deletion feature so that no drafts were deleted during the downtime. Users should log back in and check on their drafts, though, since the feature will turn back on starting November 29 so that drafts longer than 30 days old will be deleted.

It's still unclear what the cause was, but OTW confirmed it was a "security incident" and that it would "not be sharing specifics about what mitigating changes are being made at this time." OTW added that it partnered with a security firm to review the incident and analyze the site to prevent future incidents. The update post mentioned that OTW has "no reason to believe that the user database was compromised, though we cannot rule out that possibility," recommending that consumers change passwords, update linked emails and change passwords of any other sites that share a password with AO3 accounts.

The tech products we enthusiastically recommend this holiday season

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1497 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We’ve been reviewing a bunch of latest gadgets and hardware at TechCrunch this year: dumb phones, bird feeders, health trackers, slushy machines, AI mattress pads, you name it.
  • If these products can impress a group of (sometimes) curmudgeonly tech reporters, then they’re sure to please whoever you’re shopping for this holiday season.
  • We’ve reviewed a lot of e-readers this year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We’ve been reviewing a bunch of latest gadgets and hardware at TechCrunch this year: dumb phones, bird feeders, health trackers, slushy machines, AI mattress pads, you name it. Sometimes we think they’re unnecessary and expensive, but other times, we try out devices that we love so much that we go out and buy them ourselves.

If these products can impress a group of (sometimes) curmudgeonly tech reporters, then they’re sure to please whoever you’re shopping for this holiday season.

We’ve reviewed a lot of e-readers this year. What can we say? We’re nerds. We work for a tech website. But after trying devices from the usual suspects as well as some wildcards, we have recommendations. Evidently, 2026 was the year we fell in love with the pocket-sized e-reader.

It’s an e-reader so small that it can fit in your wallet, or even magnetize to the back of your phone. Do you dream of a world where instead of scrolling Instagram when you’re waiting in line for coffee, you actually opt to read books? There’s really something special about the X3, and it’s only $55 during Xteink’s Black Friday sale. Fair warning, it takes some fiddling with to set up, and it has no integration with Kindle, Libby, or any other apps, so only buy this for someone willing to do a bit of Reddit browsing and tinkering to get it up and running.

Recent findings suggest that if you aren’t planning to magnetize the XTeink to your phone, you’ve got to go with the X4 Pro. It’s slightly bigger, but it has a backlight, which makes it way more versatile. After using both the X3 and the X4 Pro, I find that the backlight really is a game changer, since I do a lot of reading in bed — plus, I like my Pop Socket wallet a bit too much to displace for the X3, and I’d rather just carry an extra credit card-sized device than risk forgetting my actual credit and ID cards, which I have grown too used to having on my phone.

It has been revealed that if I’m being honest, reading my colleague Aisha Malik’s review of the Boox Palma Pro 2 is making me want to buy one. I love using the Xteink e-readers, but they don’t connect to any outside apps. As a hardcore Libby power user (a phrase I am saying in earnest sincerity), it’s a bit frustrating that I can’t get my library books on Xteink e-readers. The same goes for apps like Kobo and Kindle, where any e-book you already own cannot be transferred out of the Amazon ecosystem unless the publisher agrees, which most do not.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re looking for an e-reader with a screen that’s actually book-sized, my favorite that I’ve used is the Kobo Libra Colour, which is $259. The Amazon Paperwhite line is great, but c’mon, Amazon. Branch out!

Hey, we’ve all got to eat. And if you want, you can make that eating process overly techy. Why not?

According to recent reports, the Ember Mug 3 is the latest iteration in Ember’s line of coffee/tea cups that actually stay warm. Our reviewer Lauren Forristal especially appreciated that you no longer need to use your phone app to change the mug’s temperature, which seems like it would be really annoying!

This mug is perfect for gifting to someone, or to put on your own wishlist — you might not want to spend $99 on a mug for yourself, but these sorts of luxury, nice-to-haves are what holidays are made for!

Ah, Ninja, the premiere company in the business of turning every appliance into a two-in-one air fryer. I jest, but at least Ninja knows it’s onto something. Despite the high price point, Lauren states that this newly introduced product made “a pretty convincing case for ditching two appliances and making room for one.” You can’t buy more counter space (without moving), but you can buy more versatile appliances.

Sure, there are cheaper ice makers on the market. But Aisha clarifies that this is the ice maker for “those who crave what’s called ‘the good ice.’” If you feel so passionately about the ice in your beverages that you know what she means, then maybe this is for you.

What they really want is a Mac mini or Claude subscription, but if that’s out of budget, we have some other ideas that might impress your AI-pilled, vibe-coder loved ones….

When I asked my colleague Lucas Ropek what about his favorite product he reviewed this year, he mentioned the Codex Micro. Some hard-core coders — who the product is aimed toward — have found this thing less than pleasing, but Lucas seems to have had fun figuring out this first attempt by OpenAI at hardware.

Recent findings suggest that best case, it’s a productivity game-changer for your friend who has a hardworking team of AI agents within the OpenAI ecosystem. Worst case, this will be a great piece of tech history in a few years.

As people have become more conscious about how much time they spend online, upcoming tech has emerged that, ironically, is designed to keep you away from tech. Some of these products can really make a difference in your life.

For about six months, I’ve consistently used the Brick to prevent me from using social media as the last thing I do before bed, or the first thing in the morning. Some people use it to help them focus during the work day, but evidently, I was not the only one who needed Brick’s help with sleep. The organization recently rolled out its second device, Brick Night, which “Bricks” your phone when you are in the same room. You can customize the times that the Brick Night is active, so it’s not as though you can never, ever use social media in your room. Both Brick and Brick Night are very customizable, so you can create the perfect set-up tailored to your needs.

According to recent reports, it’s embarrassing how whole-heartedly I recommend the Brick, which is basically just a hunk of plastic with an NFC chip in it and a companion app. But my sleep has improved significantly — I even do 8 AM Pilates now. Who am I?

I’ve tried out far pricier smart phone alternatives, but the Dumb Phone was both the most affordable, and the most usable for me. In the humble shell of a $20 TCL flip phone, Dumb Co loads its own software so that users can access apps like WhatsApp, Spotify, Apple Music, and Uber. You can even access iMessage through a third-party app, though Apple could probably get that shut down… no one tell Apple, please!

The Dumb Phone is particularly usable because it’s not intended to be a complete replacement for your smartphone — it’s more like a companion device that you can take out with you when you want to feel more present in the world but still may need to call an Uber home.

Wearable health trackers are pretty common nowadays, but after reviewing several different rings and wristbands, Aisha has named a winner.

Recent findings suggest that there are a lot of ugly health trackers. And then there’s the Oura Ring 5, the leading smart ring maker’s first product that’s thin enough to wear without loudly broadcasting to the world that you’re monitoring your heart rate. (For what it’s worth, I tried the RingConn 3 — which is about the same size as Oura Ring 5 — but returned it, unsatisfied. Womp womp.) Aisha notes in her review that the newest Oura ring is more durable, has a better battery life, and looks more premium than its predecessors.

Airline executives have voiced support for the rollout, but the US labor union representing air traffic controllers has mentioned it was not involved in designing or testing the AI-driven system.

Recent findings suggest that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says the $875 million SMART system has helped reroute 180 flights since being implemented in airspace over Washington, DC, on September 21. The agency claims that this saved an average of 10 minutes per flight and almost 80 gallons of fuel per flight—and it is apparently hoping such results can be replicated nationwide through the expanded deployment.

“After a successful initial rollout to the National Capital Region in September, the FAA will now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 centers across the country to reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption and improve the travel experience for the flying public,” according to the agency statement posted on November 10.

In a recent development, the FAA fact sheet describes SMART as a cloud-based system that combines information about “weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow and controller staffing metrics” to predict air traffic patterns. It is designed to make scheduling recommendations, identify optimal flight routes, and determine the best order of arrivals for aircraft.

However, a human team of FAA specialists based in DC is ultimately responsible for validating the SMART system recommendations before passing them along to air traffic control facilities across the country, according to the agency.

According to recent reports, furthermore, the AI-powered SMART system “cannot be used to replace the critical role air traffic controllers play or take over control of an aircraft,” the FAA clarified in the September 21 announcement about the initial deployment. Local air traffic controllers can decide whether or not to accept the SMART system recommendations.

The previous FAA announcement included supportive statements from Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian and American Airlines CEO Robert Isom.

But the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, which represents more than 15,000 members, also told Flying magazine that it was not consulted or involved in the “design, testing, or implementation of SMART and therefore cannot speak to its effect on the air traffic control workforce.”.

Following the initial deployment in airspace above DC, the FAA expanded the SMART system’s coverage to air route traffic control centers in Atlanta along with Jacksonville and Miami in Florida, according to The Dallas Morning News.

The FAA also shared an example with The Dallas Morning News about how SMART recommended a shorter and faster route for a cargo flight arriving at Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport, although the newspaper noted that the agency did not identify the flight involved and has not provided information about how SMART may have assisted passenger flight traffic.

Ars has previously covered the SMART system’s development and lingering questions about how it works, as well as the air traffic controller shortage and other challenges facing the FAA.

#107. Nvidia Was Already in Trouble Before the Jensen Huang Mess

Nvidia Was Already in Trouble Before the Jensen Huang Mess

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1190 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that nvidia played a key role enabling the AI gold rush thanks in large part to its recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang.
  • But just as he’s leaving, the manufacturer has a growing list of competitors with a range of newly introduced, advanced technology breathing down its neck.
  • “Everything sold today was designed two-to-three years ago,” states the CEO of a large AI manufacturer, who spoke to WIRED on condition of anonymity to avoid hurting business relationships.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that nvidia played a key role enabling the AI gold rush thanks in large part to its recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang. Huang was a master of foreseeing technological changes, investing in chips to train AI earlier than most.

But just as he’s leaving, the manufacturer has a growing list of competitors with a range of newly introduced, advanced technology breathing down its neck. For Nvidia, where CFO Colette Kress has now taken the reins, the timing isn’t great.

“Everything sold today was designed two-to-three years ago,” states the CEO of a large AI manufacturer, who spoke to WIRED on condition of anonymity to avoid hurting business relationships. Kress, or whoever replaces her permanently, will have to chart the course that the chip industry will take two years from now, the CEO says.

Already, competitors have started to move in.

Nvidia dominates the market for AI accelerators, capturing 80 percent of sales, according to Silicon Analysis. Longtime nemesis AMD is now making a concerted effort to build competitive AI chips. Its share of the market has crept up from just two percent in 2022 to between 7 and 10 percent in 2026.

Sources indicate that significant US cloud players—Google, Amazon, and Microsoft—are all developing more specialized chips to power the training and serving of AI models. Each has seen similar gains. These companies are designing their own silicon to reduce costs and to gain some independence from Nvidia.

Several startups now offer more specialized chips that promise improvements over Nvidia’s core products. Cerebras, for instance, sells giant ones meant to power giant AI models. AMD recently bought Taalas, a manufacturer that burns models’ weights into silicon to make computations ultra efficient. Using these chips requires rewriting a lot of code, however, to make them work with cutting-edge AI models.

Patrick Moorhead, chief analyst at MoorInStrat, a organization that tracks the chip industry, indicates the rise of AI agents makes inference, or running models that have already been trained, more important. That’s an area where Nvidia has less of an edge compared to cloud hyperscalers and startups. Nvidia did, however, acquire a startup making specialized chips, called Grok, in December of 2025.

And because of the rise in AI assistants and agents, there’s also growing demand for general purpose central processing units (CPUs), Moorehead said, an area where Nvidia barely competes.

Sources indicate that nvidia still maintains a huge lead in AI thanks to Huang’s foresight. Huang cofounded the manufacturer in 1993 to design graphics chips for PCs. In the mid-2010s, he saw the promise of AI. He funded academic research on the topic, developed software to support AI engineering, and gave hardware to labs and startups.

In 2022, ChatGPT took AI mainstream and sales of Nvidia chips skyrocketed. The company’s revenue went from $26.91 billion in January 2022 to $215.94 billion in January 2026. The challenges it faces may not be existential—but they do add up, especially on a global scale.

Recent findings suggest that while Nvidia’s fortunes have risen in the US, they have declined in the world’s other major market for AI, China. Washington is trying to restrict access to its most advanced chips, while Beijing is trying to develop its own chip industry. Nvidia is not allowed to sell its most powerful chips in China, but it can sell previous generations. Sales of these chips as well as non AI chips doubled over the past year, but China now accounts for only eight percent of the organization’s overall revenue, compared with 20 percent in 2024, according to its fillings. It remains unclear how many chips exported to other countries may either end up in China or end up being used remotely by Chinese firms.

Huawei, a Chinese tech giant targeted with US sanctions for several years, has developed new kinds of supercomputers that harness many more chips than usual to train and run AI models. Some Chinese AI companies, such as Z.ai, which makes one of the world’s best open source models, say they’ve trained their models entirely using Huawei’s chips. If Chinese open-weight models gain traction in other countries, it could create a market for Chinese chips elsewhere.

Huang’s dealings with China played a major role in his downfall. He had a romantic relationship with Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang, a Chinese executive at a Singaporean company called Megaspeed who the US government suspects of being an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Megaspeed and its subsidiaries have reportedly imported between $4.6 and $7.5 billion Nvidia chips into southeast Asia. Reports suggest that the company may have provided access to the chips to Chinese AI firms.

Recent findings suggest that babak Minovi, a senior analyst at the Eurasia Group, a consultancy that focuses on technology and geopolitics, says Huang was right to point out that cutting off access to China would empower domestic rivals. “Huang was taking a pragmatic line, and he knows competition,” he says.

Even in markets that it dominates, Nvidia may turn out to be a victim of its own success. The AI models built using Nvidia’s chip are automating the very elements of coding, data analysis, and scientific research that help design chips.

Most chip design firms use specialized AI models to arrange components on processors—something that traditionally required deep engineering expertise and experience. And both OpenAI and Anthropic have recently touted the ability of their newest models to design electronics from scratch.

Moorhead says the shift towards AI chip design may not pose a huge threat to Nvidia because it’s riding the same wave.“They have access to AI too,” he notes.

Sources indicate that but Moorhead indicates the way AI models can now quickly rewrite code to run on different hardware may prove a problem. For years, Nvidia has attracted developers by providing software that makes it easy to write programs and build models for its silicon. Its Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, has long been seen as a moat to ensure AI companies continue to rely on Nvidia chips.

But AI models are now so good at reading and writing code that they can port an AI model over to a competitor's silicon at speed.

Wafer, a startup that uses AI to port models to AMD and then serves them more cheaply, has seen revenue grow spectacularly in recent months, boasts CEO Emilio Andere.

According to recent reports, every time a major new open weight model is released Wafer can have it running on AMD hardware at least 80 percent as efficiently within hours, he says. Andere says AI is getting so capable that his engineers barely have to edit or review the code.

Dan Hutchinson, a veteran chip analyst, notes Nvidia may be entering its “Intel swan moment,” referring to the 2019 replacement of engineering-focused CEO Brian Krzanich with its CFO Bob Swan. (Sound familiar? Krzanich also resigned after a relationship with an employee; Huang is alleged to have had multiple.) From there, the manufacturer’s focus shifted to sales more than technical progress. Bureaucracy ballooned and revenue tanked.

“Nvidia is now an Intel waiting to happen,” he states.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most newer cars do, but there are a few exceptions.
  • Industry observers note that apple CarPlay is one of the most useful pieces of in-car software out there, unifying navigation with the other iPhone features you might want to use while driving, like a music player.
  • Apple maintains a list of every car model that right now supports CarPlay online.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most newer cars do, but there are a few exceptions.

Industry observers note that apple CarPlay is one of the most useful pieces of in-car software out there, unifying navigation with the other iPhone features you might want to use while driving, like a music player. It's good enough that it can be a selling point to help you decide between two cars when you're looking to buy one. Fortunately, it's extremely easy to tell whether your car supports Apple CarPlay, and there are a few options for integrating it even without built-in support.

Apple maintains a list of every car model that right now supports CarPlay online. The list is extensive, covering basically every new car model from major manufacturers. A few notable exceptions are Tesla and Rivian, which don't support CarPlay at all. GM previously attempted to pull away from supporting Apple's software on newer models in favor of its own version but has since added CarPlay back.

There are also a few ways to check in person if a particular car you're looking at supports wireless CarPlay. With Bluetooth and Wi-Fi on your iPhone turned on, also set the car's dashboard to Bluetooth or wireless. Press the voice command button on the car's steering wheel, then see if the car appears on the list of available devices in Settings > General > CarPlay on your iPhone.

If you can connect your phone to the car's USB port, you'll get a prompt to activate wired CarPlay if the car supports it. You can also check the dashboard screen for a CarPlay option or look for a CarPlay symbol on the USB port, though even supported cars may not have the symbol in every case.

It has been revealed that if you find yourself with a car that doesn't have integrated CarPlay support, there are a few ways you can add it yourself, though not without some hassle and expense. The easier method is to buy a third-party CarPlay screen to add to your car. Made by a variety of manufacturers, these screens can be mounted to your dashboard, essentially replacing your car's existing screen or adding one if you don't have one already. Most brands can interface with both CarPlay and Android Auto, letting you use all the software's functions on any vehicle. They're fairly inexpensive, typically around $100 or less, and can be moved from car to car. The downside is that you'll be relying on an extra piece of third-party hardware, and finding a good place to mount it can be tricky depending on your vehicle.

A permanent but more complicated solution is to install a CarPlay-compatible head unit. This will replace the car's stereo receiver (and screen if your car already has one) with a latest screen capable of using Apple CarPlay. This option will likely be more expensive than just buying a screen, though some units can still be found in the $100 range. You'll also have to go through a more complex installation process or pay someone to do it for you, but the advantage is having an integrated unit rather than an extra peripheral to wrangle.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A little over two years ago, SpaceX launched a Starship into orbit and then caught the Super Heavy booster when it returned to Earth, a feat it has since repeated multiple times. The organization is taking the next step in rocket reusability by catching both the booster and the upper stage of its Starship on Flight 15, something never achieved before.

Industry observers note that spaceX is launching Flight 15 into orbit on Friday, Nov. 13, with the 75-minute launch window opening at 5:45 p.m. ET.

In a recent development, on its mission, the Starship will deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites, orbit Earth 14 times and return on Saturday. All of that is in line with most of SpaceX’s launches, of which there have been over 280 dating back to 2025.

What makes the launch interesting is that SpaceX is attempting two things it hasn’t attempted before.

The first is catching its latest booster, the Super Heavy V3, using Mechazilla, the informal name SpaceX gave to the launch-and-catch tower located at its facility in Boca Chica, Texas. SpaceX has caught the Super Heavy V1 successfully three times, but this is the first for the V3 rocket. The tower will use its arms like chopsticks to catch the Super Heavy V3 out of midair.

It has been revealed that the second is recovering both stages of the rocket. Prior Starship launches featured just the Super Heavy booster getting caught by Mechazilla while the upper stage landed in the ocean. This time around, SpaceX wants to catch the upper stage when it returns on Saturday with Mechazilla.

“The upcoming flight is planned to be the first to return both Starship and Super Heavy to the launch site for catch,” SpaceX said in a statement. “If successful, this will mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system and a breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket.”.

SpaceX is streaming the flight from its X account and the company’s website. Coverage starts Friday at 5:15 p.m. ET, 30 minutes before the launch window opens.

The stream should continue through the launch and the Super Heavy V3 catch, expected approximately 6.5 minutes after launch. The organization promises “hours of live views” of Starship as it orbits Earth, offering viewers excellent views of the planet from space.

Sources indicate that spaceX hasn’t specified if it’s going to stream the entire mission, including the second catch when Starship returns to Earth on Saturday, Nov. 14. The expected time of arrival for that landing is 4:17 p.m. ET, assuming no delays or technical problems, which is a little more than 22 hours after launch. SpaceX streams from the same places every time, so if the manufacturer does stream it, the links above will be where to go.

Should the launch be delayed due to weather, technical complications or something else (after all, it is Friday the 13th), SpaceX has not declared a backup launch date at this time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I am traveling through Portugal now that Web Summit has wrapped up, so please enjoy this shortened edition.

Industry observers note that web Summit leaned heavily into Chinese founders and companies this year. The opening remarks from Web Summit co-founder Paddy Cosgrave drove the point home when he said the superstars of the future are coming from China, not California. He also gave a strong endorsement of China and open source technology when he noted that Chinese companies are building more of our shared future than anyone else.

These remarks carried a different kind of weight just a few days later as the news spread throughout the conference that Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang had resigned from his leadership post after admitting to an affair with an alleged spy.

Sources indicate that the former CEO, after all, has been one of the strongest proponents for open source in the United States. And anyone who has followed the emergence of autonomous vehicle tech knows how central Nvidia is to that ecosystem.

Recent findings suggest that nvidia is a major supplier of AI computing technology to the industry — although the degree of reliance varies. Some companies are using Nvidia’s automotive processors to run automated driving software, while others are using Nvidia GPUs to train autonomous driving models. And then there are the full-stack partnerships, which includes Mercedes-Benz, Zoox, and Wayve.

Sources indicate that I spoke to Leo Wang, the CFO of Chinese autonomous vehicle company Pony.ai, this week. I asked him about the challenges China’s self-driving industry faces and what he thinks will happen if the fallout from Huang’s resignation results in even stricter export controls on Nvidia chips shipped to China.

Demand is already far greater than supply, Wang noted, noting that it’s one of the pain points Pony.ai struggles with. The company’s strategy is twofold. Engineers are directed to be as efficient as possible when deploying its training models. That might mean using midtier compute resources instead of high-end ones, he said.

Pony.ai is also turning more to domestically produced chips to help close the gap.

In a recent development, “If you look at the whole ecosystem, especially in recent years, definitely domestic chips in China also get lots of attention and development,” he stated, noting that these chips provide another option for AI training. “I think that gives us some flexibility.”.

When asked what he thinks will happen if export restrictions on Nvidia chips tighten, Wang stated Chinese companies have already been preparing.

“If you look at the whole situation, this has been developing for already a couple of years,” he stated. “Everyone, I would say, is also practicing kind of like a Blueprint B for a few years, so at least if you think about that, I would say there are alternatives. #100. Tech Report: The paradox of AI safety

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (881 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thenextweb ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: The paradox of AI safety

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (881 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a child, I dreamed of understanding the universe.
  • Recent findings suggest that at Google DeepMind, I worked alongside some of the most brilliant and ambitious researchers in the world.
  • As the person responsible for making some of the most sensitive decisions about the data we would train Gemini on, I couldn’t ignore those questions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a child, I dreamed of understanding the universe. That dream eventually led me to physics, and later, somewhat unexpectedly, to artificial intelligence. I promptly found that AI offered the same intellectual thrill, along with an entirely upcoming mystery to explore: intelligence itself. The challenge got me hooked. What got me to stay was the growing discomfort around the way we were building it.

Recent findings suggest that at Google DeepMind, I worked alongside some of the most brilliant and ambitious researchers in the world. Yet, I could never quite understand how so many could be so absorbed in improving the models without ever questioning what we were actually building. It felt like way too few people truly cared what would happen once people started using them.

As the person responsible for making some of the most sensitive decisions about the data we would train Gemini on, I couldn’t ignore those questions. Besides, they rarely came with a straightforward answer. I took that responsibility so seriously that it often kept me up at night. In such a high-stakes environment, I obviously knew there was no guarantee my voice would be heard; still, I hoped being on the inside would allow me to make a difference.

In a recent development, when that hope vanished, the weight of a responsibility I could no longer meaningfully influence became too much to bear. I knew I couldn’t stay. Yet I left with a different fear: that one day, I would watch the consequences unfold from the outside, and perhaps regret having walked away.

It didn’t take long for my fears to feel justified. Leaving gave me the freedom to question the assumptions I had worked within. Having contributed to building some of the most powerful LLMs, I knew firsthand the limitations of how they learned from data. I wanted to go back to first principles instead of building yet another, better LLM, or tools to patch its weaknesses.

This is why I decided to start Dyssonance.

Today’s AI is good at remembering information. But remembering isn’t the same as understanding.

AI systems like ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini can process enormous amounts of information, answer complex questions, and carry on conversations. Yet they still struggle with something fundamental: making sense of conflicting information, recognizing when they’re wrong, and continuously updating what they understand.

We believe the next substantial breakthrough in AI won’t come from giving machines more information or larger memories. It will come from teaching them how to handle ambiguous situations.

Imagine reading dozens of books but never connecting the ideas, questioning contradictions, or changing your opinions when you learn something new.

It’s one of the most significant limitations we see in AI today.

True intelligence isn’t just about collecting facts. It’s about understanding how those facts fit together, recognizing when something doesn’t make sense, and adjusting your thinking as upcoming information becomes available.

AI needs to move beyond remembering more to understanding better.

According to recent reports, today’s AI is largely built around language. It learns patterns in words and uses them to generate responses.

But communicating an idea and actually understanding it are two different things.

We’ve taken a different approach to AI: building a system that develops and continuously refines its own understanding of information; a common-sense reasoning engine.

Instead of simply storing facts, these systems would maintain evolving interpretations that can change as new evidence emerges.

Think of it as the difference between memorizing the answers to a test and truly understanding the subject.

Some of our greatest discoveries begin when something doesn’t add up.

Scientists question unexpected results. Detectives investigate conflicting clues. Entrepreneurs recognize problems others have overlooked.

We believe intelligence works much the same way.

When new information conflicts with what we think we know, that contradiction creates an opportunity to learn.

For the first time, AI now has the ability to call out these dissonances.

Rather than ignoring contradictions or simply storing more information, AI should actively work to resolve them.

The ability to recognize what doesn’t make sense, and figure out why, is the very definition of intelligence.

Our vision goes beyond making AI better at answering questions.

We want to help build the underlying technology that allows AI systems to reason, learn, adapt, and develop a more consistent interpretation of the world.

Think of it as creating a foundation that different AI capabilities can share, rather than asking one system to do everything.

With this approach, AI could become more adaptable, its reasoning easier to evaluate, and its capabilities easier to improve and combine.

Dyssonance exists to rethink the foundations of artificial intelligence.

We believe the future of AI isn’t simply about bigger models, faster answers, or more powerful memory.

It’s about building systems that can continually question, learn, adapt, and make better sense of the world.

The future of AI isn’t about remembering more. It’s about understanding better.

Sources indicate that contributed by Dr. Jennifer Prendki, PhD.

How to get warnings about speed cameras in Apple CarPlay

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (668 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • CarPlay is just the messenger, while your navigation app does all the hard work.
  • Sources indicate that with all the rage and controversy over Flock cameras, speed cameras (or speed traps) have taken a back seat.
  • Industry observers note that mobile speed detectors (in some form or another) have been around since the first speeding arrest in the US in 1899.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CarPlay is just the messenger, while your navigation app does all the hard work.

Sources indicate that with all the rage and controversy over Flock cameras, speed cameras (or speed traps) have taken a back seat. Most of us have to deal with speed cameras (though they're banned in some states and limited in others), and Apple CarPlay is one way to handle them. While CarPlay itself doesn't send out speed camera warnings, alerts can be turned on for whichever navigation app you use. It stands to reason that Apple CarPlay owners default to Apple Maps, but there are other, equally useful alternatives like Waze and Google Maps. There's always a caveat, however. Regardless of the nav app you use, mobile speed traps, by definition, move around a lot. Unless someone reports the fresh position on a given app, you won't get a warning.

Industry observers note that mobile speed detectors (in some form or another) have been around since the first speeding arrest in the US in 1899. A NYC taxicab driver named Jacob German was caught going 12 mph in an Electrobat (nearly the speed of light back then) in an 8 mph zone. The mobile units in those days were police officers on bicycles. Fortunately, modern technology provides drivers with information as it changes, but there's no such thing as a navigation app that knows where every camera is at all times.

According to recent reports, in Apple Maps, there is no camera switch to toggle on or off. Camera alerts are automatic in supported regions. Waze, a compatible CarPlay navigation app, turns camera alerts on by default. You have the option to fine-tune them as well. In the Waze app, open Settings > Alerts and Reports > Reports > Cameras. Each camera type has its own toggles for "Show on map" and "Alert while driving." Make sure any changes made in the Waze app take place before connecting to CarPlay, because Waze only applies them the next time you connect and go for a drive.

Google Maps is similar yet has slightly different settings. On CarPlay, tap "Report" to pinpoint a mobile speed camera so other drivers can see when using the app. If you want information provided by other drivers, open Google Maps in CarPlay and tap Settings > Alert options > All alerts.

Some navigation apps will send warning alerts without actively navigating, as long as the app is running passively in the background. Radarbot sends alerts for fixed and red light cameras through CarPlay if you have a Gold membership. Roadar adds Flock cameras to the mix, along with other license plate readers mixed in, with speed and red light camera alerts. If you're more concerned about Flock cameras, FlockHopper is free and works with CarPlay as well.

In a recent development, it can, though it depends on what navigation app you're using. With Apple Maps, the Speed Limit toggle is in Settings > Apps > Maps > Driving. The posted limit will appear on screen while you navigate. With the Waze app, make sure you're disconnected from CarPlay, open Waze and tap Settings > Speedometer > Show Speedometer > Set Preferences > Show Speed Limit. Google Maps is similar to Waze, with the speed limit located in the speedometer settings. Open the Google Maps app, tap your profile picture and tap Settings > Navigation > Driving > Speedometer.

Sources indicate that stock CarPlay doesn't include a speedometer, but apps like Waze and Google Maps will display current speeds through CarPlay if you want. Both Google Maps and Waze will warn you if your speeds climb too high, and Waze will give you a heads-up if speed limits are about to drop sharply. In response to car manufacturers ditching CarPlay, Apple introduced CarPlay Ultra, which displays your current speed on the instrument cluster, unlike regular CarPlay. CarPlay Ultra is fully integrated, so it's not an informational speed display, as Google Maps makes clear about its own speedometer.
