#97. Millions of Americans are not taking their GLP-1 drugs as prescribed

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (577 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Millions of Americans are not taking their GLP-1 drugs as prescribed

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (577 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GLP-1 medications are everywhere these days.
  • In a study published this week, researchers at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention broke down survey data of GLP-1 use collected between July and August of 2025.
  • Among GLP-1 people, nearly half (44 percent) reported using their GLP-1 in a way that was different from how it was prescribed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GLP-1 medications are everywhere these days. The peptide-based drugs are both highly effective and wildly popular for diabetes, weight loss and a growing range of connected chronic health conditions, including cardiovascular disease and obstructive sleep apnea. But, amid the boom, the latest data suggests millions of Americans have turned to unapproved versions and are using the potent drugs in ways doctors never intended, raising questions about what that real-world use means for safety and efficacy.

In a study published this week, researchers at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention broke down survey data of GLP-1 use collected between July and August of 2025. Based on responses from over 8,000 US adults, the researchers estimate that about one in 10 US adults (9.8 percent) used a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, aka GLP-1 medication, in 2025. That’s around 27 million adults. The study was published in the CDC’s Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report.

Among GLP-1 people, nearly half (44 percent) reported using their GLP-1 in a way that was different from how it was prescribed. Users skipped doses, delayed getting refills, and used smaller doses than prescribed, among other changes. More than half of the people modifying how they used the drug stated the changes were because of cost or availability reasons. Cost and access barriers were most pronounced among younger GLP-1 users. Fifty-eight percent of adults 14­–39 years old who modified their use cited cost as a barrier, compared with just 20 percent of adults 65 or older who said the same.

Modified use of GLP-1 medications was particularly common among those using compounded versions of GLP-1 medications. Among all GLP-1 customers, at least 23 percent used a compounded version; an additional 9 percent said they didn’t know whether their GLP-1 was compounded or not.

These versions of GLP-1 drugs are made by compounding pharmacies and are intended to mimic a medication approved by the Food and Drug Administration, such as Wegovy or Ozempic. But compounded drugs themselves are not approved by the FDA; the regulatory agency does not review their safety, effectiveness, or quality before they’re sold. While compounded drugs are considered more accessible and affordable, they generally have higher rates of preparation errors, contamination, and other manufacturing problems compared to non-compounded drugs.

According to recent reports, among people who used these unapproved, potentially riskier GLP-1s, 62 percent were not taking them as prescribed. That’s compared to just 36 percent of GLP-1 people who took brand-name drugs.

In a recent development, the potential risks of taking unapproved GLP-1 drugs at all or taking them in unapproved ways may be missed by consumers, the CDC researchers note. A 2025 study assessing websites selling compounded GLP-1 medications found that nearly 40 percent of sites stated or implied the drugs were FDA-approved, making it harder for consumers to differentiate the compounded versions from FDA-approved ones. Further, nearly 80 percent of sites used brand names in their advertising, which could further mislead consumers. The researchers noted that using brand names violated FDA regulatory standards.

“Given the substantial use of compounded GLP-1 medications, understanding the safety and quality of compounded GLP-1 medications is an vital public health consideration,” the authors conclude. They also call for more research on the common modifications people are using, such as dose and frequency adjustments, saying the data on the safety and effectiveness of these real-world practices “could help guide the development and implementation of clinical guidelines and support appropriate medication use.”.

  • Sources indicate that then, you can pull up @Google Wallet in Gemini to roast — or more respectfully, analyze — your purchase history.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that google is giving Gemini another way to make itself useful by connecting the AI assistant to Google Wallet. The integration opens up possibilities for spending summaries and budgeting suggestions, making Gemini more like a personal financial assistant.

According to recent reports, starting today, users in the US on Android, iOS and the web can link Google Wallet to the Gemini app via Plaid, a third party service that connects bank and credit card accounts. The integration is done through Gemini’s Connected Apps feature, which gives the assistant access to information from supported Google services.

Sources indicate that then, you can pull up @Google Wallet in Gemini to roast — or more respectfully, analyze — your purchase history. Gemini can then visualize cash flow, track asset allocation and help you build budgets based on actual spending rather than rough estimates.

Google has some real-world examples. You can ask Gemini to look at your spending last quarter and find a way to save $1,000 over the next three months. It can also identify recurring subscriptions, flag services that increased their prices, and use last year’s holiday spending to suggest a more realistic budget for the next shopping season.

Sources indicate that of course, there are some reasonable privacy questions about giving an AI access to your financial activity. According to Google, Gemini can view your information, but it can't transfer money, manage accounts, make investments or complete transactions. You can also control the connection and turn it on or off anytime you want.

The feature is part of Google’s broader Personal Intelligence push, which already ties Gemini to services like Gmail, Google Photos, YouTube, and Search.

In a recent development, to try it, open Gemini, go to Settings, tap Personal Intelligence>Connected Apps, and add Google Wallet. You can also prompt @Google Wallet to start with a tag.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

Industry observers note that the expansion makes Gemini more useful for people who want help keeping their finances organized, though giving an AI access to transaction history won't be for everyone. At least Google isn’t handing over the keys to your bank account.

It's not hard to guess whether consumers will trust Gemini enough to incorporate it into their financial routine. But at least, for now, Google is keeping the assistant on the advisory side of the equation.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tired of moving solar-powered Christmas lights, a seventh grader built a tracker that lets gravity do the work.
  • Industry observers note that jason Chang was sick of his mother asking him to adjust the family's solar-powered Christmas lights to get more sun, so he devised a solution with big potential.
  • The prototype was less than $25 and generated about 20 percent more voltage than a stationary panel in outdoor tests, CBS Boston reports.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tired of moving solar-powered Christmas lights, a seventh grader built a tracker that lets gravity do the work.

Industry observers note that jason Chang was sick of his mother asking him to adjust the family's solar-powered Christmas lights to get more sun, so he devised a solution with big potential. The 13-year-old seventh grader at Worcester Academy in Massachusetts created a solar tracker that utilizes water and gravity to move a solar panel without the need for a motor, a sunlight sensor or electricity to power the mechanism.

The prototype was less than $25 and generated about 20 percent more voltage than a stationary panel in outdoor tests, CBS Boston reports. The contraption tackles a basic limitation of fixed solar panels: the inability to change position as the sun moves across the sky. This teenager's bright idea is attracting national attention. Here's how it works.

Chang's invention is similar to a seesaw. A small solar panel is mounted on a rotating wooden structure, with water dripping into a bucket on one side. The frame tilts the panel throughout the day as the bucket fills, increasing its weight. There's no sensor needed to determine the sun's position, and the drip rate is adjusted to keep the panel tilting at approximately the correct speed.

Recent findings suggest that it's not difficult to get the process started. Simply pull the plug to set the water in motion. However, it took a lot more work to get that flow just right. Chang spent over a year refining the project, jotting down his tests in a notebook and using recycled materials for much of the construction. And while gravity is free of cost, trying to make it work on a schedule takes a little engineering.

The reported 20 percent improvement also needs to be examined. In the outdoor comparisons, Chang's setup was able to generate higher voltage, but that doesn't necessarily translate to a 20 percent increase in power or total energy output. To calculate those gains, current readings and energy measurements over time would be required, but were not included in the report. It's a positive outcome for a student prototype, but not a guarantee to save you 20 percent on your electric bill.

Using water and gravity to follow the sun isn't entirely latest. There are commercial trackers on the market that can move with the sun, but they cost more than fixed units. There are also some build-it-yourself designs similar to Chang's concept. Engineering for Change promotes a SunSaluter rotating solar panel kit with a suggested retail price of $50. That cost doesn't include the panel, battery, and other components. Chang's version offers another inexpensive DIY take on the idea, rather than a commercially ready replacement for existing trackers.

In a recent development, there's a practical reason why most rooftop solar panels aren't designed to move around. Trackers can boost energy yields from ground-mounted arrays, but they also add costs and maintenance. It's easy to tilt a small wooden frame, but mounting moving panels on a roof where they have to withstand wind and rain is where it gets complicated. Any extra electricity would have to be worth the investment and maintenance. Another fixed panel might be a lot less hassle for some homeowners.

It has been revealed that sure, motor-free tracking could still appeal to people running small off-grid systems, where every bit of power counts. However, water has its own set of issues. While cold weather can actually boost solar panel efficiency, a mechanism that relies on flowing water has an unwelcome winter issue: ice, which is why Chang is working on a winter version.

CBS did not say how often the water needs to be refilled, how often the tracker needs to be reset, or whether the design has been tested with full-size panels in strong winds. Regardless, Chang's work as a seventh-grader is exceptional. In 2026, he was one of 55 students recognized as National STEM Champions.

Flaming Hydra’s newly introduced Kickstarter campaign rethinks e-book ownership and digital lending

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s a big promise: A fresh Kickstarter campaign aims to usher in the “return of the human internet.”.

Recent findings suggest that that’s the tagline of a crowdfunding campaign for The Phoenix Project, an initiative from the online culture and commentary magazine Flaming Hydra. If you back The Phoenix Project, you’re supporting three things — a one-off print magazine designed to celebrate “the values and fun of the early internet,” a new e-book service for libraries, and a newsletter subscription/archiving program that’s also designed for libraries.

To Flaming Hydra’s lead editor Maria Bustillos, these disparate projects are “basically all one thing,” tied together by the goal of “protecting freedom of information” and fulfilling the “promise of the early internet, where you’re making information available to as many people as possible, while still protecting the right of artists and authors to make a living.”.

According to recent reports, bustillos told me that these problems have been highlighted on Flaming Hydra itself, for example when Tal Levin wrote about finding countless AI-generated clones of his book on Amazon. By “creating an ecosystem that is based in people working together, who are offering their stuff in a context that is controlled and doesn’t allow” others to create and sell AI-generated clones, Bustillos mentioned Flaming Hydra is “part of the human project.”.

Recent findings suggest that “AI is not this unstoppable force,” she added. “If people just set up publishing pipelines and networks and organizations that are dedicated to the human internet, people who want to read stuff can go to them, and it’s actually completely isolated from mechanistic interference.”.

The Phoenix Project fits into this vision by making the work of human writers more accessible to libraries.

In a recent development, back in 2020, Bustillos wrote about the e-book systems dominating libraries and schools. In one example, instead of just buying a book, a school had to pay $27 per student per year for continued access to copies of “The Diary of Anne Frank.”.

In a recent development, this is symptomatic of a broader system that treats true ownership of e-books and other digital media as a thing of the past. Instead, we “license” these e-books from their publishers, and they can be altered or removed at any time.

“E-books are books,” Bustillos said. “They’re not some other thing. They are books, and people should be able to own them, and libraries should be able to own them, and media should be able to be owned. All digital media should be able to be owned.”.

In her view, ownership boils down to a simple question: “If you are at the mercy of somebody who can shut the book off, you do not own it.”.

Sources indicate that so even beyond the question of ongoing payments, there have also been examples of e-books being altered or removed from readers’ devices long after their purchase. Bustillos acknowledged that for individual pieces of media, this distinction may not seem like a big deal, “but if it’s all the textbooks for everybody, if it’s all the books,” then it’s a real problem.

Flaming Hydra and The Phoenix Project seek to solve this by letting libraries truly purchase and own e-books. They can then lend those e-books to their patrons through a newly introduced, open source “library in a box” system called Lenny for Libraries.

The Phoenix Project is starting by offering five fresh e-books from Flaming Hydra writers, including collections of writing from The Awl, and of essays by Tom Scocca and Bustillos herself. That might sound like a relatively small start, but Bustillos remarked she’s talking to library consortiums and author groups, and the goal here is to “change the conversation” around e-books and digital archiving and lending. So The Phoenix Project could be paving the way for other initiatives that follow a similar model.

It has been revealed that similarly, The Phoenix Foundry Archive is designed to make paywalled newsletter content available to libraries. Bustillos noted that “so much of the best journalism, criticism, essays” is now being published in paywalled newsletters that are inaccessible to libraries (as well as the Internet Archive).

Sources indicate that flaming Hydra has been working on all this even before launching the Kickstarter, and Bustillos mentioned she was grateful for the financial support from backers like Anand Raganathan, Brewster Kahle, and Paul Ford. But by turning to crowdfunding, Bustillos said Flaming Hydra can better protect the work, ensuring that it remains sustainable and independent.

Industry observers note that “We don’t have to be at the mercy of anybody, and it also protects editorial independence,” she noted. “Those things go hand in hand.”.

Flaming Hydra seeks to raise $30,000 for The Phoenix Project, with the campaign ending on November 27.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Federal Administration lifted its third-ever nationwide ground stop after several hours Friday evening.
  • “Today’s nationwide ground stop happened because our air traffic control system is operating on DECADES-OLD analog equipment that simply cannot compete with the demands of the 21st century,” Duffy posted on X.
  • Sources indicate that over a million travelers have been affected by the delays, with some airlines cancelling flights for the remainder of Friday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Federal Administration lifted its third-ever nationwide ground stop after several hours Friday evening. Domestic flights were cleared to begin taking off at 8:35 pm EST. FAA Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy cautioned that, barring massive system updates, there will be “more of these” ahead.

“Today’s nationwide ground stop happened because our air traffic control system is operating on DECADES-OLD analog equipment that simply cannot compete with the demands of the 21st century,” Duffy posted on X.

Sources indicate that over a million travelers have been affected by the delays, with some airlines cancelling flights for the remainder of Friday. “Due to the ongoing ground stop, Air Canada has cancelled all flights to and from the United States for the remainder of the evening,” the airline said.

Recent findings suggest that the stoppage began at 3:36 pm EST Friday afternoon, days after expanding use of an AI tool, when the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop, halting departures from all US airports. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy declared the ground stop on X, citing a “communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.” Duffy promised updates as more information is known and stated FAA staff was troubleshooting the problem.

Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that the ground stop was not prompted by a security threat. “This is a telecommunications outage out of the FAA. Out of an abundance of caution, we have grounded all of the flights,” Mullin said. “There’s no indication as of yet that this is a nefarious attack against us.”.

Mullin had remarked the FAA would handle incoming international flights on a case-by-case basis.

Industry observers note that this was only the third nationwide ground stop issued by the FAA. The first, and most memorable, came during the attacks of September 11, 2001, when the FAA stopped all civilian departures nationwide and subsequently ordered all airborne aircraft to land. Commercial flights did not take off again until September 13. Flights were also grounded for less than two hours the morning of January 11, 2023, after its Notice to Air Missions system suffered an outage.

In a recent development, unfortunately for travelers, it turned out to be a lengthy ground stop. Airlines were quick to cancel flights scheduled to leave later in the day, with American Airlines warning that disruptions were expected for the rest of the day.

“This is going to take some time,” Mullin mentioned. “Flights are accounted for, and there should be no fear to the public at all.”.

This story was updated at 10:03 pm EST to report the ground stop was lifted.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that you’ve probably seen a smart bird feeder or know someone who has one. The best smart bird feeders are easily recognizable with their clear housing, cameras, and solar panels. Perhaps a friend or family member has sent you a photo or video of a bright goldfinch or a handsome woodpecker (guilty). But are these feeders really worth their $100-plus price tag? Are they durable? And what about the squirrel problem?

Sources indicate that to answer these questions, I’ve been testing the most popular smart bird feeders, including models from Birdfy and Birdbuddy, for more than two years—in rain, snow, and heat, and in a yard with persistent varmints. I’ve explored the apps and notification settings, examined the photo and video quality, noted which features are hidden behind a subscription paywall, and used Cornell Lab’s All About Birds—as well as Google Lens and my own expertise—to verify the accuracy of AI identifications. The recommendations below are what I would buy with my own money, having tested dozens of brands and models for a minimum of four weeks each.

Recent findings suggest that updated November 2026: I’ve added the Birdbuddy Nook as a upcoming Best Budget pick, Kiwibit's Feeder 2 Pro as an Honorable Mention, and information on Birdfy's rollout of free AI ID. I've also removed a couple of discontinued feeders and updated links and prices.

According to recent reports, this cheery blue- or yellow-roofed feeder, from security company Netvue, was the first smart feeder WIRED tested, back in 2022, when it earned a 6/10 rating due to its high price and wonky AI. Both metrics have improved dramatically since then—Birdfy's app is now the second-most user-friendly on the market, behind only Birdbuddy's, and this feeder is often on sale for around $130. Its AI identification, which is decent, used to be paywalled but is now free with every tier of feeder.

The 1080p/2K camera isn't the best quality you'll find, but it does have one of the widest viewing angles of any smart feeder, at 155 degrees, so you're more likely to get full bird shots, as opposed to just heads and butts. The plastic housing (available in blue or yellow) also makes this feeder durable and easy to clean, and the 50-ounce seed reservoir is super easy to fill with its convenient flip-up top. Not all bundles come with a solar panel, but you can buy one separately. Unlike with other feeders, the solar panel is not built in and needs to be mounted and connected separately with the included 9.8-foot charging cable.

It's not the fanciest feeder on the market, nor the one with the best camera, but I've never had a problem with the two models I've been rotating in and out throughout the years, and the reliability and price point make it the best bet for most backyard birders.

Target (Solar + Extended Perch).

Birdbuddy's brand-new Nook model is a lot of bird feeder for the price; it won our recent head-to-head test of sub-$100 smart feeders. The base $99 model doesn't come with a solar roof or extended perch, as seen in the photo above, but you will get a 2K HDR camera that can shoot vertically or horizontally (it pops in and out via a magnet), as well as the same sturdy, high-quality construction as Birdbuddy's pricier Home model. The seed capacity isn't the greatest at 0.9 liters, but the app is easy to use and can even identify birds nearby that don't land on the feeder, so long as its excellent onboard microphone hears their sounds.

It has been revealed that birdbuddy's Achilles’ heel has always been its sensor, which is slow to wake up and regularly misses bird visits. The new Birdbuddy feeder supposedly has a faster wake-up time than previous models, and though it still lagged behind Birdfy's competing Rookie feeder in capturing all visits, the Nook's rate was substantially better than the Home's. It also has more mounting options, allowing for hanging in addition to wall and pole mounts (though the latter is a loose fit), and allows for no-cost manual AI ID of all visitors.

Recent findings suggest that camojojo's original Hibird feeder has long been a reliable model in my testing stable, one of the first to run on both 2.4-GHz and 5-GHz Wi-Fi bands, and last year saw the debut of an upgraded model, the Hibird Pro. The update has built-in solar panels, an option for pole-mounting, and supposedly improved AI identification, though it still frequently misidentifies even common birds in my West Coast backyard as East Coast species. The app is not as streamlined or user-friendly as Birdfy's or Birdbuddy's, but it's still easy enough to navigate, with options for changing video length (default is 10 seconds) or viewing in slo-mo. The default media type it saves is video, though this is 4K Ultra HD, and the images are—as expected—extremely sharp. Without a subscription, you can't search past videos by bird, and cloud storage is capped at 5 GB over 60 days; however, the feeder does come with a 128-GB SD card. You'll also get “smarter” chats with the app's AI Q&A function, “Dr. Bird,” and the ability to share across two devices with a subscription ($45 per year or $4 per month).

Industry observers note that I appreciate the generous 1.5-liter seed hopper, although this, combined with the solar panel and battery, makes it extremely heavy. When filled, it tips the scales at 5 pounds, meaning that if you do pole-mount it, you will need to use both included hose clamps and wrench them tightly. I also wouldn't attempt to mount it on anything unstable, like a wobbly fence. Other original Hibird features that made it to the Pro include the little handles on the assembly screws (so you won't need any assembly tools) and the chunky plastic body. The latter was subjected to a little bit of squirrel-chewing during my test, but it still held up well.

Recent findings suggest that the Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 is one of the most thoughtfully designed feeders on the market. You don't have to take down the whole feeder when refilling, as the 1.5-liter dual-hopper plastic seed reservoir is removable from the body. The 8-megapixel photos and 4K HD video have much better quality than you'll find from most competitors, and the components come apart for easy cleaning. I also tested the original version, which features a separate solar panel, and my only complaint was that the panel stopped charging the camera after about six weeks. This version features a built-in solar roof, which did an excellent job keeping the feeder charged during its six-week-long test, even on cloudy days. The plastic body is extremely thick and sturdy, and unlike lighter-weight feeders like Birdfy's, it's designed to hold up in more extreme weather.

The app is easy to navigate, and the whole setup is functional without a Kiwibit Plus subscription ($90/year, purchasable online or through the Kiwibit app) but you'll be losing out on a lot of features, including 60-day storage and the ability to record up to three minutes of video if a bird is doing something interesting—a unique feature among smart feeders, and one I discovered that I love. (There's nothing more frustrating than having a video cut off right as a bird is about to do something funny.) This smart feeder costs a bit much for what it is, but if you know you like having a smart feeder, I think it's worth the investment. Note, however, that it only works on 2.4-GHz Wi-Fi, and the warranty is half the length you get from many competitors. I also tested Kiwibit's newer model, the Feeder 2 Pro, and while its camera does have an interesting auto-zoom lens, I didn't think it was worth the $120 premium over this model.

In a recent development, birdbuddy is known for its user-friendliness and thoughtful app—its Pro Smart Hummingbird Feeder is no exception. The feeder is intuitive and easy to use, and you don't need a subscription to access fun features like AI identification, 5 MP photos, and 2K HD video with slo-mo. A subscription unlocks features like family sharing and a higher bit rate, but the feeder is perfectly functional without those. With the panel being built into the feeder's roof, there’s also no auxiliary solar panel to worry about. Pairing with your phone is a cinch, integrating it into the Birdbuddy app with other feeders is a snap, and even refilling it is no problem. Unlike other hummingbird feeders that have weirdly cavernous capacities and/or need to be filled upside down, the Birdbuddy’s bottom screws off and holds a reasonable 1.75 cups of liquid. This detail is notable; as the Cornell Lab of Ornithology points out, the easier it is to clean a hummingbird feeder, the more likely you are to do it often and well.

According to recent reports, this feeder also comes with extra plastic flowers and a little brush for scrubbing them, and the app sends reminders when it's time to clean. You'll find fun, seasonal touches in the app, like the ability to send digital bird holiday cards with the photos your feeder captures, and a tool that superimposes hats, clothes, and various accessories on the birds, which is actually funnier than it sounds. However, as with the Birdbuddy seed feeders, the big downside is that the feeder's sensor doesn’t always pick up every bird that visits. This can definitely be a bummer, particularly when you see something interesting out the window but it doesn’t show up in the app.

After experiencing connection problems with the Birdfy Polygon, I swapped it out for the newer Birdfy Nest Duo and have had no issues. The sleek, contemporary Duo is a fir box fitted with two cameras—one facing the hole and one tucked discreetly inside the feeder. That gives you a full-spectrum view of what's going on. Both cameras have night vision (the internal one is infrared). Like the Polygon, the Duo sports a remote for rebooting and recharging the camera (though the separate solar panel, which can be pole-mounted, has kept the cameras reliably charged), as well as different-size holes for different species, each with its own chew-proof predator guard.

There's a metal grate with drainage holes that you can slot into grooves in the lower third of the Nest to make the cavity larger or smaller. Birdfy's user-friendly app presents 2K HD images and video with free lifetime AI ID, and it's easy to share photos and videos with others. There's a solar panel you can mount separately, but I didn't do this and was impressed that the camera ran for nearly two months on an indoor USB-C charge.

What to Look for When Buying a Smart Bird Feeder.

The world of smart bird feeders is vast and can seem overwhelming, but there are some key features that will really make a difference in your user experience. I've tested dozens of feeders for years from many different brands, and this is what I think you should pay attention to when comparing models.

Industry observers note that subscription: Most, if not all, smart bird feeders require a subscription to access all features. That's in order to support the manufacturer's continued investment in user experience. There are few things more disappointing than giving or receiving a smart bird feeder as a gift, only to find out it's not actually usable without shelling out an additional $70 a year. Reputable companies will note subscription requirements up front, and some even offer models that have a lifetime subscription built in. Note that if a feeder costs less than a hundred bucks, odds are it will require a subscription to capture photos, whether it says so in the marketing materials or not. You will need to do your due diligence before buying.

Recent findings suggest that mounting options: If you live in an area with squirrels, your best bet is to pole-mount your bird feeder—especially a more expensive smart feeder, which often has cords that squirrels and other rodents like to chew. Not all feeders offer a pole-mounting option, though, which is another important detail to confirm before buying.

Wi-Fi network: The vast majority of smart feeders only work on 2.4-GHz Wi-Fi frequencies. If you only use 5 GHz, you will need to look for a feeder that specifically works with a shorter transmission range or has dual range, such as the Camojojo Hibird, above.

App: An app can make or break your smart bird feeder experience since it's where all of your bird viewing, sorting, and saving will take place. Apps with added features like useful facts, the capacity to share feeds with others, quality AI identification, and the ability to sort by bird are sometimes worth the added cost over a less-expensive feeder. Many companies use security cameras in their bird feeders that don't have a separate app—this means you'll just get a utilitarian list of image captures with no detail or context. To help buyers with their decision-making, I am currently building a rubric to grade and rank smart bird feeder apps, which I hope to add to this guide within the next couple of months.

How Does WIRED Test Bird Feeders?

I test all feeders in my rural-suburban backyard in the Pacific Northwest. I mount seed feeders on a 1-inch pole with a baffle, using the provided mounting hardware and hose clamps. If pole-mounting isn't feasible, I mount on a fence or a shepherd's hook. I hang hummingbird feeders from a shepherd's hook mounted on the side of my house. I fill the seed feeders with Audubon Wild Park bird seed and the hummingbird feeders with a nectar mixture of 4-to-1 granulated sugar and water. I keep each feeder up for a minimum of four weeks, with all app notifications enabled.

Recent findings suggest that I look at all app features available both with a subscription and without, seeing how often I get notifications and noting whether they are accurately picking up just birds or any type of outdoor movement, and how well the AI feature is able to distinguish bird species. I also look at connectivity, seed capacity, video quality, and how well the feeder bodies hold up to squirrels and inclement weather.

Sources indicate that the majority of feeders I tested were provided as press samples by the tech giant. I keep some for longer-term testing, put others in storage for future testing or comparison purposes, and donate others locally via the Buy Nothing Project.

What Do I Need to Know Before Setting Up a Smart Feeder?

Why Do Most Smart Feeders Only Run on 2.4 GHz?

This section was inspired by an email from a reader who installs home Wi-Fi systems and did not appreciate my recommending a feeder that has the option to run on 5 GHz. He's not wrong that this isn't the preferred band for a smart bird feeder, but I'll explain why someone might want 5 GHz below.

First off, what is 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz? In simplest terms, these are the main radio frequency bands Wi-Fi uses to send data wirelessly between your smart bird feeder and your router. One gigahertz (GHz) is 1 billion hertz, the unit of measurement for how fast radio waves oscillate. Both bands are the accepted standards for Wi-Fi, which yes, is a name brand.

It follows, then, that 2.4-GHz waves oscillate more slowly than 5-GHz waves. This also means the slower waves can travel farther and pass through walls and other obstacles more effectively. With Wi-Fi-enabled products placed outside the home, the ability to penetrate walls, trees, and other potential barriers is more crucial than speed. These slower waves also result in less power consumption by devices. It makes sense that 2.4 GHz would be a preferable band for a smart bird feeder, which likely would be in or near a tree-filled area.

However, 2.4 GHz is a more crowded band and thus prone to interference from other Wi-Fi networks and devices, so it can be less stable. It also results in slower overall performance, leading to sluggish downloads and lag during streaming and video calls. Most modern routers offer both 2.4-GHz and 5-GHz bands, but some may be configured (for whatever reason) to broadcast only 5 GHz. Other routers feature something called band steering, which automatically diverts devices to the less-crowded 5 GHz. A smart bird feeder that offers dual connectivity simply provides more options. If the bird feeder is right outside your window where the router is located, you may want the faster speed. Or maybe you just don't want to try to figure out how to turn off band steering. If you're not dialed in to your router, no pun intended, it may make sense for you to consider a bird feeder with dual-band connectivity.

As is the case with any bird feeder, squirrels love to eat at smart bird feeders, most of which are not squirrel-proof, regardless of marketing claims. However, most of the smart feeders we’ve tested are just as sturdy, if not in some cases sturdier, than analog bird feeders. The worst-case scenario is likely the squirrel eating all the seed, chewing the edges, and covering up the camera with its fuzzy butt.

The yard where I test smart feeders year-round is lousy with the large and persistent rodents, and the squirrel damage I’ve sustained on test feeders has been minor. With the Birdfy Pro Duo, above, the animals chewed off the edges to better get at the seed supply when it was low, and the FeatherSnap Scout had its mounting bent. Top of mind is the 5-7-9 method of siting a bird feeder—at least 5 feet off the ground, at least 7 feet away from any structures, and at least 9 feet away from anything a squirrel could jump from (branches, fences, roofs). I explain this in more detail in my guide to keeping squirrels away from your bird feeder.

Another option is an aftermarket baffle added to feeders hanging on shepherd’s hooks, or a pole with a built-in baffle, like this one from Birdfy. Or you could use seed treated with capsaicin, or hot pepper. The taste doesn't affect birds, since they don’t have capsaicin receptors like mammals do. That noted, I’ve found capsaicin only keeps squirrels away for a couple of days, whether because they’ve gotten used to it or the pepper loses its potency when exposed to the elements. As a last resort, you could always just learn to live with the squirrels and dedicate a feeder to them, although my neighbor does this, and I'm of the mind that doing so brings even more squirrels to the area.

SNL sketches often go viral, but it's not often they generate quite this much conversation.

On Saturday, SNL featured a pre-taped skit called "Sister" — a parody ad narrated by a man (this week's host John Mulaney) struggling to find care for his ageing father.

Industry observers note that "My dad means the world to me," Mulaney says in the sketch. "So when I noticed him start to slow down, I knew I needed to get him the best care possible. I didn't want to put him in a nursing home, but a private health aid could cost thousands a week. I didn't know where to turn. That's when I heard about...Sister. Sister is a live-in, 24/7 elder care provider that is completely free, and also your sister.

"Now I don't have to worry about my dad getting the care and attention he needs, because my sister will do it. And I can get back to my life, and the stuff I like to do.".

Although the sketch made people laugh, it also filled many — including people who have found themselves in the situation depicted in the ad — with rage.

Recent findings suggest that sounds like "Sister" may end up acting as a WhatsApp family group chat shorthand for families going through a similar situation. Invisible labor has never been so succinctly demonstrated.

HBO Max — top pick for premium content.

Disney+ — best for families.

Hulu — popular choice for originals.

Peacock — low-cost choice for live sport.

The manufacturer hasn't shed any light on when Quick Measure or AR Doodle might return, or if it will move their features into other offerings.

As long as you're quick on the draw, you can download Quick Measure and AR Doodle to compatible devices from Samsung's Galaxy Store.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that an open letter asking Nvidia’s board to bring back Jensen Huang had more than 175,000 names on Monday, four days after he resigned as chief executive.
  • It asks the board to reinstate Huang while an independent investigation runs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang at NVIDIA GTC 2026 in San Jose.

It has been revealed that an open letter asking Nvidia’s board to bring back Jensen Huang had more than 175,000 names on Monday, four days after he resigned as chief executive. The Stand with Jensen site counted 8,766 people who say they work at Nvidia. It puts that at about 21% of the company’s 42,000 staff. Every affiliation on the site is self-reported, and TNW has not verified the signatures.

The letter makes three demands. It asks the board to reinstate Huang while an independent investigation runs. It wants the inquiry’s scope and timeline disclosed, with a hearing for Huang before any final decision. And it asks for a public explanation of the concerns behind his exit.

“Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice,” the letter indicates.

The site also urges institutional investors to raise the matter on Nvidia’s earnings call on Tuesday, 17 November, at 5pm ET.

In a recent development, the site lists Elon Musk first among its public signers, dated 13 November, the day after Huang stepped down. It also indicates 26 people who describe themselves as vice presidents or above at Nvidia. The letter notes it is not endorsed by Nvidia or by Huang.

It has been revealed that the count has not been clean. Business Insider reported on Saturday that the organisers, who post as @TheJensenLetter on X, were removing fake signatures. The tally then stood at more than 108,000.

Sources indicate that the letter is one of several moves by Huang’s allies. Investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker wrote to the board on Friday. On Sunday, the Financial Times reported that Huang had discussed a comeback with confidants. TNW covered both in its report on the return talks.

Industry observers note that the letter says no evidence has shown that the woman at the centre of the case was a spy. A separate report deals with what Huang told his own executives.

It has been revealed that reuters reported on 14 November that Huang misled several Nvidia leaders about his relationship with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang. They included general counsel Tim Teter and chief marketing officer Alison Wagonfeld. Reporters Max A. Cherney and Jeffrey Dastin cited two people familiar with the matter and internal messages from October that the agency reviewed.

In those messages, Huang described his dealings with Alice Huang as standard business with a customer, according to Reuters. She was a senior executive at Megaspeed, the Singapore manufacturer that bought Nvidia chips, and the two are not related. The company said on Sunday that she left in August 2025.

Reuters also reported that Huang discussed legal action against The New York Times over an October 2025 article about their public meetings. No suit was filed. A Times spokesperson told Reuters the paper received no legal demand.

Industry observers note that nvidia’s independent directors hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz on 10 November to run the board’s investigation. Nvidia told CNBC on Sunday that it was choosing a search firm for the chief executive role and had not formally engaged any candidates.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent spoke about Alice Huang on Fox News Channel’s Sunday Morning Futures. He noted whether she is a spy “doesn’t matter to me”. His concern, he said, was whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance with US export restrictions.

Wedbush analyst Dan Ives told CNBC he does not expect a return.

“We see no chance Jensen comes back to Nvidia as CEO,” Ives said.

In a recent development, colette Kress, the interim chief executive, presents Nvidia’s quarterly results on Tuesday. It is her first public appearance in charge, according to The Information. TNW found no public response from the board to the letter.

While awkward, creepy tech executives have become a recurring theme on Saturday Night Live, this week’s episode gave the cast a chance to show off all their impressions at once.

In a single sketch, we got James Austin Johnson as Peter Thiel, Ben Marshall as Sam Altman, Jane Wickline as Dario Amodei, Jeremy Culhane as Elon Musk, Andrew Dismukes as Mark Zuckerberg — and eventually, the recently departed Bowen Yang joined the fun as Jensen Huang.

Huang’s ouster from Nvidia (after admitting to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy) could have serious implications for the tech industry; it also provided a hook for some obvious jokes about rich nerds being easy marks for women (or men) who are out of their league.

In the sketch, a CIA agent played by host John Mulaney (hilarious as ever, if not entirely confident about how to pronounce “Palantir” or “Nvidia”) attempts to painstakingly explain why these execs should be suspicious when someone attractive suddenly seems interested in them romantically. For Altman and Thiel’s sake, he added, “I hope this is obvious: Even though you’re gay, you can still be tricked by a spy.”.

Johnson’s version of Thiel pushed back, insisting that tech tycoons deserve more respect, given all they’ve done for the country. “Name one time technology has let us down,” he said, giving Mulaney a chance to remind viewers about flights being halted all across the United States on Friday night.

“Okay, name one more time,” the fictional Thiel noted, leading to an obligatory mention of Microsoft Outlook going down on Thursday. When asked for a third example, Mulaney said, “No, I’m done naming times.”.

“Look, I get it,” he stated. “I can’t imagine how disorienting this has been for you, to go from being bug-eyed weirdos to being gods. I mean, never in the history of our species have people as pale and as strange as you a) survived, and b) been given all the world’s wealth and power.”.

#80. Tech Report: Razer’s Wild $1,000 Gaming Chair Has Six Motors, Built-In Speakers and RGB Lighting

Tech Report: Razer’s Wild $1,000 Gaming Chair Has Six Motors, Built-In Speakers and RGB Lighting

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1128 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that there are different levels of gaming immersion when it comes to haptics.
  • On the other side, you have Razer’s two fresh gaming chairs, the $1,000 Soma Pro and the $570 Soma Sense HD Haptics, which feature some serious motors to really shake your spine.
  • This isn’t an entirely new line for Razer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that there are different levels of gaming immersion when it comes to haptics. On one side, you have controller haptics, which provide a bit of stimulation in games. You might feel a nice little rumble from explosions or gunshots and maybe a bit of vibration to give you some feedback while driving off-road.

On the other side, you have Razer’s two fresh gaming chairs, the $1,000 Soma Pro and the $570 Soma Sense HD Haptics, which feature some serious motors to really shake your spine. Both incorporate Razer Sensa HD Haptics, which the company first debuted as part of Project Esther back in 2024. The chair also has THX Spatial Audio support and Razer Chroma RGB lighting built in.

This isn’t an entirely new line for Razer. The Soma series is one the tech giant has been working on for some years now. The Soma Chroma was the first wireless RGB gaming chair confirmed this summer for $499. Now Razer is rounding out its gaming chair lineup.

Recent findings suggest that “The Soma Pro is where the chair finally joins the game,” said Addie Tan, Razer’s global head of its lifestyle division in a press statement. “For years, gamers have upgraded everything they see and hear, while the seat they spend every session in stayed on the sidelines. With Soma Pro, the chair becomes part of the game — you feel it, hear it and see it.”.

It has been revealed that both chairs come with six haptic motor actuators built into each seat, unlike the $300 Razer Freyja, which was essentially a wired cushion you placed on top of your existing chair and plugged in. I actually owned the Freyja, and while it worked OK for some games, for a lot of others I tried it with, it just used a generic rumble without really customizing things. It was also very uncomfortable to sit on long-term. Plus, I didn’t like the feeling of being tethered to a cable and ended up getting rid of it. A built-in wireless option, like these latest chairs, seems like a much better solution to me.

It has been revealed that both fresh chairs deliver “multizone feedback” via Razer Sensa HD Haptics, and Razer says they should match the intensity, direction, and distance of in-game events. For example, an explosion off to the side will feel different from one that’s up close to you. So this isn’t just a generic rumble that applies to every situation; it’s customized based on the gameplay.

Razer lists more than 100 PC games that support integrated Sensa HD Haptics, including Battlefield 6, Borderlands 4, Marvel Rivals and S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2: Heart of Chornobyl. For everything else, the chairs use Audio-to-Haptics via Razer Synapse, converting audio into vibration, so the effect also works with games without native support, as well as with movies and music.

In a recent development, in theory, this should allow the feature to work on anything that supports controller vibration, but a Razer representative did not immediately respond to a request for clarification. On the Soma Pro, you can dial the overall intensity up or down in Synapse or adjust each of the six motor zones individually.

In a recent development, it’s worth noting that, unlike the Freyja, both chairs are wireless, though that doesn’t mean they’re completely untethered since Razer hasn’t managed to break the laws of energy yet. Each chair draws power over a single USB-C connection, from either a wall outlet or a compatible power bank, to preserve what Razer calls a wireless-aesthetic setup.

A power bank isn’t included in the box, so budget for one if you want the cable-free look. (You’ll also need a power adapter if you don’t have one handy, as the company doesn’t provide one.) That’s a downside because my LiberNovo Omni chair, which comes with adjustable lumbar support, a motorized spine, and even a massager setting, shipped with a rechargeable 2,200-mAh power bank.

Both Soma chairs carry a three-year warranty on mechanisms and moving parts and a two-year warranty on electronic parts.

Recent findings suggest that both Soma chairs share the same hardware, at least where you rest your backside. There’s a built-in lumbar arch intended to encourage a neutral sitting position, a dual-density cold-cured foam seat cushion with a softer top layer over a firmer core and a backrest that reclines up to 132 degrees. Both have a steel frame and are rated for people up to 331 pounds. Razer lists the Soma Pro for people 5 feet, 5 inches to 6 feet, 6 inches tall, and the Sensa model for people who are 5 feet, 3 inches to 6 feet, 6 inches.

For $1,000, the Soma Pro offers sound and light in addition to haptics. Built-in speakers deliver THX Spatial Audio directly from the chair. Yes, that’s right: You don’t need computer speakers — they’re right behind your head now. You can use them on their own or pair them with front speakers to widen the soundstage, with the chair effectively handling the rear of the setup. It is the same idea Razer has used with Razer Clio headrest speakers before, now integrated rather than clipped on.

In a recent development, the Pro is also the only model in the line with Razer Chroma RGB. The reactive lighting uses 16.8 million colors, responds to on-screen action in more than 300 integrated games and syncs with the rest of a Razer setup via Synapse. While I love a good light show, this isn’t really meant for the person seated in the chair. It seems designed for streamers and people watching you since it doesn’t look like you can really see the light show unless you take your eyes off the stream.

The Pro also gets the line’s most adjustable fit — 4D armrests, a magnetic head cushion and a frog tilt mechanism — on a powder-coated aluminum alloy wheelbase.

The controls are on a built-in panel that switches between Razer HyperSpeed Wireless (2.4 GHz) for PC and Bluetooth LE for mobile, with a companion Razer Furniture app on the Pro for adjusting haptics, audio and lighting from a phone. The controls are a nice alternative to using Razer’s annoyingly overlapping and often invasive Synapse and Chroma software.

Sources indicate that the $570 Soma Sensa HD Haptics chair keeps the same six-actuator haptic system and drops the speakers and the RGB. That makes it $71 more than the lighting-only Soma Chroma ($499), and $430 less than the Soma Pro ($1,000). If you already have a headset or speakers, which I’d assume you do as a gamer who’s considering a product like this, the Soma Sensa HD Haptics gets you most of the key features without the unnecessary extras.

#79. Tech Report: How long can a 1000 watt-hour power station run your devices?

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (663 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: How long can a 1000 watt-hour power station run your devices?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (663 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Determining the stamina of your portable power station is more complicated than you might expect.
  • It has been revealed that this is anecdotal, perhaps, but based on the number of ads I'm bombarded with, it feels like portable power stations have become a hot commodity in the last several years.
  • Sources indicate that A critical question to ask is how much power you actually need.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Determining the stamina of your portable power station is more complicated than you might expect.

It has been revealed that this is anecdotal, perhaps, but based on the number of ads I'm bombarded with, it feels like portable power stations have become a hot commodity in the last several years. And it makes sense — in a society increasingly dependent on phones and laptops, not to mention other electronics, even the best small power banks just won't cut it during a prolonged outage. And of course, these stations have always had uses outside the home, such as camping or job sites.

Sources indicate that A critical question to ask is how much power you actually need. More isn't always better, since a high-end station is not only expensive, but considerably larger and heavier. A multi-kilowatt station might cost as much or more than the devices it's powering and require help to lift if you've been neglecting the gym.

Let's take 1,000Wh (watt-hours) as a baseline. How long can you reasonably expect that to last when the power goes out at home or you're watching YouTube in the Adirondacks? The answer is surprisingly complicated. It depends on what you plug in, how it's actively operating, and how efficient your power station is at converting energy.

Recent findings suggest that while there are plenty of options out there from brands like Anker and EcoFlow, let's take the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 as an example. It's rated at 1,024Wh, and can deliver up to 1,500W of output. Simple math suggests that a 200W fridge, for example, could run for over five hours, or that a 65W laptop could last for well over 15 hours.

Industry observers note that in practice, however, even Jackery only promises four hours for that fridge and 11 hours for the laptop. So what gives? The answer is power conversion. When you plug into a station's AC outlet, that power has to be converted from DC, possibly wasting anywhere from 5 to 20 percent in the process. Total efficiency is impossible, and you might make things even less efficient if you plug in something like the wall adapter for your phone or tablet, which converts AC back to DC.

It's also worth noting that the rated consumption for devices can vary wildly in practice. A gaming laptop might consume a few dozen watts when it's browsing the web, but well over 200W when it's running full tilt. Even your phone is going to have ebbs and flows, based on what it's trying to do — it takes a lot more more juice to stream a TV show over 5G than it does to add those crackers to your calorie counter.

Sources indicate that for a start, if a station has built-in USB ports, plug your phones, tablets and other mobile devices into those whenever possible. You'll reduce the inefficiency created by plugging in adapters. Naturally, this also frees up AC outlets, allowing you to plug in other critical gear.

Recent findings suggest that pay attention to ambient temperatures, too. While something like the Jackery 1000 is rated for output at temperatures from 14 to 113F (-10 to 45C), the optimal range for its LiFePO4 (lithium iron phosphate) batteries is actually around 59 to 95F (15 to 35C). You'll get less power out a battery that's extremely cold or extremely hot, so simply keeping a station in the shade or properly ventilated could make a world of difference.

In the long term, consider the impact of charging cycles. There's a difference between battery capacity and battery life, and as with any rechargeable battery device, the usable capacity of your portable power station shrinks over time, based largely on how many full cycles (or their equivalent) you've gone through. It may be hard to put a dent in something with a kilowatt-level supply, but that should be a reason to avoid draining a power station unless you really need it.

Vulcan rocket failure destroys 40 Amazon Leo satellites in ULA’s first loss

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (775 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that united Launch Alliance is investigating why its Vulcan rocket failed on Sunday.
  • Vulcan lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida at 12:40pm ET (17:40 UTC).
  • Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle released from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that united Launch Alliance is investigating why its Vulcan rocket failed on Sunday. The loss took 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites with it. It was the first mission ULA has lost since Boeing and Lockheed Martin formed the company in 2006.

Vulcan lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida at 12:40pm ET (17:40 UTC). About 10 minutes later, ULA stated, the rocket suffered an anomaly and failed to deliver the satellites to orbit. The tech giant said in a post on X that it did not yet have specific data on what went wrong.

Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle released from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.

Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us something. Since the anomaly just occurred, we don’t have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today.

It has been revealed that ULA exists to provide assured access to space for our nation and for the customers who depend on us. That purpose is why we take on some of the hardest missions in spaceflight, and why we hold ourselves to the standard of mission success. Today, we did not meet that standard.

We will work closely with our customer and other appropriate organizations to find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action, and return to flight as rapidly as possible.

ULA is committed to full transparency with our customers, and they will have visibility into the investigation process, which utilizes rigorous methodology and corrective action.

We will provide further updates when new information becomes available.

ULA (@ulalaunch) November 15, 2026.

ULA added that engineers will find the cause and the fix, then return to flight quickly. Blue Origin makes Vulcan’s BE-4 main engines. It is working with ULA on the investigation, a person familiar with the matter told Reuters.

Industry observers note that early accounts differ on which part of the rocket failed. Several sources told Stephen Clark of Ars Technica that the problem lay in the booster stage. They said it was not in the Centaur V upper stage or the six solid boosters. According to Ars, the two BE-4 engines kept firing at least 30 seconds past their planned shutdown. The rocket’s telemetry animation then highlighted it starting to spin.

Reuters reported it was unclear whether the BE-4 engines played a role. The failure appeared to come after the upper stage, which carried the satellites, separated from the booster.

According to recent reports, the question matters beyond Vulcan. Blue Origin’s own Latest Glenn rocket uses a similar engine. A faulty BE-4 valve caused its launch pad explosion in May. Blue Origin has already delayed New Glenn’s return to January.

It has been revealed that sunday’s flight, LV-01, was the first of 38 Vulcan launches Amazon bought for Leo. Leo is its rival to SpaceX’s Starlink. Amazon had about 400 Leo satellites in orbit before Sunday. Its first-generation network needs more than 3,200. It noted last month it had built its 1,000th satellite, so hundreds are waiting for rockets.

“There is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01,” Amazon said.

Amazon called ULA a trusted partner and said it expects ULA to learn from the mission. Its next launch is an Ariane 6 flight with 36 satellites. It is set for 23 November at the earliest, according to GeekWire. Amazon also has 10 more missions booked on SpaceX’s Falcon 9, Ars reported.

Recent findings suggest that amazon already missed a July deadline to have half its network in service, and the FCC gave it more time while stripping some spectrum priority. It still has until July 2029 to deploy the full first generation.

The failure also reaches the US military. The Pentagon had not yet cleared Vulcan to resume national security launches, pending Sunday’s result, according to Reuters. Ars put Vulcan’s share of those missions at about half over the next few years. The rest go mostly to SpaceX, which has squeezed launch rivals and has stopped taking upcoming Falcon 9 bookings.

NASA, which picked a version of ULA’s Centaur upper stage for future flights of its Space Launch System, offered to help.

In a recent development, “Artemis, Moon Base, and the nation need ULA. We are in your corner and here to help,” NASA’s administrator wrote on X.

Starship flight 15 powers to orbit—setting up a possible catch on Saturday

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (736 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • STARBASE, Texas—Starship lifted off right on schedule Friday from South Texas, making its 15th test flight in more than three years.
  • Sources indicate that the largely successful launch took place in the early evening; as the massive rocket rose into the atmosphere, the Sun sank toward the western horizon.
  • The first stage ascended toward space flawlessly, releasing the upper stage above the Gulf of Mexico.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

STARBASE, Texas—Starship lifted off right on schedule Friday from South Texas, making its 15th test flight in more than three years.

Sources indicate that the largely successful launch took place in the early evening; as the massive rocket rose into the atmosphere, the Sun sank toward the western horizon. Conditions were ideal for the launch, with the atmospheric winds so calm the rocket’s white plume did not dissipate for many minutes. The weather in South Texas is not always comfortable; summers are long and hot. Friday evening was perfect at Starbase.

The first stage ascended toward space flawlessly, releasing the upper stage above the Gulf of Mexico. From there, the Starship upper stage ignited its Raptor engines and powered its way into a nominal orbit. This was the second time SpaceX has flown Starship into low-Earth orbit.

When it came time for the first stage to return to the ground, it dropped like a rock. However, due to an unspecified problem, the vehicle was commanded to divert into the Gulf rather than return to the Starbase facility to be caught by the launch tower. It created a fantastically powerful explosion, even for observers more than 10 miles away.

Sources indicate that the primary aim of Friday’s launch was the deployment of 26 Starlink V3 satellites from a narrow door at the base of the spacecraft. This occurred about 40 minutes into Starship’s flight, and all 26 satellites—which have solar panels that stretch 60 meters end to end when fully deployed—safely made it into orbit, where they will now use onboard propulsion to raise their altitude.

This means that Starship is now an operational, orbital rocket. It is the largest and most powerful machine humans have ever launched into space. The challenge for the organization now is to make Starship reusable and dramatically increase its flight rate.

In a recent development, in that sense, the first part of Friday’s mission was not a success. SpaceX had hoped to return the first-stage booster, refurbish it, and fly it again. The organization has previously landed and reflown Starship boosters but has yet to do so with the latest iteration of the vehicle, version 3.

In a recent development, however, SpaceX still has a chance to make history on Saturday with the potential return of the Starship upper stage. SpaceX has never attempted to catch the vehicle’s upper stage.

Doing so will require Starship to pass a series of tests in orbit and subsequently during its return to Earth to ensure it is fully healthy. This is critical because Starship will be passing over parts of Mexico and the United States before returning to Starbase, and SpaceX does not want to endanger people on the ground. Additionally, it does not want to risk damage to its launch towers.

In a recent development, if Starship passes these health checks, it would land at about 3:15 pm local time in Texas (21:15 UTC). If it does not, the manufacturer has earlier options to de-orbit the vehicle into an ocean.

In a recent development, successfully returning Starship’s upper stage would be historic, as well as significant for SpaceX’s efforts to reuse the massive rocket. It would also give the company valuable information about the vehicle’s performance during reentry.

In a recent development, one of the biggest hurdles left in Starship’s development is the vehicle’s heat shield, which must protect the upper stage during its return through Earth’s atmosphere. More than that, SpaceX aims to make Starship rapidly reusable, and to do this, Starship’s tiles must be light and resilient.

Industry observers note that spaceX has been experimenting with tiles since the beginning of the Starship program, trying to find the right combination of low mass, heat resistance, and durability so the tiles require minimal refurbishment between rolls out. For this flight, SpaceX noted it is applying learnings from the previous test flight in September, including additional retention mechanisms on tiles in areas deemed to be at the highest risk of falling off during ascent and addressing areas with a flow path for plasma to get behind the tiles.

Another problem on recent flights has been heat incursion into the small gaps between the edges of the tiles. According to SpaceX, this Starship has a large portion of the heat shield equipped with a curved tile design that has shown the ability to reduce heating in the gaps between tiles.

Samsung's upcoming Galaxy S27 Ultra could come with a major camera downgrade, as a newly leaked design render seems to suggest.

Samsung has been offering four rear cameras on its Galaxy S Ultra smartphones for quite some time now. The current Galaxy S26 Ultra features a 200MP primary camera, a 50MP ultrawide, and two dedicated telephoto lenses offering 3x and 5x optical zoom.

According to recent reports, however, we've already seen several reports suggesting Samsung could ditch one of these zoom cameras next year. And now, a new leak seems to further support those rumors.

Sources indicate that according to tipster Ice Universe on X, the Galaxy S27 Ultra will feature a redesigned camera setup with just three rear lenses. The tipster shared a latest design sketch of the Galaxy S27 Ultra and Galaxy S27 Pro, claiming that this is the final design and that he's "100% sure" about its accuracy.

100% sure this is the real design for the Galaxy S27 Pro and S27 Ultra https://t.co/hXF0g1QViNNovember 15, 2026.

In case you haven't been following the leaks, Samsung appears to be trying a fresh design with the Galaxy S27 Ultra and Galaxy S27 Pro, introducing a horizontal camera plateau similar to the iPhone Pro series. The new design reportedly features two large camera lenses on the left, alongside two smaller circles housing an additional sensor and the camera flash on the right.

This means the Galaxy S27 Ultra could lose its fourth rear camera, which is expected to be the dedicated 3x telephoto lens. A previous leak has already suggested that the phone will feature a 200MP primary camera, a 50MP ultrawide, and a 50MP telephoto lens with 5x optical zoom.

Of course, having fewer cameras doesn't necessarily mean the Galaxy S27 Ultra will deliver worse image quality than this year's model. However, if Samsung does remove the dedicated 3x telephoto lens, users will lose the flexibility of having a separate optical zoom camera at that focal length.

That said, the 200MP primary sensor already does a pretty good job with 2x sensor cropping, so the difference might not be as noticeable as it sounds.

In a recent development, there are also reports suggesting that the Galaxy S27 Pro could swap the 5x telephoto lens for a 3x telephoto camera instead. Of course, all of this is still up in the air, with Samsung a few months away from unveiling its next-generation flagships. So, plenty could change before the company officially reveals the Galaxy S27 series next year..

Latest Update: Is bad news for Jensen Huang also bad news for the AI industry?

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we didn’t see this coming.
  • On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Rebecca Bellan, Tim De Chant, and I discussed how Huang’s ouster went down and what it means for the larger AI economy.
  • It has been revealed that “Jensen is Nvidia, right?” she added.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we didn’t see this coming. Or at least, I didn’t — a week ago, when I wrote about Nvidia’s board opening an investigation into then-CEO Jensen Huang, I assumed his job was safe.

On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Rebecca Bellan, Tim De Chant, and I discussed how Huang’s ouster went down and what it means for the larger AI economy. While Tim noted he saw it coming (albeit not this swiftly), Rebecca said, “I didn’t think it was going to happen at all.”.

It has been revealed that “Jensen is Nvidia, right?” she added. “And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia.”.

In a recent development, similarly, I marveled at how quickly Huang’s support seemed to crumble, with more scandals seeming to emerge every day. (At the same time, there are many who’d still like to see him return.) And we also took a moment to wonder what will happen to Nvidia’s investments in the larger AI ecosystem.

Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity; you can listen to the whole episode here.

Tim De Chant: I figured this was coming. I didn’t think it would happen this rapidly. I thought there would be at least a few days.

Industry observers note that rebecca Bellan: I didn’t think it was going to happen at all. I mean, Jensen is Nvidia, right? And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia. And we’ve got nothing but the last few years of data to show us that billionaires can do whatever the hell they want. So it was surprising to me  — it almost restored my faith in humanity, that he resigned.

But someone stated to me, “If this were Elon, nothing would happen.” He would not be resigning. Nothing would be going down.

Anthony Ha: Which is interesting, because I would have mentioned, as of a week ago, or even just a few days ago, that Jensen is in the same category as Elon. I mean, no one is quite as special as Elon is, but it’s a big, incredibly successful manufacturer. Like you said — in a lot of ways, the entire AI economy is built on top of Nvidia.

Recent findings suggest that and for most people, Jensen Huang is Nvidia. He’s the biggest shareholder. He has family members who work at the manufacturer, and probably most importantly, there was no succession proposal in place. So this was not something that they were prepared for at all.

Rebecca: I think we should actually take a step back, because we just debuted into this conversation assuming — rightly so — that our listeners will know what the heck we’re talking about.

But for those who somehow don’t, Jensen resigned on Thursday, after it came out he was having an affair with a former executive at an Nvidia customer called Megaspeed, who’s alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence. And then there was another reported affair with an Nvidia executive.

So he’s resigned. Nvidia CFO Collette Kress is jumping in as the interim CEO. She’s a longtime board member. I think it’s always interesting when a CFO steps in to be a CEO. It just means we’re going to manage expenses right now, like that’s the key.

In a recent development, anthony: I think a big part of the message is: This is not necessarily someone you should expect to be in this role for the long term. No disrespect to her, but it feels like a caretaker appointment while they figure things out.

Industry observers note that just to get into that backstory a little bit more, what has been really remarkable to me has been this sense that a lot of what ultimately brought Huang down, [that] stuff was at least known in intelligence circles for a while. Apparently, this report that [raises] questions, concerns about his relationship with Alice Huang is something that was circulating a year ago, or close to a year ago.

Sources indicate that and then suddenly, everything really accelerated, Starting over the weekend, with Jensen Huang admitting to having an affair, the board saying it was investigating, but that it still had a lot of faith in him. And then this week, this other affair being reported on, and it just felt like there was all this bad news coming fairly swiftly.

But also, it wasn’t this thing that no one had known before. I guess a lot of the general public hadn’t known. So it’s this combined feeling of, “Wow, the ground kind of shifted so quickly under him,” even though the worst stuff, the possibility that somehow national security might have been threatened, is something that actually has been known by the government for nearly a year, if not more.

Rebecca: That’s exactly right. Trump was given some warnings about Huang’s affair with someone who has ties to Chinese intelligence, potentially, and it seemed like he didn’t really mind.

I think what’s notable here, though, is to note that Jensen Huang has been an advocate for loosening chip exports to China. And so this is where the crux of it is. Can anyone trust him as the CEO of this firm when he’s advocating for loosening chip exports to China? Which a lot of people believe is a national security glitch, because that means it will give Chinese AI companies access to our powerful chips, which will help them improve their AI, which could threaten America.

I mean, there’s two sides of this coin. And I think, honestly, that Jensen does not need a woman to tell him that  — he just wants to sell more chips, and to anybody and everybody, and whether or not that’s good for national security or not, I think is honestly secondary to him.

In a recent development, tim:  I completely agree. I think the big turning point seems to happen on November 9 — so that would have been earlier this week, Monday, when the Bloomberg report came out and suggested that Nvidia’s head attorney had some role in inquiring about the Department of Commerce’s investigation into Alice Huang.

According to recent reports, things seem to have accelerated in the last few days following that. And I don’t know what role exactly that report played in it, but it seems to be maybe there was a shift within government or within the board, a kind of a daunting realization of the extent to which this had spread just beyond Jensen and some affair.

Industry observers note that anthony: There’s also just the question of: What does this mean for Nvidia? What does this mean for the broader AI industry? And one of the reasons those two things are very tightly connected is not just Nvidia chips themselves, but also the fact that under Jensen Huang, the organization has invested very, very heavily in a number of AI startups.

In a recent development, people talk about the idea of an AI circular economy, and I think Nvidia has been one of the biggest players in that, in terms of both funding a lot of things, [but] also, obviously, providing the infrastructure for a lot of AI projects. So if Nvidia is going into this stage of lockdown, circle the wagons — even if it just means a small pullback, that could have really dramatic repercussions.

Rebecca: Yeah, that’s what I want to know: What happens to the Bank of Nvidia without Jensen? Is he the one leading this?

Industry observers note that just to throw some numbers at you, Nvidia apparently accounts for roughly 80% of the AI GPU market. It reported $99 billion in investments and another $25 billion in commitments, plus $36 billion dollars in cloud service commitments. A lot of those include investments into CoreWeave, Nebius, OpenAI, Anthropic, major data center projects. They’ve got their fingers in literally everybody’s pie.
