#69. Why your Wi-Fi slows down when more devices connect

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (731 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

Why your Wi-Fi slows down when more devices connect

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (731 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Your Wi-Fi router is like a busy train station, and once you get a sense of how things work, it's easier to keep the incoming and outgoing traffic humming.
  • According to recent reports, demands on home Wi-Fi have increased considerably over the past decade, never mind the launch of the first routers way back in the 1990s.
  • Recent findings suggest that that can create a real crunch on performance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your Wi-Fi router is like a busy train station, and once you get a sense of how things work, it's easier to keep the incoming and outgoing traffic humming.

According to recent reports, demands on home Wi-Fi have increased considerably over the past decade, never mind the launch of the first routers way back in the 1990s. It used to be that homes had a handful of connected devices at most, typically major-ticket items like PCs and game consoles. Today, there's a good chance your watch is online too, and that you've got a plethora of cool smart home gadgets ranging from lamps to smart speakers.

Recent findings suggest that that can create a real crunch on performance. But why is that, exactly? You probably know part of the answer, yet there may be more going on than you imagine. Your Wi-Fi router isn't just a series of tubes — a better analogy might be a central train station with complicated lines of incoming and outgoing traffic.

Industry observers note that once you have a sense of how things work, it's easier to keep this congestion under control. It's not just about minimizing the number of connected devices — controlling how and when gadgets connect can also have a substantial impact.

In a recent development, all Wi-Fi routers have an internal bandwidth cap, but there are some differences between types of home internet. Wi-Fi 6 and 6E routers top out at 9.6Gbps, whereas Wi-Fi 7 ups the ceiling to 46Gbps. Although you're unlikely to approach even the 9.6Gbps mark, which is well beyond the scope of most internet plans, we should emphasize that these limits represent total available bandwidth — going not just to and from the internet but locally between devices. If someone's transferring a few dozen gigabytes of video from their camera to their laptop, it could create momentary congestion if a bunch of other devices are also trying to run full-tilt.

Complicating matters is the issue of band congestion. Wi-Fi 6 provides 2.4 and 5GHz bands, while 6E and 7 add a 6GHz option. Each band is allocated only so many channels, so if a band fills up, the result is likely to be delays or a kick over to another band, assuming a device supports it and that your router isn't using separate band IDs. The 2.4GHz band is particularly easy to overwhelm, since there are only three non-overlapping channels, and many low-power accessories don't have 5 or 6GHz has a option.

In fact, all routers have an invisible limit on simultaneous connections, which is why you should upgrade immediately if you're still using Wi-Fi 5. That protocol may only be able to handle as few as 10 to 25 active devices, and it's going to boot older connections to make room for new ones once that limit is reached. I learned this the hard way when I started reviewing smart home gear in the 2010s.

Upgrading to Wi-Fi 7 may help, but be warned that it's not a magic bullet. It's still possible for a band to become overloaded. To truly take advantage of Wi-Fi 7's features — such as "preamble puncturing," which allows a channel coping with interference to be carved out for its remaining bandwidth — both your router and connecting devices need to support it. Chances are, most of the devices you own are still limited to Wi-Fi 6 or 6E.

According to recent reports, with or without Wi-Fi 7, it may help to steer as many devices as possible over to 5 or 6GHz if your router allows the creation of separate band logins. It's a win-win. While those bands have shorter range than 2.4GHz, they offer both less congestion and faster connection speeds for the devices that support them.

That's not an option on mesh routers, however, so you may need to resort to other tactics, such as using your router's app controls to pause unnecessary devices when a particular upload or download is crucial. In the long term, you should consider migrating as many smart home accessories as possible over to hub-based setups, particularly light bulbs. While standalone Wi-Fi bulbs are cheap and easy to set up, each one has to compete for available channels. Conversely, a hub can link dozens of products via protocols like Thread or Zigbee while only demanding a single Wi-Fi connection.

#64. Here's what actually happens if your laptop battery is completely drained

Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

Here's what actually happens if your laptop battery is completely drained

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (520 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A dead battery might do more damage than you think.
  • Sources indicate that if your laptop has ever run out of battery unexpectedly, you know what an inconvenience it can be — especially if you're out in the world without a charger.
  • In a recent development, granted, there's a lot of information on the internet about the best ways to take care of your battery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A dead battery might do more damage than you think.

Sources indicate that if your laptop has ever run out of battery unexpectedly, you know what an inconvenience it can be — especially if you're out in the world without a charger. One minute you're cranking away on some crucial spreadsheet for work, and the next, you're staring at your own face reflected in a black screen. Aside from the jump scare of the latter, there could actually be a bigger risk to letting your laptop battery completely drain.

In a recent development, granted, there's a lot of information on the internet about the best ways to take care of your battery. Some of it hinges on the type of battery and how you use it. No matter how you cut it, though, a total drain isn't ideal, even if it won't set off a disaster if it happens from time to time. Nevertheless, here's what happens when you fully drain your laptop battery.

Recent findings suggest that on the whole, lithium-ion batteries, like those you'd find in a laptop, are pretty low maintenance and have several perks, such as being able to charge fairly promptly. In a perfect world, you wouldn't get all the way down to 0%. HP explains that if you want to extend your laptop battery's life as long as possible, it's best to keep the charge somewhere between 20% and 80%. Others might recommend charging to 40% to 80%. Either way, this also takes a bite out of the myth that you should drain your battery before recharging it in the name of longevity.

Industry observers note that repeatedly letting your battery drop to low levels can cause wear to the battery. Staying within a safe range helps keep the lithium ions in a stable state. Battery degradation could affect charging capacity. It should also be noted that some systems, like Windows, will actually shut down or hibernate before your battery hits 0%.

In a recent development, if you find yourself flirting with that 0% a little more often than you'd like, it might be worth investigating whether there are reasons your battery is draining faster than normal. Most current laptops will last between 4 and 12 hours on a single charge, with some lasting even longer. This will vary depending on your laptop and what you're doing with it. For instance, gaming laptops won't last as long.

According to recent reports, otherwise, you could have apps running in the background that you don't need. Depending on the laptop you have, you might have some energy options to check out and tweak. Older software, higher temperatures or even plugged-in devices could all be contributing to your battery drain.

According to recent reports, in any case, it's worth keeping an eye on how much battery you have left if you're not connected to your charger. On the whole, draining your battery is mostly a self-inflicted annoyance. It's also not something you want to make a regular habit of doing, particularly if you're interested in making your battery last as long as possible.

Tech Report: SK Hynix’s $654m Trinity Fab lets small suppliers test on a real line

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (519 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, SK Hynix mentioned on Monday it will spend 1.4tn won ($1.05bn) over five years on South Korea’s smaller chip suppliers.
  • Sources indicate that the support covers four stages, from research and testing to mass production and sales, Reuters reported.
  • Trinity Fab sits inside Y1, the first fab at SK Hynix’s Yongin cluster south of Seoul.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, SK Hynix mentioned on Monday it will spend 1.4tn won ($1.05bn) over five years on South Korea’s smaller chip suppliers. The plan includes Trinity Fab, an 874.6bn won ($654m) test site. There, suppliers can try their materials and machines on 12-inch wafers under factory conditions.

Sources indicate that the support covers four stages, from research and testing to mass production and sales, Reuters reported. SK Hynix will pay up to half of a supplier’s early development costs in advance. It will also pay for the work if a project misses its targets.

Trinity Fab sits inside Y1, the first fab at SK Hynix’s Yongin cluster south of Seoul. SK Hynix plans to open it in May 2027. Its 3,305-square-metre cleanroom will hold about 50 tools, from lithography to etching and measurement, according to Bloomberg.

Three backers share the bill. SK Hynix puts in 443.2bn won and the central government 373.6bn won, with 57.7bn won from local governments, Reuters reported. An independent non-profit foundation will run the site, so suppliers can test without exposing their intellectual property.

SK Hynix calls it the world’s first open-access testbed for mass-production readiness. Suppliers can rent about a fifth of the space and install their own equipment there, MoneyToday reported after a site visit.

In a recent development, smaller Korean firms struggle to prove their products in a real factory. Cleanrooms are costly, and chipmaking links hundreds of processes that no small supplier can copy on its own.

Yang Ji-dong, who leads SK Hynix’s Yongin planning team, compared it to a race.

“In a marathon, the final 10-kilometer stretch is called the ‘wall of the marathon’ because it is the most difficult,” he told MoneyToday.

Sources indicate that expectations for the time saved differ. Equipment development and certification usually takes about five years. Lee Jae-ho, vice chairman of equipment maker TES, told MoneyToday that Trinity Fab could cut about one year. Seeking Alpha cited a bigger goal: 30% to 50% off validation times of two to three years.

The plan adds to a 2tn won financing programme for suppliers. SK Hynix launched it in October with four banks and the Korea Trade Insurance Corporation. SK Hynix is also doubling its interest-free payment support fund to 100bn won.

Sources indicate that korea’s two memory makers are riding an AI boom. SK Hynix posted record quarterly profit in October, and Samsung did too. Seoul has also put chips at the centre of its 2027 budget.

Rivals are closing in. China’s CXMT aims to make AI memory despite low yields. SK Hynix plans to invest 600tn won in four fabs at Yongin, and its suppliers will have to keep pace.

Lee Hyun-cheol, SK Hynix’s head of purchasing strategy, framed it as a national effort in remarks to MoneyToday.

“As global semiconductor hegemony competition intensifies, a ‘one team’ system where the upstream ecosystem and large corporations move as one is essential,” he said.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The investment comes as the nearly five-year-old, pre-revenue startup says it has secured design wins with U.S.
  • India has committed billions of dollars to build up a domestic semiconductor industry, with a hope to become an alternative manufacturing hub as U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bharat Semi, an Indian semiconductor startup, has raised $24 million in seed funding to develop AI-enabled image sensors, as it seeks to win customers in the United States and elsewhere.

The investment comes as the nearly five-year-old, pre-revenue startup says it has secured design wins with U.S. defense technology company General Atomics and India’s Kaynes Semicon. Its image sensors, however, remain under development, with the startup targeting its initial commercial production in 2027.

India has committed billions of dollars to build up a domestic semiconductor industry, with a hope to become an alternative manufacturing hub as U.S. companies look to diversify supply chains beyond China. The country, however, has yet to establish itself as a major chip manufacturing hub. Meanwhile, the AI boom is also giving Indian startups such as Bharat Semi an opportunity to develop specialized chips for global markets.

The New Delhi-based startup is developing programmable image sensors that combine image capture, processing, and AI capabilities on a single chip, reducing the need to send visual data to separate processors. The move could cut system costs by at least 70% compared with conventional setups that use a separate image sensor, image signal processor, and a system-on-chip, co-founder Vrinda Kapoor (pictured above, right) mentioned in an interview.

“Our aim here is to move from sensors to sense-making solutions,” Kapoor told TechCrunch.

Kapoor, a South Park Commons fellow who earlier worked in healthcare technology, co-founded Bharat Semi in late 2021 with Vinayak Dalmia (pictured above, left), the startup’s managing director, who previously worked at McKinsey and in private equity. Its chief technology officer, Boyd Fowler, previously held the same role at image-sensor maker OmniVision.

Bharat Semi is targeting smart homes, industrial automation, surveillance, and aerospace. Without disclosing specifics, Kapoor pointed to air conditioners that could detect when a room is empty and adjust automatically and drones that could process visual information — even with the absence of more expensive computing hardware elsewhere in the system.

The startup’s first-generation sensors are already in prototyping, while its second-generation sensors, which will incorporate more advanced AI capabilities, are expected to reach the prototype stage by mid-2027, Kapoor mentioned. Moreover, the startup plans to get those newer sensors into customers’ hands by the end of 2027.

Industry observers note that the all-equity seed round was led by Info Edge Group, South Park Commons, and Indus Bridge Ventures, with participation from Valour Capital, Micromax, Gaingels, and individual investors. Bharat Semi, Kapoor noted, looks to use the funding to expand its engineering team, complete product development, and bring its sensors to market.

Sources indicate that bharat Semi has about 75 employees across India and the U.S., including 10 to 12 in its American operations, which span engineering and business development in Santa Clara. The startup plans to increase its U.S. headcount to around 20 by mid-2027, Kapoor said. It has also begun hiring engineers in Europe.

“It’s a story of can we build a global technology firm out of India,” Kapoor mentioned.

In 2024, Bharat Semi confirmed plans for a semiconductor fabrication project in India involving a technology partnership with the U.S. Space Force. The initiative, Kapoor noted, remains in development and the startup is working to identify domestic partners that would build and operate the facility.

The project is separate from Bharat Semi’s image-sensor business, Kapoor added. The startup aims to remain fabless, outsourcing chip manufacturing while focusing on semiconductor design and software. The upcoming funding will not be used to finance the proposed fabrication facility.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • We’ve long suspected that our devices are listening to us, but what about when we invite them to do it?
  • Along with the general sensor, processor, and battery upgrades, the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 introduced Audio Intelligence, a new set of features that allows the watch to listen in on conversations.
  • Siri Recap generates summaries of what you’ve discussed throughout the day, while Live Rewind gives you a transcript of the last 15 seconds of audio in case you missed something.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We’ve long suspected that our devices are listening to us, but what about when we invite them to do it? That’s what testing Audio Intelligence has felt like on the Apple Watch. But despite how disturbing it may sound to have your smartwatch listening and taking notes of your entire day, the reality has been a lot more mundane.

Along with the general sensor, processor, and battery upgrades, the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 introduced Audio Intelligence, a new set of features that allows the watch to listen in on conversations.

Siri Recap generates summaries of what you’ve discussed throughout the day, while Live Rewind gives you a transcript of the last 15 seconds of audio in case you missed something.

It’s similar functionality as AI-powered recording pins like Plaud or Amazon’s Bee, but within the context of your smartwatch and without the additional cost or subscription.

It has been revealed that and it’s completely optional. You have to first opt-in to the features to activate them, then choose to turn the feature you want on whenever you want to start using it. Then you can leave it on all day, set it on a schedule or toggle it manually whenever you need it. If you’re like me and forget that it’s on, you get reminders that it’s still listening or to check your recaps.

The fact that you have so much control over whether you use it and how much helped ease the creepy factor for me, but there’s still everyone else to consider.

Beyond a barely audible chime when I double-click the Digital Crown to activate Live Rewind, there’s no way to alert others that the feature is in use and that whoever’s in earshot is inadvertently getting roped into my little experiment as well. Other wearables like smart glasses have an indicator light on the front to alert spectators when they’re recording video.

Recent findings suggest that apple has built-in privacy safeguards for the audio, how it’s processed and then deleted. I’ve broken all that down in a separate Audio Intelligence FAQ. This is about what it’s like to use it in the wild.

I’ve been testing Audio Intelligence in the WatchOS 27.3 (and iOS) public beta for two weeks. Because this isn’t the final version (Apple claims it will release publicly later this year), consider this a sneak preview.

Recent findings suggest that let’s get Live Rewind out of the way because there’s not a lot to say about it. Whether from a lack of muscle memory (or usefulness), I’ve had to go out of my way to remember the feature exists.

I figured it’d come in handy for those “come again?” moments during conversations, but the reality is that it’s just easier to ask someone to repeat what they mentioned than remember to double-press the Digital Crown at just the right moment. I can see it being more useful when you’re listening to a presentation or other event.

Fifteen seconds go by a lot faster than I expect and by the time I realize something might be worth revisiting, the person has moved on with the conversation. I either missed what I intended to get or just captured the silence after.

In a recent development, siri Recap has been more useful, though it’s still hit-or-miss. The feature gives you high-level summaries of what it heard — it doesn’t provide a transcript to review, and it doesn’t identify who said what. It shines brightest during dedicated meetings when there’s a single conversation to follow rather than a jumble of unrelated discussions.

One success story: I was moderating the chat for our iPhone Duo live folding test on YouTube while Matthew Murray, CNET’s lab director, answered viewer questions on the stream.

I thought I’d caught the gist of what he was saying, but the typing must’ve distracted me more than I realized because I was pleasantly surprised to learn some interesting facts that I’d missed in the Siri Recap, like “Opening a phone 20 times daily over 10 years equals 73,000 folds” or that the “machine runs approximately 22,560 cycles every 24 hours”.

But Siri’s batting average wasn’t always that good, which made it challenging to trust the notes. During a conversation with another mom about car-pool logistics, Siri Recap pulled out action items, like who I was picking up and at what time, which I appreciated, but the information wasn’t accurate. Not only had Siri gotten the names of the kids wrong, it also had me picking up the wrong kid. Clearly, the mental load of figuring out after-school logistics is challenging even for Siri.

Siri can’t handle the messy conversations (and TV shows).

Where things get interesting (and occasionally hilarious) is how Siri discerns what constitutes a conversation and how many topics belong in a single recap.

Siri is generally good at accurately labeling what conversations are about: “Parent-teacher conferences,” “Car-pool logistics,” “Folding phone durability testing.” But rather than keeping them separate, as it should, it sometimes conflates two or even three completely unrelated conversations into a single recap.

I encountered bullet points summarizing a serious conversation with a friend about a medical condition alongside notes about a chaotic (albeit funny) exploding apple cider incident with my kids. The two conversations happened within the same two-hour window, but they were by no means back-to-back.

It’s a good thing Siri Recap leaves out tone and volume cause that last bullet would’ve been in ALL CAPS.

What it did decide was worthy of a standalone recap was a discussion about wedding plans during an episode of Nobody Wants This on Netflix. To be fair, this would’ve absolutely warranted a recap if I’d been discussing my own wedding plans; however, the fact that the “conversation” happened at midnight should’ve tipped off Siri that this was a late-night binge session and not an actual conversation needing to be recapped.

Rather than coming away better informed about the notable conversations I’d had throughout the day, I came away feeling validated by the sheer chaos of it all. The constant whiplash of being pulled in a dozen different directions — bouncing between work, kids, gossip and the occasional sticky beverage crisis — was real and now immortalized (until the recap automatically expires if you don’t choose to save it).

In a recent development, for now, while novel, neither Siri Recap nor Live Rewind is reason enough to buy (or avoid) the Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4. They’re two of our top-rated smartwatches for their fitness, health and other smart features. Audio Intelligence is either an added bonus (it’s free) or something you can ignore altogether.

But if you do decide to venture into this brave new world of AI notetakers, my suggestion would be to use Siri Recap intentionally rather than leaving it running all day.

Turn it on before a work meeting, a doctor’s appointment or another conversation where you might want a few notes to jog your memory later. Just make sure everyone involved knows it’s enabled and is comfortable with it, and that you’re not relying on it for crucial information.

If the stakes are high, have a backup — whether that’s your own notes or a recording — lest you risk coming home with the wrong kid.

#59. Industry News: Winemakers are learning that conservation can be good for business

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1010 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Winemakers are learning that conservation can be good for business

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1010 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that more than 500 vineyards are scattered across the slopes and valleys of South Africa’s Western Cape, one of the world’s most biologically diverse landscapes.
  • It has been revealed that temperatures in the region have risen 1.5 to 2 times faster than the global average over the past five decades.
  • As climate variability places increasing pressure on grape production, many wine producers are building on sustainability measures that have long been part of vineyard management.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that more than 500 vineyards are scattered across the slopes and valleys of South Africa’s Western Cape, one of the world’s most biologically diverse landscapes. The region produces about 90 percent of South Africa’s wine, but winemakers there are increasingly struggling with drought, excessive heat and erratic rainfall.

It has been revealed that temperatures in the region have risen 1.5 to 2 times faster than the global average over the past five decades. And extreme storms have become more intense as climate variability increases. The late 2010s brought a significant challenge for winemakers, as three years of severe drought placed vineyards under intense stress and reduced grape production.

As climate variability places increasing pressure on grape production, many wine producers are building on sustainability measures that have long been part of vineyard management.

We are a team of geographers and sustainability scientists who study environmental change, environmental health, conservation, agriculture and land management. Our team wanted to better understand how farmers in South Africa’s wine-producing regions are responding as a range of environmental and economic pressures rise. We talked with growers, conservation practitioners and wine industry experts in the Western Cape and analyzed how 107 vineyards, about 20% of the total, were using sustainable land stewardship practices to adapt.

Sources indicate that in many agricultural landscapes, production and conservation goals are frequently viewed as competing priorities. But our research found that many vineyard operators in the Western Cape see long-term stewardship and conservation of soil and wildlife habitat as essential strategies for business success.

It has been revealed that the Western Cape is home to the Cape Floral Region, a global biodiversity hot spot. It includes fynbos, a unique biome containing thousands of endemic plant species, including types of proteas, ericas and restios that are found nowhere else on Earth.

Sustainability certification and conservation programs, such as World Wildlife Fund Conservation Champions, have helped encourage vineyards to protect biodiversity in the region. Many growers use these sustainability certifications to increase their wine’s marketability. But we found they have also embraced conservation for how it can benefit their vineyards. Rather than viewing conservation as land taken out of production, many stated they see it supporting the ecological processes essential to their business.

Sources indicate that the majority of South Africa’s vineyards today participate in the Integrated Production of Wine certification system, created by the South African wine industry and researchers in 1998 to reduce environmental harm. The system sets standards governing pesticide use, water management, wastewater treatment and environmental stewardship. It also uses independent auditing of participating farms and wineries to ensure those claiming certification meet the standards.

To manage the water supplies their vineyards depend on, growers described restoring native vegetation, including the removal of alien species, along waterways and reducing erosion to protect wetlands and rivers. Research reveals that healthy natural systems can improve water retention in the soil and contribute to the overall resilience of the landscape in the face of more extreme climate conditions.

To boost their soil’s health, some growers are planting cover crops, such as legumes, cereals like oats and rye, and brassicas such as radish and mustard, between vine rows. Growers broadly described using cover crops, compost, mulching and other practices to improve soil structure and increase organic matter in the soil. Cover crops require maintenance and can provide habitat for pests, but research shows that the right cover crops, when well maintained, can benefit vineyards by reducing erosion and increasing water retention and nutrients in the soil.

Sources indicate that several producers also described efforts to reduce their reliance on chemical pesticides, which is beneficial not only for the environment but also their businesses as chemical costs continue to rise. We heard about vineyards that monitor pest populations closely and respond in targeted ways rather than using pesticides broadly.

Sources indicate that some growers encourage beneficial insects and manage habitats that support natural pest control. The creation of habitats for natural pest predators can reduce the overall disease risk too. While chemical treatments remain part of many vineyard operations, growers reported increasing interest in other approaches that prevent disease and pest outbreaks, such as pruning, to reduce their total chemical use.

Sustainable practices like these are well established in South Africa’s wine industry, but our interviews suggest their use has been expanding in recent years. Rather than focusing solely on treating problems after they arise, these approaches emphasize prevention, monitoring and ecological balance.

The stewardship practices we observed in South Africa are investments in long-term business resilience for many growers.

Industry observers note that many of the wine producers we interviewed described facing rising costs and market uncertainty. Exports, labor and chemicals are all expensive. They emphasized that maintaining healthy soils, conserving water and reducing vulnerability to drought and disease are essential to keeping their vineyards productive.

Sources indicate that as concerns about drought, climate pressures and profitability rise, the area in vineyard production in South Africa has also decreased. Several growers described diversifying their business models and even switching crops to make their businesses more resilient to hotter, drier conditions.

Farmers around the world are confronting the realities of a changing climate. Our research highlights that effective solutions can come from recognizing the interconnectedness of nature and production.

The experience of South Africa’s winegrowers demonstrates that farms can be managed more sustainably when they’re seen as part of larger ecological systems.

Students Zoe Van der Walt, Jack Spining and Dryver Finch contributed to this article.

Recent findings suggest that hannah V. Herrero is Associate Professor of Geography & Sustainability and Director of Sustainability at University of Tennessee; Erin L. Bunting is Assistant Professor of Geography at Michigan State University; Jane Southworth is Professor of Geography at University of Florida; Jason K. Blackburn is Professor of Geography at University of Florida; and Stephanie Insalaco-Wyner is Assistant Professor of Geographic Information Sciences at Southwestern University.

#58. Industry News: What causes a sudden drop in phone battery percentage?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (692 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: What causes a sudden drop in phone battery percentage?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (692 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An aging battery or a recent software revision could be the reasons behind your phone's sudden battery drops.
  • Few things are more frustrating than noticing that your phone's battery is draining faster than usual.
  • At the same time, that doesn't mean your phone's battery is dying.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An aging battery or a recent software revision could be the reasons behind your phone's sudden battery drops.

Few things are more frustrating than noticing that your phone's battery is draining faster than usual. It gets to a point where it can no longer last a full day away from the charger. Under normal conditions, battery drain depends on what you're doing on your phone. Lighter uses like browsing the web and listening to music use less power, while taking lots of photos and playing games tend to drain your battery faster. But when your phone's battery suddenly drops without heavy use, something might be wrong.

At the same time, that doesn't mean your phone's battery is dying. Software can also cause your battery to drain faster, like when you install an iOS or Android update, or when an app is constantly running in the background. If you've been noticing that your phone's battery is draining faster, here's what you can try to fix it.

Recent findings suggest that your phone doesn't know exactly how much charge is left in the battery. In fact, it estimates that number based on the battery's voltage and current, and sometimes that estimate is far off from reality. Eventually, the software recalculates it, and that's when you see the battery percentage suddenly drop by a significant amount instead of gradually. This happens more often with batteries in poor condition. As lithium-ion batteries age chemically, they no longer retain their full charge capacity and may also fail when the phone needs a power boost to perform a demanding task, like opening the camera or using GPS. As a result, your phone may think the battery is much lower than it actually is.

Sources indicate that smartphones have mechanisms to prevent this from happening. On iPhones, Apple has implemented a system that detects when the battery fails to reduce performance in order to avoid these spikes in power consumption. Temperature also has a major impact, as most phones are rated to operate at temperatures between 0° and 35° C (32° to 95° F). Using your phone at temperatures above that range can significantly reduce battery life. When your phone gets too hot, the battery will most likely drain much faster. It's best to stop using it until it returns to a normal temperature. Don't put it in a refrigerator, though, as the introduction of cold air can create condensation within the warmer phone.

Also, it's perfectly normal to see your phone's battery drain a little faster for a few hours or even days after an update. Both iOS and Android run a series of optimizations to put all the files in their proper places, and this increases battery consumption. The good news is that this is temporary, and everything goes back to normal once the indexing process is complete. A buggy app or a process constantly running in the background, especially if it uses your location, will also drain your phone's battery swiftly.

Start by closing apps running in the background to see if your battery usage returns to normal. It's also worth taking a look at your privacy settings and limiting access to your location to only when you have an app open. This prevents your phone from constantly triggering the GPS. That alone should have a significant impact on reducing battery consumption. Also, check your phone's battery settings to see exactly which apps are draining your battery the most — both iOS and Android provide details on this.

Pixel 6 and later models have a Battery Diagnostics tool under Settings. On a Samsung Galaxy, open Settings, then Battery and tap View Details. For iPhone consumers, it's as simple as going to Settings and opening the Battery menu. These menus usually include details about your phone's battery health. Apple, for example, says that the latest iPhones are designed to retain 80 percent of their original battery capacity through up to 1,000 charge cycles. If your phone's battery health is below 80 percent, you should probably replace it with a latest one — which, at least, is much cheaper than buying a new phone.

ULA said an ‘anomaly’ led to its Vulcan vehicle failing to deliver its payload to orbit.

According to recent reports, united Launch Alliance (ULA) suffered what is reportedly its first mission failure in its 20-year history, failing to deliver 40 Amazon Leo satellites to orbit. Leo is Amazon’s competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink, but it has struggled to get off the ground so far, putting only a small portion of the necessary satellites to challenge Starlink into orbit. Today’s launch was supposed to be the first of 38 flights Amazon purchased from ULA.

In a statement posted on X, ULA said, “Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle released from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.”.

It has been revealed that the company said it was currently unclear what caused the failure, but pledged transparency as it continues its investigation. Amazon projected confidence in its launch partner despite the failure, posting on X that, “ There is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01. ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.”.

Apple is finally adding video podcasts to Apple TV in a move that trails after major rivals like YouTube and Spotify.

It has been revealed that first reported by The New York Times on Monday, the company is testing video podcasts on its streaming platform. This means if your favourite show has a filmed element (which most major podcasts currently do), you'll be able to watch it in the same spot you mainline Apple Originals like Silo and Ted Lasso.

It has been revealed that they're not quite available on Apple TV yet, as according to the news outlet, early access is only for testing with developers. However, the NYT reports that video podcasts will be available soon and free for all, even if you don't have an Apple TV subscription.

Despite leading the podcast charge in 2005 and dominating listener stats, Apple has left eyeballs on the table when it comes to video podcasts — and not just because they're celebrity magnets and dynamite for clipped viral social media moments. Notably, the manufacturer did add video to its Podcast app in February, with the NYT reporting a 20 percent audience growth for top shows.

Sources indicate that elsewhere, as of 2026, over 500 million users have streamed a video podcast on Spotify, an increase of 50 percent year over year, according to the manufacturer. Like YouTube, Spotify is aware of the impact videos can have on growing podcast audiences. During its May 2026 Investor Day, Spotify also noted, "These users engage more, use more devices, and spend more time across podcasts, music, and audiobooks.".

Industry observers note that adding a podcast section to Apple TV will inevitably increase viewership for these shows, which is great news for creators as much as Apple. However, not every podcast has a luxurious budget, celebrity hosts, and a polished studio, both of which are becoming increasingly crucial in the incessant battle for views.

10 things your iPhone's Notes app can do other than taking notes

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1868 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple Notes has a lot of tricks you might not have properly explored.
  • In a recent development, for most people, the Notes app is where grocery lists, stray thoughts and various codes go to live.
  • Recent findings suggest that A few of the features below rely on Apple Intelligence, requiring newer hardware to work as intended.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple Notes has a lot of tricks you might not have properly explored.

In a recent development, for most people, the Notes app is where grocery lists, stray thoughts and various codes go to live. If you've only used it for basic text, you've probably missed how Apple has added fresh features to the mix that can solve complex equations, draw graphs, transcribe audio and turn your doodles into images. iOS 27 brought even more, including smarter Siri integration and divider lines, so the app is more capable than ever.

Recent findings suggest that A few of the features below rely on Apple Intelligence, requiring newer hardware to work as intended. On the iPhone, that means the iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max and any iPhone 16 model or later. Those features are flagged along the way, along with anything that requires a specific version of iOS.

Industry observers note that the Notes app has a calculator hiding inside it, with the math happening while you're typing. Since iOS 18, when you type an equation and add an equals sign, Math Notes fills in the answer on the spot. It also works with variables, so if you write "dinner = $42" and change that value later, every result that uses it updates automatically. That makes it a surprisingly easy way to split the bill or plan a monthly budget.

Sources indicate that math Notes can do more than give you simple answers. After you type an equation that starts with "y =", tap the equals sign and choose Insert Graph to plot what you've typed right inside the note. If you change the variable, the graph changes automatically to match. It's a neat tool for students to check their homework without a dedicated graphing app.

If you don't have a physical scanner at home, there's no need to download a dedicated scanner app to replace it. Tapping the attachment button in any note demonstrates the Scan Documents option, where Notes will capture a page automatically, including cropping and straightening it for you. The scanner also offers a flash option and image filters if needed.

Recent findings suggest that in Auto mode, you don't even need to tap on the shutter button; the system captures the document once it detects the page's edges and you're holding your iPhone steady. You can scan multiple pages into a single document, which is useful for contracts, lease agreements or anything else that runs longer than a page.

Industry observers note that if the document needs a signature, open the scan, tap Markup, then go to Add > Signature. Use a saved signature or draw a latest one with your finger, then resize it and drag it into place. It's an easy way to sign and send a form without taking a printout of the pages. Scans are saved to the note as PDFs, which you can annotate.

According to recent reports, notes can double as a recorder: choose Record Audio in any note to record and transcribe everything your phone hears. The transcript is searchable, so you can jump into the relevant part of a long lecture instead of scrubbing through the entire session. On iPhone models with Apple Intelligence, Notes can summarize entire recorded lectures or meetings. Phone calls you record also land in Notes inside the Call Recordings folder with a transcript.

According to recent reports, the iPhone already has a dedicated recording app in Voice Memos, so it's worth knowing when to use which. Notes is the better pick when the recording is part of something bigger. For a class or a meeting, for example, you can type your own notes, add photos of the whiteboard and keep the recording all in the same note. Everything stays together, so you won't have to switch between multiple apps when you're going through your notes at home. Meanwhile, Voice Memos makes more sense when the audio itself matters most, like an interview you blueprint to edit or share.

If you need some help when drawing, sketch something rough with the Markup tools, then pick Image Wand from the same tool palette and circle your sketch. Add a few words describing the image you want, and Apple Intelligence will turn your doodle into a polished image.

Sources indicate that you also have the option to circle an empty spot in the note and create a newly introduced image based on the text around it. Afterward, fine-tune the image by adding or removing descriptive words. If your note is a packing list for a beach trip, for instance, it will generate a matching seaside illustration to sit at the top.

In iOS 27, Image Playground, which powers this feature in the Notes app, got a latest model that can make photorealistic images, not just stylized ones. Since iOS 27.2, most images you generate or edit carry a SynthID watermark, which the SynthID detection website uses to know something was made by AI.

According to recent reports, your notes don't have to be only for you; it's possible to share a specific note or an entire folder with your family, friends and coworkers, then everyone can make changes in real time. This is ideal for a household grocery list or a group plan for a trip. The person who creates the shared note remains in control of who can do what.

Just tap the Share button in the note you want to add people to, then choose whether each person can make changes or only view it. Type @ followed by someone's name and they'll get a notification pointing them to the note. If several people are editing the same note, the activity view and highlights show who changed what and when. And in iOS 27, the Shared folder now sits at the top of the folders list with a new icon, so multi-person notes are easier to spot.

According to recent reports, the Notes app can help with the actual writing you do. Select some text, tap the Apple Intelligence button in the toolbar and pick an option from the Writing Tools menu. This can proofread your text for spelling and grammar mistakes and rewrite it in a friendlier, more professional or more concise tone.

In a recent development, the suite is also useful for reshaping messy notes. It's able to create a summary of a long note or pull out its key points, which is handy after a meeting or before an exam. It will also turn a block of text into a bulleted list or even convert it into a table. If you've jotted down a few phone looks with their prices and data limits, for example, the Table option can organize them into neat rows and columns so they're easier to compare.

Recent findings suggest that writing Tools isn't limited to just the Notes app; it works almost anywhere you can type on the iPhone, including third-party apps. In iOS 27, Apple Intelligence also suggests ways to improve your writing.

In a recent development, long notes quickly become messy and hard to organize, but Notes has a few tools to keep them neat. With iOS 18 and newer, you have the option to collapse any heading to minimize sections you're not working on. This means the final version is a bit cleaner to view, while it's also easier to manage everything while writing.

Sources indicate that if that's not enough, you can also highlight text in different colors, curating them by sections, information or any other preference. To do so, select the text, tap the Aa format button and pick a color. Notes offers five color options to choose from: pink, purple, orange, mint and blue. iOS 27 also added divider lines, which gives another option to tidy up a mess. Place your cursor where you want a break, open the edit menu and choose Insert Divider Line. If someone views the note on iOS 26 or prior, the divider lines show up as three hyphens(—), so nothing breaks.

According to recent reports, iOS 27 also added section links to the mix, letting you link to a specific section of a note where tapping the link jumps straight there. That's particularly useful for a table of contents in a long note. Pasting Markdown now converts it to formatted text automatically, and a new Copy as Markdown option easily brings notes to other apps with the formatting intact.

According to recent reports, iOS 26 added a reed pen to the Markup tools, which is designed for a traditional calligraphy experience. Like the actual writing instrument, your strokes get thicker or thinner depending on the direction you draw in. It's a unique way to write, especially for special occasions like birthdays and invitations. You'll find the reed pen in the list of Markup tools; tapping it again after selecting it is how you pick a preset.

According to recent reports, there are five angle presets to choose from, with the one you pick deciding which stroke direction gives the thickest line. The angle is fixed no matter how you hold your finger, so your strokes stay consistent. Apart from the Notes app, the reed pen also works in Freeform, Journal and Preview — basically anywhere the Markup tools are available.

Recent findings suggest that the search bar in the Notes app is smarter than it looks and than how most people casually use it. Beyond your own typed notes, it can search handwriting, objects in images and text in scanned documents. Tap the search button, then type a word from a page or a photo. If you scanned a receipt months ago, searching for the store's name should bring it up. It's an easy way to find snippets from longer notes, especially when you're transcribing lectures or meetings.

This turns your Notes library into a practical place to store paperwork you might need in the future. Consider storing information like warranty cards, appliance manuals, prescriptions and receipts all in Notes, then you can find them by searching for a word on the page instead of scrolling through dozens of scans and navigating file names.

It has been revealed that siri and Notes finally work together properly in iOS 27. Siri can create notes with generated content, like information it pulled from the web, instead of only typing what you say. Ask it to put together a packing list for a trip and save it to a newly introduced note, and it will comply. This really comes in handy for smaller notes or basic reminders, as well as capturing ideas on the spot when you can't stop to type.

It can also add to an existing note or clean up a list before saving it. If you've got a messy, unformatted list, ask Siri to tidy it up and add it to the right note. Of course, the full power of this requires Siri AI, which launched in English first. iOS 27.2 added French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish. Older iPhone models can also create notes with Siri, but without the AI-generated content, which slightly limits the feature. But the basics are still there to jot down ideas.

#52. The EPA’s Chemical-Detecting Plane Isn’t Doing Its Job Anymore

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2436 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

The EPA’s Chemical-Detecting Plane Isn’t Doing Its Job Anymore

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2436 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When an ammonia leak outside a hotel in Weatherford, Oklahoma, injured 74 people last November, the federal government's chemical-detection plane stayed on the ground.
  • When a fire tore through a Valero refinery in Port Arthur, Texas, in March, the plane sat idle.
  • And when massive blasts killed two workers at an industrial recycling plant in Toledo, Ohio, in August, it stayed put, despite a fire surrounding tanks of flammable solvents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When an ammonia leak outside a hotel in Weatherford, Oklahoma, injured 74 people last November, the federal government's chemical-detection plane stayed on the ground.

When a fire tore through a Valero refinery in Port Arthur, Texas, in March, the plane sat idle.

And when massive blasts killed two workers at an industrial recycling plant in Toledo, Ohio, in August, it stayed put, despite a fire surrounding tanks of flammable solvents.

“Ten years ago, it would have gone to all of them,” indicates Mark Thomas, a former EPA official who for years managed the airborne detection effort.

Industry observers note that the program, known as ASPECT, was designed to respond around the clock to emergencies involving toxic chemicals, oil spills, and radiation. The plane’s sensors could identify chemicals in the air within minutes, giving emergency responders crucial information about the dangers nearby communities face.

For more than two decades, the plane has flown over many of the country’s worst disasters, from Newly introduced Orleans after Hurricane Katrina to the deadly West Fertilizer explosion in Texas to the Deepwater Horizon oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico.

Sources indicate that but since early 2021, the single-engine Cessna has responded to just seven emergencies. And former ASPECT scientists say two of those missions—the 2023 train derailment that sent toxic clouds over East Palestine, Ohio, and the 2025 fire at Smitty’s Supply in Louisiana—were badly mismanaged.

In a recent development, at Smitty’s, the EPA declared the air safe, but a former ASPECT scientist later found toxic chemicals the agency had missed. And the agency’s inspector general is now auditing the response to the East Palestine derailment, including the data behind its public assurances about air quality.

In a recent development, in June, the EPA inspector general found a more fundamental problem: The plane could no longer identify chemicals within minutes, as designed. Instead, the data had to be analyzed by hand, a process that takes about a week. That’s far too long to help anyone on the ground who’s deciding whether to evacuate.

The EPA noted the plane's chemical sensors are wearing out and expects replacements to be working by mid-2027.

But five people who helped build and run the program told Floodlight that the EPA is fixing the wrong problem. The old sensors still work, they say. What the agency lost, in their view, is the initiative and expertise that made the program a powerful tool when disaster struck. Replacing the old sensors, they warn, could leave the EPA even less capable of detecting hazardous chemicals in an emergency.

Sources indicate that “I fear that the public is at risk,” indicates Robert Kroutil, a longtime ASPECT scientist who helped develop the program and later became a whistleblower. “It’s such an crucial program, and they've allowed it to waste away to nothing.”.

The EPA did not respond to Floodlight’s requests for an interview or questions about ASPECT’s decline, its handling of emergencies, the replacement of its sensors, and allegations of mismanagement by former program scientists and managers.

The country’s need for a chemical-sensing plane grew from the smoldering, toxic debris in Manhattan on September 11, 2001, when the EPA’s monitoring trucks were stranded on the wrong side of the Hudson River, unable to cross after bridges and tunnels into the city closed.

Kroutil was a program manager for the Department of Defense at the time, leading a research team that had developed the technology that would become ASPECT, short for Airborne Spectral Photometric Environmental Collection Technology.

The military transferred the program to the EPA for use in detecting hazardous chemicals during civilian emergencies.

It became a critical tool for emergency responders over the next 20 years.

For 72 hours after Hurricane Katrina struck, it was the only emergency response aircraft flying over Latest Orleans, where it helped locate a missing 55-gallon drum of potentially lethal chloroacetic acid.

During the Deepwater Horizon disaster, it became a key tool for tracking oil slicks in the Gulf of Mexico.

And when a fire engulfed 15 massive tanks at a chemical storage terminal east of Houston in 2019, the ASPECT plane helped emergency responders track the plume, which contained the carcinogen benzene.

It has been revealed that richard Lawhorn, an assistant chief with Harris County’s hazardous materials response team in Texas, claims the plane could detect chemicals at elevations beyond the reach of ground crews and survey a much wider area in a short time. Unlike ground monitors, the plane can scan a swath of air three-quarters of a mile wide, capturing a far broader picture of potential hazards.

“They’re monitoring the products we can’t reach,” he says.

Recent findings suggest that the program’s success lay in its intellectual rigor: Kroutil and the program’s radiological lead held PhDs, as did Mark Thomas, the former EPA official. The team wrote the code, designed the mounts that held gear, and analyzed the raw data themselves.

“We were very, very hands-on and intimately familiar with every part of that aircraft,” notes Thomas, who later went to work for a company that develops chemical-sensing technology.

The decline began with the departures of key ASPECT personnel during President Donald Trump’s first administration.

As part of an agency reorganization, the EPA told the program’s staff in 2019 that they had to relocate to Texas, where the plane was based, or face termination, documents show.

Industry observers note that the mandate was unnecessary, according to Thomas, because the program had been designed for remote operation. Rather than leave his elderly parents in Kansas, he retired. Then, ASPECT’s radiological lead left the division, and the engineer who helped build and manage the plane’s sensors accepted a demotion to stay in Kansas.

According to Kroutil and two of his former colleagues, the EPA then failed to fill those vacancies with scientists who had any experience with airborne chemical detection.

“They lost the institutional knowledge of the program, and quite frankly, lost the momentum of the program,” Thomas states.

During its first two decades, the plane flew almost 80 emergency missions—an average of roughly four a year. In the past five years, however, it has flown an average of just one a year.

In October, hundreds were evacuated—and more than 50 were treated at hospitals—when a 5,500-gallon industrial tank in Toledo, Ohio, leaked glycidyl methacrylate, a chemical used in making plastics that is a probable carcinogen suspected of causing genetic defects. It was one of at least 80 chemical emergencies this year that the plane did not respond to.

The decline comes as accidental chemical releases are becoming more common. The US Chemical Safety Board tracked 133 last year, up from 83 in 2021.

The Trump administration, meanwhile, has proposed rolling back federal safeguards designed to prevent chemical disasters, including requirements for some plants to undergo independent safety audits and provide hazard information to nearby communities.

Former ASPECT program managers say they used to actively track chemical emergencies and urge EPA on-scene coordinators—who manage environmental emergencies—to deploy the plane. After they left, that proactive approach vanished: The plane stayed in a Texas hangar until coordinators requested it, they say.

According to recent reports, scott Smith, an independent environmental tester who’s often called on by local communities to investigate chemical contamination after industrial accidents, indicates ASPECT could help him target his soil and water testing by mapping the path of chemical plumes. Deployed regularly, he says, the plane could save lives. Instead, “it's being shut down and not used.”.

On February 3, 2023, a Norfolk Southern freight train carrying the carcinogen vinyl chloride and other hazardous chemicals derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, near the Pennsylvania border.

As fires from the derailment smoldered, emergency responders feared an explosion—and made the controversial decision to vent and burn five railcars containing vinyl chloride, sending a towering plume over the town.

According to recent reports, ASPECT missed the vent-and-burn operation, and its services weren’t requested until more than two days after the initial disaster. Even then, it was used sparingly. Despite the derailment being one of the nation’s worst chemical disasters in years, Kroutil claims, the plane collected just eight minutes of chemical data when it finally flew over East Palestine on February 7—a fraction of what it typically gathered during an emergency.

Had the plane been deployed earlier—or flown over the site en route to Pittsburgh, the nearest major airport—its thermal detection equipment might have helped determine that the tank cars were not in danger of exploding, Kroutil later remarked in an affidavit.

The National Transportation Safety Board concluded that the vent-and-burn operation had been unnecessary. It found no evidence of the dangerous chemical reaction that Norfolk Southern and its contractors stated threatened an explosion. Temperature readings revealed the railcars were cooling.

An EPA inspector general investigation later found a series of errors in the East Palestine response: The agency had poorly documented its procedures and failed to adequately inform emergency responders of the plane’s capabilities. The on-scene coordinator, who didn’t request the plane until two days after the derailment, wrongly believed that ground-level monitoring would provide better data.

Recent findings suggest that frustrated by how EPA officials were running the program, Kroutil retired. Two of his colleagues also left, further draining the program’s pool of experience and expertise.

On August 22, 2025, a massive explosion ripped through Smitty’s Supply, a facility that blended and packaged oil and other engine lubricants in Roseland, Louisiana.

Less than 4 miles away, Ronnie Polezcek and his family heard something hitting their roof that afternoon. At first, they thought it was raindrops.

But when they walked outside, Polezcek says, “It was just like it was raining oil.”.

The dark residue covered the family’s 23-acre farm. Polezcek states he had to burn his hay, move his cows temporarily to Mississippi, and replace a metal roof that could not be scrubbed clean. Two of his cows miscarried soon afterward, he says, and a veterinarian found arsenic in one of them. Polezcek filed a lawsuit against Smitty’s in September 2025 that has been consolidated into an ongoing class-action case.

The Smitty’s fire burned for nearly two weeks, sending a huge plume of smoke into the air. Local authorities ordered a 1-mile evacuation around the plant, and the EPA dispatched ASPECT—the plane’s first emergency deployment in 19 months.

Industry observers note that the agency didn’t publicly post findings from the ASPECT flights until August 31, nine days after the fire began. Those reports show the air around Smitty’s contained ozone and three other pollutants but at levels far below those considered harmful to human health.

A later analysis of the raw flight data, though, told a very different story.

Working with the Government Accountability Project, a nonprofit that advocates for whistleblowers, Kroutil obtained data from ASPECT’s third flight over the disaster area. He says it took him weeks to analyze it, doing by hand what the plane’s software was designed to do in minutes.

Recent findings suggest that kroutil identified high concentrations of the neurotoxicant toluene and the carcinogens trichloroethylene and naphthalene, among other toxic chemicals. He concluded that the levels of toluene were so high, they could have put nearby communities at risk.

Many of the findings also matched what Smith, the independent environmental tester, detected in soil and water after the fire.

The EPA later acknowledged a similar problem, according to records that the Government Accountability Project obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request.

According to recent reports, in a May 2026 email, an EPA manager said some target chemicals might have been present in data from the third flight but weren't flagged at the time the data was collected. The manager suggested that deterioration of the aging sensors might have contributed to the failure.

Polezcek believes officials should have evacuated a larger area.

“I really think it was a pitiful job,” he notes. “They just kept saying, ‘There’s nothing to worry about, you’re good to go.’”.

In June, the EPA inspector general confirmed that Kroutil’s warnings were justified: The plane could no longer provide chemical-monitoring data within five minutes.

Industry observers note that instead, scientists had to conduct manual analysis that would take about a week. The EPA also failed to tell on-scene coordinators that the program isn’t working as designed.

In a recent development, EPA officials blamed the delays on old sensors. The agency bypassed competitive bidding to award a Canadian tech giant, Telops, a $1.7 million contract for replacement sensors designed for several applications, including gas detection and mineral mapping. Integrating the new sensors won’t be complete until “early to mid 2027,” according to the EPA.

In contract documents, the EPA cited peer-reviewed studies showing the Telops sensors had been field-tested and proven. But much of the research on the new equipment has focused on tracking methane leaks, not the wide range of toxic chemicals released during complex industrial emergencies.

Five people formerly involved with ASPECT have raised concerns that the latest sensors will be less capable than the old ones at detecting hazardous chemicals during industrial emergencies.

Exosens, the parent organization of Telops, told Floodlight that its system and the old one use “different measurement architectures.”.

Sources indicate that the latest sensors, it says, can identify hundreds of chemicals and distinguish chemical plumes from surrounding objects. The original infrared sensors, built by the Canadian firm Bomem, were rebuilt multiple times and equipped with new software.

Chris Manning, an infrared spectrometer expert with no ties to Telops, the EPA, or the firm where Thomas now works, says the latest Telops sensors could complement ASPECT’s older sensors but would be a poor replacement. They are slower, less sensitive, and less suited to moving targets, he says.

“To say, ‘We're just going to replace these other two instruments’ … I mean, that’s ludicrous,” he indicates.

In a recent development, the old sensors had problems, too. Their artificial intelligence software had not been retrained after an electrical malfunction several years ago, Kroutil and Thomas say. In early 2023, contract scientists with the program presented the EPA with a plan to retrain the software, emails show. But the EPA never took the required steps, according to Kroutil and Rick Turville, a former ASPECT manager who left the program in 2025.

According to recent reports, kroutil and his former colleagues say they have no confidence that the newly introduced sensors will fix the problem. They expect the program to deteriorate further.

In the affidavit submitted to the Government Accountability Project, Kroutil offers a dim prognosis: “Unless major changes are made at EPA and with the ASPECT program, it is not going to get any better and EPA will be flying blind.”.

Apple launches latest app to study how people use AI for health

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (582 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Big AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic have made their bets on offering chatbots that can answer health-related queries with specialized features.
  • The iPhone maker is partnering with healthcare-focused AI organization OpenEvidence to launch a new study app.
  • According to recent reports, the fresh app will allow users to ask health-related questions, as they do with ChatGPT or Claude, with answers grounded in clinical data, from sources including The New England Journal of Medicine, Journal of the American Medical Association, and Nature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Big AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic have made their bets on offering chatbots that can answer health-related queries with specialized features. Apple is debuting a new study to understand how people use AI for health. But it isn’t quite following other AI startups just yet; it wants to study how clinically grounded answers can help people.

The iPhone maker is partnering with healthcare-focused AI organization OpenEvidence to launch a new study app. Apple is inviting customers in the U.S. over 21, using iPhone 15 or later, and running iOS 26 or later, with Apple Intelligence enabled. The company is aiming to run this study with up to 200,000 participants for more than 12 months.

According to recent reports, the fresh app will allow users to ask health-related questions, as they do with ChatGPT or Claude, with answers grounded in clinical data, from sources including The New England Journal of Medicine, Journal of the American Medical Association, and Nature. Apple said that the app will try to give simplified answers to everyday medical questions. Users can rate those answers and provide feedback about the responses; they’ll also be asked to participate in monthly surveys.

According to recent reports, participants can share data from HealthKit such as resting heart rate, activity, sleep, or lab results to get more personalized and pointed suggestions from the app. The manufacturer stated the app can also help prepare participants better for a doctor’s visit, and it will guide owners to specific providers for answers related to concerning medical issues.

Apple specified that the data will be anonymized before sending it to a secure third-party cloud provider, and it won’t be used to train any kind of AI models. The company stated that OpenEvidence deletes the query and response data after 24 hours.

Sources indicate that “At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life,” Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, remarked in a statement, adding, “Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey.”.

It has been revealed that the app is available to download starting today for U.S. customers. It’s not clear if Apple wants to release AI-powered answering to its Health app or Siri yet. The potential is huge — earlier this year, OpenAI said users were asking over 300 million health-related queries each week.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dario Amodei, chief executive of Anthropic, at Fortune Brainstorm Tech in Park City, Utah, in July 2023.
  • In a recent development, orders for Anthropic’s IPO have reached close to seven times the shares on offer, people familiar with the matter told Bloomberg on Sunday.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dario Amodei, chief executive of Anthropic, at Fortune Brainstorm Tech in Park City, Utah, in July 2023.

In a recent development, orders for Anthropic’s IPO have reached close to seven times the shares on offer, people familiar with the matter told Bloomberg on Sunday. Demand is much hotter than it was for SpaceX at the same stage, one of them noted. The only comparable deal, that person said, was Snowflake’s 2020 listing, whose shares jumped 112% on their first day.

In a recent development, goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, which lead the deal, expect to close the order book on Tuesday, Bailey Lipschultz and Carmen Reinicke reported. That is the day Nvidia reports its first results without Jensen Huang. The Anthropic IPO is set to price on Wednesday. The shares should start trading on the Nasdaq under ANT on Thursday.

Anthropic and some of its backers are raising up to $90.4bn, counting a $26bn private placement. That would beat SpaceX’s $75bn base deal and make it the biggest listing ever. The manufacturer set its IPO terms on 10 November, at $70 to $78 a share and a $1.4tn valuation.

Orders were about twice the shares available by the end of the roadshow’s first day, 10 November, according to Reuters. By Thursday demand had hit six times the offer, Milana Vinn, Echo Wang and Krystal Hu reported. Bloomberg had reported a similar figure a day earlier, alongside the founders’ share sale.

Recent findings suggest that not every investor is welcome. Banks have turned away orders from institutions in mainland China and Hong Kong, Bloomberg reported on 13 November. US defence-trade rules known as ITAR are part of the reason, some of its sources said. Some are trying other routes, including a trust in the British Virgin Islands and swap arrangements, the people said.

Investors on the roadshow asked whether Anthropic can keep its lead as Google and others catch up, Reuters reported. They also asked whether Claude can win beyond coding. One investor said the manufacturer had not given detailed answers to some questions. Another said one group meeting had no dial-in line for questions, which breaks with normal practice.

Industry observers note that the valuation rests on forecasts. Banks put Anthropic’s 2028 revenue at about $270bn to $280bn, two people told Reuters. One investor who passed on the deal uses a 2028 figure about 30% lower. Goldman Sachs, which has forecast $685bn in revenue by 2030, does not expect positive annual free cash flow until then, according to Bloomberg.

Dario Amodei took some of those questions in public on 13 November, at a livestreamed JPMorgan event with Jamie Dimon. He stated buying computing power a year or two ahead was his hardest call, Business Insider reported.

“Compute is the deepest business dilemma that the tech giant faces,” Amodei said.

According to recent reports, he remarked Anthropic buys relatively little compute in advance. If demand runs high, its cash lets it buy more on the spot market. Its commitments top $900bn, with about $71bn due by September 2027, Bloomberg reported.

Recent findings suggest that howard Marks, co-founder of Oaktree Capital, doubts any AI leader can stay ahead for long. He made the case in a memo last week.

“If companies can forge ahead that fast in the world of AI, can they likewise be supplanted by others, or at least challenged?” he wrote.

In a recent development, anthropic’s public-benefit structure leaves it wide room to define what counts as benefit, governance experts told the Associated Press. Its Long-Term Benefit Trust elects a majority of the board, but the founders keep 50.1% of the general vote. A protest group, Stop Funding Billionaires, has demonstrated outside Anthropic’s offices in Fresh York and San Francisco, Business Insider reported.

Industry observers note that nvidia has agreed to buy about $10bn of the private placement. Huang resigned as chief executive on 12 November, five days before the order book closes.
